messages.body_plain:
"Error in function stan::prob::bernoulli_logit_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): Logit transformed probability parameter[0]  is 1.#QNAN:0, but must not be nan!Rejecting proposed initial value with zero density."

A common reason to have a NaN is that you've forgotten to fill in a parameter somewhere.

In this case, I'm guessing your problem is just a little typo in line 47, which uses c2 instead of c3.  I hope changing lines 46-48 to the following will fix it.

  for (i in 1:c3) {
    alpha3[c3_idx[i]] <- 0;
  }

> >   }
> >
> >
> >   ...

> >
> > and the data you'd pass to it would be generated in R as,

> >

> > beta2_const_n <- 4

> >

> >
> >
> >
> > but I presented it in a more general form that would scale to larger numbers of groups and allowing the model to be reused with different numbers of groups.  In general, I try to preprocess the data as much as possible outside of Stan, so that the model does as little data manipulation as is necessary.
> >
> >
> >
> > Similar ideas are discussed in the section on Missing Data in the Stan manual.  When you are dropping the coefficient for some groups, it is equivalent to constraining it to 0.

messages.subject: Model Consultation on change point model in RStan
messages.subject_clean: Model Consultation on change point model in RStan
messages.body_plain:
Has anybody fitted a change point model in Stan, please?

We are interested to fit a change point (broken stick) model in RStan to model longitudinal continuous outcomes measured about three to ten times (at baseline and follow-ups) for each of about hundreds of subjects (i.e. patients in a clinical trial); (So this is different from a time series on a single outcome for a single unit of observation, say a NYSE stock.). The timing of the outcome observations is different for each individual (the patients come in for appointments at different, irregularly), as are the slopes before and after the change point, the intercept and the actual change point itself.

The model:

y[i,k] = beta[pre, i] * (t[i, k] – tau[i]) * I(t[i, k] < tau[i]) + beta[intercept, i]+ beta[post, i] * (t[i,k] – tau[i]) * I(t[i,k] > tau[i]) + epsilon[i,j]

where the error term epsilon [i,k] ~MVN (0, Sigma), iid;

y[i,j,t] is the continuous outcome of the ith subject at the kth observation at time t[i,k]; beta[pre,i] is the random slope for each subject before,  beta[post,i] is the random slope for each subject after the subject specific change point tau. We think a reasonable prior for beta may be ~MVN, iid, but the slopes and intercept are certainly not iid.

 I( t[i,k] > tau[i]) is the indicator function used to define a linear spline: (t[i, k] – tau[i]) * I(t[i, k] < tau[i]) = t[i,k] - tau[k]  iff t[i,k] < tau[i] ; 0 otherwise;

tau [i] is the random change point (to be estimated for each subject i); tau [i] is the time of the ‘kink’ in the spline measured before say a diagnosis of dementia.;

See for example attached: Hall CB, Ying J, Kuo L, Sliwinski M, Buschke H, Katz M, Lipton RB. Estimation of bivariate measurements having different change points, with application to cognitive ageing. Stat Med. 2001 Dec 30;20(24):3695-714. PubMed PMID: 11782027.

We are interested to learn from similar models other users may have fitted or know about or to share related functions, now possible in Rstan.

Thank you.

Michael Andreae

There is a recent discussion about a change point model, although that one seemed simpler than the one you propose: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/stan-users/QlgX00f6JG8. Nevertheless, it might provide some inspiration.

In short, you will probably have to specify a mixture model, marginalizing over the different possible values of the changing point in time for each individual.

Luc

messages.subject: Re: Stan 2.3 released (RStan, PyStan, CmdStan)
messages.subject_clean: Stan 2.3 released (RStan, PyStan, CmdStan)
messages.body_plain:
The new manual says,

"The CmdStan documentation used to be part of this document, but is now its own standalone document. The CmdStan home page, with links to download and installation instructions and the manual is code and manual is http://mc-stan.org/cmdstan.html "
But going to that URL, there is no CmdStan manual. Downloading CmdStan, the only manual found is the Modeling Language Manual. The README.txt file says that

"Stan's user's guide and reference manual, including installation
instructions and a quick start guide, are in:

  $STAN/doc/stan-reference.pdf"

But that is just the modeling language manual, and it contains nothing specific to CmdStan (like all the info it used to have on command-line parameters, how to build Stan, what tools you should have installed, etc.)

So it appears that this release is lacking any documentation for CmdStan.

On Thursday, June 26, 2014 10:50:46 AM UTC-6, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> We're happy to announce RStan, PyStan and CmdStan 2.3.
> Instructions on how to install at:
>
>    http://mc-stan.org/
>
> Release notes below.
>
> As always, let us know if you're having problems or have comments
> or suggestions.
>
> - Stan Development Team
>
>
> v.2.3.0 (18 June 2014)
> ======================================================================
>
> We had a record number of user-submitted patches this go around.
> Thanks to everyone!
>
> New Features
> ------------
> * user-defined function definitions added to Stan language
> * cholesky_corr data type for Cholesky factors of correlation matrices
> * a^b syntax for pow(a,b)  (thanks to Mitzi Morris)
> * reshaping functions: to_matrix(), to_vector(), to_row_vector(),
>   to_array_1d(), to_array_2d()
> * matrix operations: quad_form_sym() (x' *Sigma * x), QR decompositions
>   qr_Q(), qr_R()
> * densities: Gaussian processes multi_gp_log(), multi_gp(),
>   and alternative negative binomial parameterization neg_binomial_2()
> * random number generator: multi_normal_cholesky_rng()
> * sorting: sort_indices_*() for returning indexes in sorted order by
>   value
> * added JSON parser to C++ (not exposed through interfaces yet; thanks
>   to Mitzi Morris)
> * many fixes to I/O for data and inits to check consistency and
>   report errors
> * removed some uses of std::cout where they don't belong
> * updated parser for C++11 compatibility (thanks to Rob Goedman)
>
> New Developer
> --------------
> * added Marco Inacio as core developer
>
> Optimizations
> -------------
> * turned off Eigen asserts
> * efficiency improvements to posterior analysis print
>
> Documentation
> -------------
> * Clarified licensing policy for individual code contributions
> * Huge numbers of fixes to the documentation, including many
>   user-contributed patches (thanks!), fixes to parallelization in
>   CmdStan, Windows install instructions, boundaries for Dirichlet and
>   Beta, removed suggestion to use floor and ceiling as indices,
>   vectorized many models, clarified that && doesn't short circuit,
>   clarified von Mises normalization, updated censoring doc (thanks
>   to Alexey Stukalov), negative binomial doc enhanced, new references,
>   new discussion of hierarchical models referencing Betancourt and
>   Girolami paper,
> * Avraham Aadler was particularly useful in pointing out and fixing
>   documentation errors
>
> Bug Fixes
> ------------
> * fixed bug in lkj density
> * fixed bug in Jacobian for corr_matrix data type
> * fix cholesky_cov_matrix test code to allow use as parameter
> * fixed poisson_rng, neg_binomial_rng
> * allow binary operations (e.g., < and >) within range constraints
> * support MS Visual Studio 2008
> * fixed memory leaks in categorical sampling statement, categorical_log
>   function, and softmax functions
> * removed many compiler warnings
> * numerous bug fixes to arithmetic test code conditions and messages,
>   including calls from
> * fixed model crashes when no parameter specified
> * fixed template name conflicts for some compiler bugs (thanks Kevin
>   S. Van Horn)
>
> Code Reorganizations & Updates
> ------------------------------
> * CmdStan is now in its own repository on GitHub: stan-dev/cmdstan
> * consolidate and simplify error handling across modules
> * pulled functionality from CmdStan command class and PyStan and RStan
>   into Stan C++
> * generalized some interfaces to allow std::vector as well as Eigen
>   for compatibility
> * generalize some I/O CSV writer capabilities
> * optimization output text cleaned up
> * integer overflow during I/O now raises informative error messages
> * const correctness for chains (thanks Kevin S. Van Horn)
>
>
>

We don't have a solution for label switching, I'm afraid.
There's a discussion in the manual, but all the possible solutions
we've come up with or seen from others are flawed.

I don't know about the rotational indeterminancy.  Is there
a mathematical constraint on the params that solve it?

Also, using group-level predictors doesn't solve the basic
indeterminacy problem.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: change point models?
messages.subject_clean: change point models?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all.  I generally don’t like change point models because it’s my impression that real life does not usually have sudden changes—and when sudden changes exist, we usually know when they happen.

But, setting those qualms aside, the model seems well-enough specified.  I see the potential HMC problem, though, as there is a discontinuous derivative.  One way to handle this would be to allow the change to be continuous, which in some way is an application of the folk theorem in that I expect actual changes really are continuous.

Beyond this, we (Stan-dev, that is) might want to think more generally about how to patch models that have bits of discontinuity so they work ok in HMC.  Maybe we can map to some latent continuous model?

A

> Has anybody fitted a change point model in Stan, please?
>
> We are interested to fit a change point (broken stick) model in RStan to model longitudinal continuous outcomes measured about three to ten times (at baseline and follow-ups) for each of about hundreds of subjects (i.e. patients in a clinical trial); (So this is different from a time series on a single outcome for a single unit of observation, say a NYSE stock.). The timing of the outcome observations is different for each individual (the patients come in for appointments at different, irregularly), as are the slopes before and after the change point, the intercept and the actual change point itself.
>
> The model:
>
> y[i,k] = beta[pre, i] * (t[i, k] – tau[i]) * I(t[i, k] < tau[i]) + beta[intercept, i]+ beta[post, i] * (t[i,k] – tau[i]) * I(t[i,k] > tau[i]) + epsilon[i,j]
>
> where the error term epsilon [i,k] ~MVN (0, Sigma), iid;
>
> y[i,j,t] is the continuous outcome of the ith subject at the kth observation at time t[i,k]; beta[pre,i] is the random slope for each subject before,  beta[post,i] is the random slope for each subject after the subject specific change point tau. We think a reasonable prior for beta may be ~MVN, iid, but the slopes and intercept are certainly not iid.
>
> I( t[i,k] > tau[i]) is the indicator function used to define a linear spline: (t[i, k] – tau[i]) * I(t[i, k] < tau[i]) = t[i,k] - tau[k]  iff t[i,k] < tau[i] ; 0 otherwise;
>
> tau [i] is the random change point (to be estimated for each subject i); tau [i] is the time of the ‘kink’ in the spline measured before say a diagnosis of dementia.;
>
> See for example attached: Hall CB, Ying J, Kuo L, Sliwinski M, Buschke H, Katz M, Lipton RB. Estimation of bivariate measurements having different change points, with application to cognitive ageing. Stat Med. 2001 Dec 30;20(24):3695-714. PubMed PMID: 11782027.
>
> We are interested to learn from similar models other users may have fitted or know about or to share related functions, now possible in Rstan.
>
> Thank you.
>
> Michael Andreae

messages.body_plain:
My mixed model is a little bit special.
It has a term beta1*log[S(i)-X(i)], where X(i) comes form the observed data but S(i) is the parameters. Only if S(i)>X(i), the model works.
Otherwise if I still have to write an expression, I can give an extremely large constant.
i.e., my model is
y=beta0 + beta1*log[S(i)-X(i)] if S(i)>X(i), otherwise y=200

Note that f(y|parameters) can be written out ( i.e., the likelihood of y is known).

I explored the Stan manual 2.3.0, and found these ways:

1. In Chapter 21.5, Page 195, it gives us the conditional statements,  if (condition1)  statement1.... else statement2.
    Each condition must be a real or integer value.
> I'm wondering if I put the "if else" condition in the model part, will the Stan model work.
> Or if it is possible to use the "While" statement.

2. Since the likelihood is able to be written down, I'm also thinking to use the Log Probability Increment Statement, increment_log_prob.
    I found an example in the Manual Page 66, Section 9.2, it specifies
> increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(log(0.3)+ normal_log(y,-1,2),
> log(0.7)+ normal_log(y,3,1));

    Also in the FAQ https://groups.google.com/forum/#!msg/stan-users/4gv3fNCqSNk/VonPUkdcZuUJ
    To utilize the Kumaraswamy distribution, it uses log-likelihood:

// log-likelihood
  lp__ <- lp__ + N * (log(a) + log(b)) + (a - 1) * sum_log_x;
  for (i in 1:N) {
    summands[i] <- (b - 1) * log1m(pow(x[i],a)); // log1m(y) := log(1 - y)
  }
  lp__ <- lp__ + sum(summands); // faster than doing inside loop
(I believe in Stan version 2.3, it is replaced by statement increment_log_prob)

can I fit the above model in the same way?

I'll be really grateful if anybody can come up with some ideas.

Dora

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Anyone using stan for Bayesian Network models?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Anyone using stan for Bayesian Network models?
messages.body_plain:
Stan can do posterior inference based on MCMC sampling for
any model expressible in BUGS, as long as:

 * all parameters are continuous, and

 * all the distributions used are in the Stan library
   (or coded by the user in the Stan modeling language).

So we can't program the Asia model (which is from the BUGS examples)
because of the discrete nodes (well, technically we could probably code
it up in our Turing-equivalent generated quantities block,
but it wouldn't be pretty, wouldn't sample efficiently,
and I wouldn't recommend it).

But Stan doesn't do anything with graphs per se.  It's just
that you can use BUGS-style models to define log densities, which
is what Stan deals with.  In particular, we don't do any reasoning
over the graphical structure of models.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] The condition of my mixed model contains an unknown parameter
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] The condition of my mixed model contains an unknown parameter
messages.body_plain:
Stan doesn't give you an easy way to encode the constraint

  S[i] > X[i]

when S is a parameter vector and X a vector computed from data.

The simplest way to program it is to use a parameterization:

  vector<lower=0>[N] S_minus_X;

with your model term now implemented as

   beta1 * log(S_minus_X[i]);

so that S_minus_X[i] is the amount which S[i] is above
X[i].  Then you can define S as a transformed parameter:

transformed parameters {
  vector[N] S;

  for (i in 1:N)

    S[i] <- S_minus_X[i] + X[i];
}

But if you don't need to use S anywhere in the model, you're better of
defining it as a generated quantity.

Because it's only a linear increment with data, there's no Jacobian
adjustment needed.

You may want to use

  multiply_log(a,b) = a * log(b)

where

  multiply_log(beta1, S_minus_X[i])  = beta1 * log(S_minus_X[i]);

Some more comments below.

- Bob

This won't sample well --- you really want the support of
a parameter to match its constraints.  Hence the parameterization
above.

> increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(log(0.3)+ normal_log(y,-1,2),

messages.subject: modeling normal measurement noise for counts in stan
messages.subject_clean: modeling normal measurement noise for counts in stan
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Does anybody have experience with modeling measurement noise for count data in stan.  Assuming that true count data from observation to observation are distributed according to poisson (perhaps with the addition of overdispersion parameter as in Gelman & Hill) measuring instrument adds some normal additive/multiplicative/log normal noise.  It could be expressed as:
true_counts[i]~poisson(lambda[i])
observed_counts[i]~normal(true_counts[i],sigma)

Problem with this is that Stan doesn't allow integer parameters true_counts.  observed_counts are real since the instrument returns real values (current).

I appreciate any comments on this.

Thanks,
Linas

messages.subject: Re: modeling normal measurement noise for counts in stan
messages.subject_clean: modeling normal measurement noise for counts in stan
messages.body_plain:
Hi Linas,

To clarify: you say that the observed_counts data are reals, rather than integers. Does this mean that the data are counts per some unit (volume, time, etc)? Similarly, does it perhaps mean that your instrument is actually counting something but returns an expected count as a result of some regression it is performing internally (e.g. as in qPCR)? Either way, I would start with a log-normal distribution for the observed_counts (which might actually be rates). It would be great of course if your instrument would actually return the data that it's basing its "result" on in the first place. That way, you could incorporate all that information in your Stan model.

What do you need the true_counts for? Is it ok to just produce them in the generated quantities block or do you need them somewhere else in your model? In the latter case, it sounds like you need to marginalize over all possible outcomes of true_counts, which doesn't sound pretty.

Best,

Luc

messages.body_plain:
Hi Luc,

Observed counts are particle counts in liquid per volume.  I think the idea is to pass the light and measure the current.  Then based on the current reading and instrument calibration (assuming that particles are spherical) infer particle counts.  I always thought that count data is best represented by poisson (with extension to overdispersion) and not log normal.  In fact poisson with overdesispersion works very well (Bayesian p-value is close to 0.5, Pearson residuals look random, histogram of mean and standard deviation is replicated - actual mean and sd are in the middle of replicated mean and sd histograms - basically I did lot of model checking suggested by Gelman).  However, when I start predictions I see large uncertainty. Therefore I thought about improving the model by adding additional layer for instrument.

Technically true counts are not needed, I just wanted to separate count variability between samples and measurement error.
Thank you,
Linas

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: modeling normal measurement noise for counts in stan
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: modeling normal measurement noise for counts in stan
messages.body_plain:
Hi Linas,

Thanks for the clarification. Based on what you are saying, I would argue that your data are not counts but concentrations (i.e. rates), and therefore Poisson, negative binomial or whatever other discrete distribution you can think of are not formally appropriate. In my experience, concentrations/rates are often treated as following a log-normal distribution, with sigma representing your tool's measurement error on the log-scale. If you think there is overdispersion, I suggest you fit a log-T-distribution or a hierarchical model, depending on the setup of your experiment. The large uncertainty you are getting in your estimates probably comes from your Poisson distribution (sigma^2 = mu). BTW, as you may know, the measurement error of lab instruments in general is usually not constant, but relatively higher (beyond log-normal) for very low (and sometimes high) values of observations. Also, an important cause of so-called "overdispersion" or "zero-inflation" is actually that most instruments have a minimum detection threshold. You can take account of this by modeling observations under the detection limit ("zeroes") as right-censored observations (using the CDF given expectation, measurement error, and the detection limit (assuming you know this)).

Best,

Luc

On Thursday, July 3, 2014 5:27:10 PM UTC-4, Katherine Grace Jonas wrote:
> When using this method to sample in parallel, does each chain use the same initial values?  If the initial values are set in running this single iteration, and that iteration is passed to the parallel operation, would each chain would follow from the same set of initial values?  What if, in the example above, iter=0?

Regardless of whether you run the chains in parallel or serially, (R)Stan does not "continue" a previous run, even if you pass a stanfit object to the fit argument of stan(). In other words, each chain starts fresh currently. [I think we are working on having the ability to continue a previous run, but it is not much of a priority].

By default, (R)Stan randomly draws initial values. Even if you specify a seed (which you should probably do), as long as you specify the chain_id (which you should definitely do), then the state of the pseudo-random number generator will be different for each chain because it is advanced by a function of the chain_id.

If you wanted to specify initial values for each chain (rarely is this necessary), then you could do something like

initial_values <- list(something, different, for, each, chain)
posterior <- sflist2stanfit(mclapply(1:5, mc.cores = 5, FUN = function(i) {
  stan(fit = eight_schools, seed = 12345, chain_id = i, chains = 1, inits = initial_values[[i]])
}))

Ben

messages.body_plain: I think the issue here is appropriately quantifying the uncertainty in predictions rather than "reducing" it. If there is a lot of uncertainty due to measurement error from your instrument, this should be propagated into predictions (assuming that by predicting you mean that you are trying to predict new data points). You could use posterior predictive checks (or better, cross-validation, if possible) to see how well the model actually predicts the data. messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] typo in ARM model
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] typo in ARM model
messages.body_plain:
If I am not mistaken, for a d-dimensional model, if we specify a normal(0,1) prior on  each on the ability parameters (factors), we would still need d*(d-1)/2 additional constraints on the discrimination parameters. So for a two dimensional model, we would need to impose one restriction on the discrimination(loading) matrix. But these restrictions won't take care of reflective invariance and label switching. In Bayesian Factor Analysis, the positive lower triangular identification scheme is usually used to to mitigate rotational invariance, sign flips, and label switching. Has anyone fit a model in stan using the positive lower triangular identification scheme?

On Wednesday, July 2, 2014 10:15:53 AM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> We don't have a solution for label switching, I'm afraid.
> There's a discussion in the manual, but all the possible solutions
> we've come up with or seen from others are flawed.
>
> I don't know about the rotational indeterminancy.  Is there
> a mathematical constraint on the params that solve it?
>
> Also, using group-level predictors doesn't solve the basic
> indeterminacy problem.
>
> - Bob
>
> On Jun 28, 2014, at 7:27 PM, Rick Farouni <rfar...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> >
> > For ideal point models, Gelman and Hill discuss an approach to deal with reflection invariance using group level regression predictors. Simon Jackman has an example ("legislators") on his website that implements the approach in Winbugs. http://jackman.stanford.edu/mcmc/index.php. I would be very interested to see how to code a similar model in STAN but for a two-dimensional case. In two dimensions, two more indeterminacy arise if I am not mistaken: label switching and rotational indeterminacy.
> >
> > On Saturday, June 28, 2014 1:02:49 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > It's a reparameterization.  You have an
> > additive non-identifiability, which you can fix
> > by fixing one of the coefficients.  And you have
> > a multiplicative non-identifiability that can get
> > fixed by fixing one of the scales, say the student
> > abilities, to normal(0,1).  And then there's a sign
> > non-identifiability, which you can fix by constraining
> > the discrimination (g) to b positive.  (Unless it's
> > an item-response model, then I'm not sure what to do
> > about the sign --- Andrew and Jennifer discuss in their
> > book.)
> >
> > - Bob
> >
> > On Jun 28, 2014, at 5:25 PM, Peter Li <li.pe...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > > I'm confused how you would fix this. If you look at how it all gets computed in p[i] for example, g(a-b) leaves you with just (a_raw - b_raw)*g_raw so why even bother shifting and scaling? And what's the point of d? Or is this all some kind of reparameterization trick?
> > >
> > >
> > > On Sat, Jun 28, 2014 at 7:50 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> > > OK, I see what's going on.  This is NOT a good way to code
> > > these models.  This model relies on Andrew's trick for BUGS of
> > > specifying an ill-defined posterior to sample from, then
> > > attempting to pull it all back into something with reasonable
> > > n_eff and Rhat through standardization.  Here's the offending
> > > code in our example:
> > >
> > > > transformed parameters {
> > > >  vector[J] a;
> > > >  vector[K] b;
> > > >  vector[K] g;
> > > >  vector[N] p;
> > > >  real scale;
> > > >  real shift;
> > > >
> > > >  shift <- mean(a);
> > > >  scale <- sd(a);
> > >
> > > >  a <- (a_raw - shift) / scale;
> > > >  b <- (b_raw - shift) / scale;
> > > >  g <- g_raw * scale;
> > > >
> > > >  for (n in 1:N)
> > > >    p[n]<-g[kk[n]]*(a[jj[n]] - b[kk[n]]);
> > >
> > >
> > > The problem here is that the raw values are not identified.
> > >
> > > The problem is that the posterior for the parameters is improper.
> > > And what you see is that Stan's HMC is effcient enough to race all over
> > > the posterior and at least realize it's undefined.
> > >
> > > There's a chapter on problematic posteriors that goes through
> > > an example of the effects of such non-identified models.  (Look at the
> > > plot of the long ridge, which is what happens for this kind of example.)
> > >
> > > This model needs to be recoded so that it's properly identified.
> > >
> > > We're working on rewriting all the ARM models, which are a pretty direct translation
> > > of what's in Gelman and Hill, and thus not guaranteed to work.
> > >
> > > This looks like a good place to start!
> > >
> > > For models that don't have data we can release, we can simulate
> > > data according to the model.  I want to bring up the question of how
> > > to simulate predictors for regressions --- it seems like for proper testing
> > > we shouldn't make them all independent.
> > >
> > > - Bob
> > >
> > >
> > > On Jun 27, 2014, at 12:28 AM, Rick Farouni <rfar...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > > Hi,
> > > >
> > > > So I manged to fit the model but  I always see to get a very low number of effective samples for the scaled variance and location parameters.Is that a reason to be concerned here? I have attached the model and here is a part of  the output.

messages.body_plain:
This thread's drifted from typos in ARM models, right?

But the answer is that I don' tknow if anyone's done that,
but I'd be interested in seeing how it works --- these problems
with identification are really important and I'd like to include
some more realistic examples in the manual.

Is there a relatively simple reference to these models I could
start with?  Or if someone sends me a working Stan model, I can
include that (with attribution, of course).

- Bob

On Jul 4, 2014, at 5:05 PM, Rick Farouni <rfar...@gmail.com> wrote:

>
> If I am not mistaken, for a d-dimensional model, if we specify a normal(0,1) prior on  each on the ability parameters (factors), we would still need d*(d-1)/2 additional constraints on the discrimination parameters. So for a two dimensional model, we would need to impose one restriction on the discrimination(loading) matrix. But these restrictions won't take care of reflective invariance and label switching. In Bayesian Factor Analysis, the positive lower triangular identification scheme is usually used to to mitigate rotational invariance, sign flips, and label switching. Has anyone fit a model in stan using the positive lower triangular identification scheme?
>
>
> On Wednesday, July 2, 2014 10:15:53 AM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> We don't have a solution for label switching, I'm afraid.
> There's a discussion in the manual, but all the possible solutions
> we've come up with or seen from others are flawed.
>
> I don't know about the rotational indeterminancy.  Is there
> a mathematical constraint on the params that solve it?
>
> Also, using group-level predictors doesn't solve the basic
> indeterminacy problem.
>
> - Bob

>
> >
> > For ideal point models, Gelman and Hill discuss an approach to deal with reflection invariance using group level regression predictors. Simon Jackman has an example ("legislators") on his website that implements the approach in Winbugs. http://jackman.stanford.edu/mcmc/index.php. I would be very interested to see how to code a similar model in STAN but for a two-dimensional case. In two dimensions, two more indeterminacy arise if I am not mistaken: label switching and rotational indeterminacy.
> >

> The stanfit object has both the samples and the

> doesn't provide a good way to continue with the same PRNG
> state.

> We do plan to enhance the C++ interface to allow proper
> restarting (though we still haven't decided what to do about
> restarting the PRNG).

> not get to it very soon.
>

>
> > So the fit argument is taking the compiled model, but not the samples generated from it.  That makes sense.  Thank you Ben.
> >
> > On Thursday, July 3, 2014 5:14:06 PM UTC-5, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> > On Thursday, July 3, 2014 5:27:10 PM UTC-4, Katherine Grace Jonas wrote:
> > When using this method to sample in parallel, does each chain use the same initial values?  If the initial values are set in running this single iteration, and that iteration is passed to the parallel operation, would each chain would follow from the same set of initial values?  What if, in the example above, iter=0?
> >
> > Regardless of whether you run the chains in parallel or serially, (R)Stan does not "continue" a previous run, even if you pass a stanfit object to the fit argument of stan(). In other words, each chain starts fresh currently. [I think we are working on having the ability to continue a previous run, but it is not much of a priority].
> >
> > By default, (R)Stan randomly draws initial values. Even if you specify a seed (which you should probably do), as long as you specify the chain_id (which you should definitely do), then the state of the pseudo-random number generator will be different for each chain because it is advanced by a function of the chain_id.
> >
> > If you wanted to specify initial values for each chain (rarely is this necessary), then you could do something like
> >
> > initial_values <- list(something, different, for, each, chain)
> > posterior <- sflist2stanfit(mclapply(1:5, mc.cores = 5, FUN = function(i) {
> >   stan(fit = eight_schools, seed = 12345, chain_id = i, chains = 1, inits = initial_values[[i]])
> > }))
> >

messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob,

For a factor model y=Lf +e, where f~ N(0,Sigma) , I think there are three important cases to consider:

1. The positive lower triangular (PLT) identification scheme mentioned here http://apps.olin.wustl.edu/faculty/zhou/GZ-RFS96.pdf , where Sigma=I (identity matrix) and the the diagonal entries of L are polarity constrained.
2.The modified PLT where the factors,f, are still orthogonal but the elements of diagonal of Sigma Aguilar, O. & West, M.(2000) Bayesian dynamic factor models and portfolio allocation.
3.. Sigma is a correlation matrix, but now instead of requiring D(D-1)/2 constraints on L, we need D(D-1) to ensure local uniqueness under rotation and the polarity constraint to ensure global rotational uniqueness.This paper lists the conditions http://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11336-012-9259-3

But as this paper shows https://www.stat.washington.edu/research/reports/2011/tr589.pdf , imposing constraints is problematic.

I'll try work on something and if I get a working Stan model, I'll send it to you.

Rick,

messages.body_plain:
This code doesn't work for a large number of variables (time series). When I run the code for two time series, it takes a long time to simulate (about an hour) and the results adequate. When I want to include something like 10 variables (in this case have 10 time series in my SUR), it takes a minute and gives values of all parameters around zero.

Why does including more variables (in this case having a larger K) give inadequate results? (My thought is that the parameter space is too big / constrained and its not sampling properly.. Just a guess)

Thanks Again

Below is code:

code1=
  "data {
int<lower=0> N1;
int<lower=0> N;
int<lower=0> N2;
int<lower=1> K;
vector[K] y1[N1];

int<lower=1>  S;
int<lower=1>  dum[N]; // monthly dummies

}
parameters {
corr_matrix[K] OmegaV;
vector<lower=0>[K] tauV;
corr_matrix[K] OmegaW;
vector<lower=0>[K] tauW;
vector[K] theta[N];
vector[K]  alpha[S];
vector[K] mu[N];
vector<lower=0>[K] sigma_mu;

vector[K] y2[N2];

}
transformed parameters{
matrix[K,K] L_betaV;
matrix[K,K] L_betaW;

L_betaV <- cholesky_decompose(OmegaV);
for (k1 in 1:K)
for (k2 in 1:k1)
L_betaV[k1,k2] <- tauV[k1] * L_betaV[k1,k2];

L_betaW <- cholesky_decompose(OmegaW);
for (k1 in 1:K)
for (k2 in 1:k1)
L_betaW[k1,k2] <- tauW[k1] * L_betaW[k1,k2];

}

model{

vector[K] y[N];
for(n in 1:N1) y[n] <-y1[n];
for(n in 1:N2) y[N1+n] <-y2[n];

//prior
mu[1] ~ normal(y[2]-y[1], 10000);
theta[1]~normal(y[1], 5000);

y[1]~multi_normal_cholesky(theta[1], L_betaV);
//likelihood
for(n in 2:N){
mu[n]~normal(mu[n-1], sigma_mu);

theta[n]~multi_normal_cholesky(mu[n-1]+theta[n-1],L_betaW);

y[n]~multi_normal_cholesky(alpha[ dum[n] ]  + theta[n],L_betaV);

}

}

"

data1=list(N=length(data[,1])+12, N1=length(data[,1]),N2=12 ,K=10, y1=data.1[,c(1:10)], S=12, dum=rep(1:12,12)[1:(length(data[,1])+12)])

> There are two ways to do this.
>
> Both involve adding new data variables for the number of items to
> predict/forecast and any inputs necessary to do that prediction.
> Then you can either:
>
> 1.  Define new parameters for the predictions and give these parameters
> predictions just like in the original model.  This only works for continous
> predictions.
>
> 2.  Define new generated quantity variables for the predictions and
> define them using random number generators in the generated quantities block.

messages.body_plain:
As a side note (and perhaps one more for stan-dev), there are some easy ways to save/restart the PRNG.  If nothing else, one way is to reseed the PRNG before every iteration using a randomly generated seed.  This seed is generated at the end of the last iteration using the PRNG and can be saved with the state, making it easy to restart things.

Two potential downsides of this is it 1) could be a little slow depending on whether seeding is expensive for a particular PRNG and 2) you are potentially not using the entire period of the PRNG depending on how it works.  Of course for 1) it's unlikely to be so slow that we'd notice it for anything but the fastest models and for 2) I'm not sure this is really an issue but I could be wrong.

On the up side, it works for any PRNG, is simple to implement and is compatible with user-specified seeds.

Cheers,
Marcus

> the C++ interface to Stan doesn't provide a way to set

> doesn't provide a good way to continue with the same PRNG
> state.
>
> We do plan to enhance the C++ interface to allow proper
> restarting (though we still haven't decided what to do about
> restarting the PRNG).
>
> This is among the things we're going to be updating,

messages.body_plain:
There are big advantages to the vectorized forms.
See the discussion in the section following the introduction
of linear regression (p. 22 in version 2.3 manual).

We're going to rewrite all of these in a best-practices
first way rather than the other way around.  I started
by trying to make them easy to understand for BUGS/JAGS
users and most of these examples were written before we'd
finished implementing the vectorization.

- Bob

>

> Hi, thanks very much for the valuable input.
>
> It is particularly interesting to note your example of a difficult posterior, this is something I always found hard to deal with in Stan (and any other software/method), I suggest more of these examples (of dealing with difficult posteriors) in the manual (or an issue on Github, for future reference).
>
>
> On 14-07-06 03:58 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
>> On Sunday, July 6, 2014 11:35:11 AM UTC-4, Luc Coffeng wrote:
>> I always have to think hard when it comes to changes to variables. So if anybody wants to correct me in turn, please do :).
>>
>> I think Luc has the right code. It does seem very challenging to explain change-of-variables to Stan users, so here is another attempt. The main point is that the priors must always pertain to the variables declared in the parameters block; the only issue is whether the priors are expressed directly on the parameters or indirectly via functions of those parameters.
>>
>> [Technically, the priors actually pertain to the unbounded variables that are transformed into the variables declared in the parameters block, but Stan handles those (and only those) change-of-variables automatically, which is one reason why the log-posterior calculated by Stan differs from what you would intuitively calculate in R or Python. Anyway, the user is only responsible for direct or indirect priors on the possibly bounded variables declared in the parameters block].
>>
>> Direct priors are pretty straightforward, and it is often possible to respecify your model so that the variables that you have informative prior information about are declared in the parameters block and functions thereof are used in the log-likelihood. In that case, you can just specify your priors, and there is no need for a change-of-variables adjustment.
>>
>> Direct priors only get confusing when you declare a primitive variable in the parameters block that has no substantive meaning in order to sample a transformed parameter more efficiently. For example, you may want to put a Cauchy prior with a median of zero and a scale of gamma on a regression coefficient, but unless the data are fairly informative, the marginal posterior distribution of that regression coefficient may have heavy tails that are difficult to sample from efficiently. So, it can be more efficient to do something like
>>
>> parameters {
>>   real z;
>> }
>> transformed parameters {
>>   real beta;
>>   beta <- gamma *  tan( pi() * (Phi_approx(z) - 0.5) );
>> }
>> model {
>>   // use beta in the log-likelihood ...
>>   z ~ normal(0,1); // implies: beta ~ cauchy(0,gamma)
>> }
>>
>> There is no need for a change-of-variables adjustment because the standard normal prior is expressed directly on z, but z is only introduced because it is easier for NUTS to do its thing in a space that is approximately standard normal. What you care about is beta, which is related to z by an opaque formula           (that happens to be the inverse-CDF transformation for the Cauchy distribution). But, in order for Stan to work really well in a non-trivial set of situations, you often have to gunk up your Stan program with primitives like z, which is why I favor writing a // implies:  comment whenever you do that.
>>
>> Indirect priors are legal but confusing and should be avoided if it is possible to express your program using direct priors. For the sake of example, suppose you wanted efficiency but thought the above model block was too unintuitive for your audience. So, you wanted to write
>>
>> parameters {
>>   real z;
>> }
>> transformed parameters {
>>   real beta;
>>   beta <- gamma *  tan( pi() * (Phi_approx(z) - 0.5) );
>> }
>> model {
>>   // use beta in the log-likelihood ...
>>   beta ~ cauchy(0,gamma);
>>   # wrong due to absence of change-of-variables adjustment
>> }
>>
>> This model block does not imply that z is distributed standard normal a priori; thus Stan would not be sampling efficiently and moreover, it would not be sampling from the posterior distribution you intended (i.e. the posterior distribution that would arise if you eliminated z and declared beta in the parameters block). In order to restore coherence, you would have to manually increment_log_prob() by the logarithm of the absolute value of the derivative of beta with respect to z and thus you would have to invoke the chain rule three times without making a typo. And even if you did that correctly, it would             still be slower to execute than if you had just written z ~ normal(0,1) as above. Hence, the coherent model block would be even more gunked up with no benefit.
>>
>> I think the parser would warn you about having to manually increment_log_prob() in this case, but there can be "false" positives when the parser sees a sampling statement on a function of the parameters but isn't programmed to recognize that the transformation is linear inclusive of an identity transformation such as col(Y, j). Under a linear transformation, then manually increment_log_prob() by a constant just slows everything down and does not affect the probability that a proposal will be accepted.
>>
>> All of this is even less transparent when talking about multivariate and / or many-to-one transformations, but the basic principle still applies that you should specify your program with direct priors if at all possible and if that is not possible, make sure to manually increment_log_prob() correctly.
>>
>> Ben
>>

You can simple save the chains themselves:

chain1 <-stan(fit=fit1, init =my.inits(), pars=params, data=data.list, warmup = 250, iter=3250, chains = 1, chain_id=1)
save(sample1, file="G:/BackupChris/mallard_spatial_model/chain1.saved")

and then  re-import them in R and combine them into a fit object.

load("G:/BackupChris/mallard_spatial_model/chain1.saved")
...
model1 <- sflist2stanfit(list(sample1,sample2,sample3, sample4,  sample5,  sample6))
output1<-extract(model1, permuted = TRUE)

Note that if you use that method it will be really important to use the "chain_id" command otherwise some chains could be exact duplicate.

Finally, I also had problem in the past with BUGS and JAGS so I usually run the chains in different working folders. I never tried to run many chains at the same time with Stan though so you should listen to Bob instead of me.

Chris
------------------

messages.body_plain:
On Jul 7, 2014, at 6:17 PM, Tymoteusz Wołodźko <t.wol...@ibe.edu.pl> wrote:

> OK, I thought so, but didn't find clear confirmation of that in manual and was a little bit confused. In the manual there are also some mentions on that "not everything" is yet vectorized, so it can add up to confusion.
>

Sorry it's confusing.

The manual says after presenting the vectorized form:

  "The main difference is that the vectorized form is much faster."

I guess I need to more clear about what the other differences are.  The
example is complicated due to matrix arithmetic, which is only defined
for vector and matrix types.

But we're going to change the presentation eventually so at least this issue
shouldn't be a problem, starting with the vectorized version then presenting
the unvectorized one as an equivalent semantically but slower alternative.

In the lists of functions and distributions in the manual, the pseudo-types
"reals" and "ints" indicate what can be vectorized.  There's a discussion of
the notation before the functions --- maybe we should point to it on every
function definition (hundreds of references), because it's come up before,
because obviously not everyone's going to read our manual cover-to-cover.

   reals:   real, 1D array of real, vector, row vector

   ints:  int, 1D array of int

There's also a discussion in the chapter on vectors and arrays as to what
the advantages are.  For instance, using the vectorized exp() is no faster
than just using a loop, whereas vectorized sum() [and all the distributions]
are much faster in vectorized form for vectors with more than a few entries.
The point is whether we can speed things up with analytic derivatives.

- Bob

messages.subject: Interest in a Julia <-> Stan interface?
messages.subject_clean: Interest in a Julia <-> Stan interface?
messages.body_plain:
A while ago above question came up on the Julia MCMC issue list ( https://github.com/JuliaStats/MCMC.jl/issues/45 ).

I have no idea how much interest there is in such an interface, but I wanted it at least for my own use, in addition to a similar interface to Jags (which I'm working on), and of course Julia's own MCMC.jl is readily available from METADATA.

Stan.jl is an initial version of such an interface. It is assumed users have some experience with Julia (REPL, iJulia, LightTable, etc.) and some familiarity with Stan script and data files.

To test it, three steps are needed:

1. Install CmdStan as described in the Getting Started sections 2.2, 2.3 (and 2.4 to test it) of the CmdStan Interface User's Guide (Version 2.3.0, Jun 20th, 2014).

2. Set the environment variable STAN_HOME to point to the directory where CmdStan was downloaded, e.g. on OSX I added to my .bash_profile:

   export STAN_HOME=/Users/rob/Projects/Stan/cmdstan/
   launchctl setenv STAN_HOME /Users/rob/Projects/Stan/cmdstan/

   The launchctl line (on OSX) will typically only be needed for e.g. LightTable and similar apps that do not inherit the full shell environment.

3. Install Stan.jl:

   Julia >  'Pkg.add("Stan")' .

To test the setup:

   Julia > Pkg.test("Stan")

The README.md file in the Stan.jl package contains a walk-through example, somewhat similar to section 2.4 of the CmdStan Interface User's Guide.

This is a first version of Stan.jl and no doubt will need tweaking (and more!). I can't test on non-OSX platforms either, so I will need help to iron out issues on those platforms.

Dependent on the level of interest and feedback ( please file requests/issues at https://github.com/goedman/Stan.jl/issues ), additional features will be added as time permits or through 'Pull Requests'.

R and Python are in a very different stage of their life cycle compared to Julia and Stan, so I have opted to keep the package lightweight to track changes in both Julia and Stan.

The two primary features currently implemented are generating a Model() to be used to automatically generate the command to execute a Stan script and the use of make to minimize the number of compilations required.

This Stan.jl version cannot activate sub-parts of Stan, like R can through Rcpp. By default Stan.jl runs 4 chains when sampling.

Regards,
Rob J. Goedman
goe...@icloud.com

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: A counterintuitive example of change of variables
messages.body_plain:
Hi Marco,

You should add a correction for change of variables to the second model where you are sampling sigma2 as a transformation of parameter tau. When Bob said that this adjustment is already part of the inv_gamma distribution, he meant that in general (i.e. compare the probability density functions of the gamma and inverse gamma distributions, you will see that the inverse gamma contains the adjustment for the Jacobian of the transform). The adjustment of the posterior in model 2 should be;

increment_log_prob(-2 * log(tau));

- Luc

> Yes, this should have been the first thing I should have done!
>
> I've confirmed what you all said and came to understand things better:
> parameterizing a gaussian using the precision with a gamma prior
> expresses the same uncertainty as parameterizing a gaussian using the
> variance with an inverse-gamma prior. Sorry to state the obvious, I
> guess that's what inverse gamma is for in the first place.

> Thanks very much.
>

> And here's goes the code and results in case anyone is interested:
>
> require(rstan)
>
> model_code1 <- "parameters {
>    real <lower=0> tau; //precision
>    real x;
> }
> transformed parameters {
>    real <lower=0> sigma2; // variance
>    real <lower=0> sigma; //standard deviation
>    sigma2 <- 1/tau;
>    sigma <- sqrt(sigma2);
> }
> model {
>    x ~ normal(0, sigma); //likelihood
>    tau ~ gamma(1,  1); //prior
> }"
>
>
>
> model_code2 <- "parameters {
>    real <lower=0> tau; //precision

>    sigma2 <- 1/tau;
>    sigma <- sqrt(sigma2);

messages.body_plain:
Hi!

I am regurlary handling models where I need to know during initialization the number of groups which are fitted in my hierachical model. This is needed to seed the random effects defined in the model for the individual units. For that to work out the init functions needs to figure some things out about the data which I solve right now like this

attach(stan_data)
stan("mymodel.stan", data=stan_data, init=myinitFunction)
detach(stan_data)

Assume now that stan_data$J <- 20 is the number of individual units over which random effects are defined. Then the init function should look like

myinitFunction <- function() { list(randomEffect=rnorm(J,0,0.5)) }

My trick with attach works, but I would certainly consider this as a hack. So if someone else finds this useful, I would like to request that the data is made available to the myinitFunction when this function is called.

I hope this is not to confused - I am happy to work out a minimal example which even works.

Best,

Sebastian

messages.body_plain:
We're about to undertake a major overhaul on the RStan interface,
so now is the time to get feature requests in!

Sebastian's "trick" is exploiting Stan's dynamic scope to
read a global variable in the body of a function.  Perhaps not
the safest programming style, but then I'm not a huge fan of
this kind of scoping.

But R is nothing if not flexible.  Maybe you'd be happier with
a functional programming solution --- take the data as an argument
to a "factory" function that creates the init function.  For example,

  init_fun_factory <- function(stan_data) {
    return(function() { list(randomEffect=rnorm(stan_data$J,0,0.5)); }
  }

and then call with

  stan("mymodel.stan", data=stan_data, init=init_fun_factory(stan_data));

Here's a simple example of how the idea works outside the context
of Stan:

  > factory <- function(data) return(function() { return(data$alpha); })

  > data <- list(alpha=10)

  > alpha
  Error: object 'alpha' not found

   > init_fun <- factory(data)

   > init_fun()
   [1] 10

You can also just use factory(data)() to get 10.

Was there something you were suggesting we add to rstan?

- Bob

My own preference is not to have complex defaults and not under
any circumstances to play with default environments for user-supplied
functions.  The former so everything's easy to doc and test and understand
(though perhaps not so easy to use in a single step) and the latter
so that the behavior is predictible to R users who might themselves
be monkeying with environments as you did.

But I'm not the only one with my hands on the steering wheel of the
Stan bus.  And I'm more concerned that the lower-level functionality is
implemented cleanly than the high-level calls (for instance, "stan()" calls
compilers, data readers, and then one or more chain runners --- it's
the thing stan() calls that I'm most concerned with).

That %in% function looks really useful!

- Bob

On Wednesday, July 9, 2014 12:46:32 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> But I'm not the only one with my hands on the steering wheel of the
> Stan bus.  And I'm more concerned that the lower-level functionality is
> implemented cleanly than the high-level calls (for instance, "stan()" calls
> compilers, data readers, and then one or more chain runners --- it's
> the thing stan() calls that I'm most concerned with).

I'm inclined to agree that we not mess with this right now. Under my proposal for 3.0, there could be an abstract base class for the stanfit object and then we could create an child class on the fly that would have additional fields for the symbols declared in the data block of the .stan program that get populated (by reference) with the elements of the passed data list in R. Then, it wouldn't be too difficult for a function that generates initial values to refer internally to "this", as in

this$get_J()

Ben

On Wednesday, July 9, 2014 12:38:32 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> We're about to undertake a major overhaul on the RStan interface,
> so now is the time to get feature requests in!

Since you asked...

Feature request: I would like to be able to ask Stan to sample p(x|y,data) and use other code to sample p(y|x,data) to get samples from p(x,y|data). I think what is needed to make that happen is:
   1) make it easy to read/write data and read/write parameter values at any time from R without otherwise modifying the state/adaptation of the sampler.
   2) make it easy to read/write the sampler/optimizer tuning parameters from R without modifying the rest of the object, redoing adaptation, etc...

Argument:
- Stan can do a lot but it can't do everything.
- R is frustrating at times but it's a good glue language for statistical analysis because everyone feels obliged to implement interfaces there.
- I acknowledge that it is sometimes necessary to re-do the adaptation but of the many ways you give users to shoot themselves in the foot this would not be the worst.
- Right now when I do an analysis I have to ask myself whether it's easier better to write my own code OR use Stan, I would like to be able to make that an "AND".
- This would provide a path for people outside of the Stan team to show that certain algorithms/functionality are relevant for Stan without writing Stan-compatible C++ code.
- Working through R would be relatively slow but in my experience most of the wait time is due to autocorrelation caused by the model/data rather than the speed of the algorithm.

Not my first time pitching this one but thought I'd give it another try...

Krzysztof

messages.body_plain:
Let me rewrite your request following Andrew's (and hence
Stan's) notation.

You have parameters theta = (alpha,beta) and data y and
you want to sample from a posterior p(alpha,beta | y)
by doing something Gibbs-like in sampling p(alpha | beta, y)
in Stan and p(beta | alpha, y) in some other program.

Fair enough --- we'd love to make that easy to do.  In fact,
it was part of our rejected DARPA probabilistic programming
proposal.

I think we'll be adding just about everything you'll need in
the next version (more below).

WARNING:  I think this is what you meant below about adaptation,
but for everyone else's sake:  because beta now looks like "data" to
Stan (even though it's a parameter of the bigger system), every time beta
changes, it changes the posterior from which Stan is trying to sample.
This is an issue because our adaptation assumes that we're
only trying to adapt to a single posterior.

In R, we are going to be breaking the stan() command down and exposing
some more primitive operations:

  * compiling a model:  translates model from Stan to C++ and compiles
    a dynamically linkable library, but doesn't instantiate any instances
    of the model

  * create a model object with data: populate a compiled model with data,
    creating a C++ class instance corresponding to the model using the shared object
    code

We also want to be able to specify all the inputs and outputs including
adaptation, so that you can

  * extract (and then potentially save) current adaptation parameters

  * start a sampler with given adaptation parameters

Most of the time in our algorithm is spent computing gradients.
The faster that goes, the faster everything goes.  If the adaptation
gets messed up, you'll have to intentionally slow everything down by
forcing a very small step size, which can deal with different situations.

The fact that interpreted R is snail slow isn't usually a problem if
you're just calling other functions that do the heavy lifting.  But
you may find it prohibitive if you're in a tight loop doing a lot of
computation using R.  But then if you have a good general technique
prototyped in R, it's usually pretty straightforward to move it to
something faster like C, C++, Fortran, or Java.

- Bob

p(alpha|beta,y) is going to be p(alpha|data)... Stan can compute that

> > > >    [1] 10
> > > >
> > > > You can also just use factory(data)() to get 10.

Daniel

I don't see anything you're missing, so maybe Michael
will chime in.

I don't understand why Michael's talking about computing marginal
distributions in closed form --- we just have Bayes's rule and compute
everything up to a constant.  I think that'll work for your
proposal.

If we did limit models to DAGs a la BUGS, then there's more
that we could infer from the graph structure, such as Markov
blankets, which would make doing a proper per-variable
Gibbs easy to implement.  The fact that we don't do that is
why we don't have any discrete sampling.

And just to be clear about our goals, we're not planning on building these
Gibbs updates any time soon. And if you had to implement full Gibbs this way,
as in trying to code up BUGS in Stan, it'd be too much copying to be efficient
unless there were only a few blocks.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi!

Since you asked for features:

- a facility to simulate from a posterior would be nice, i.e. currently I loop over each draw of a posterior and fire up stan for each draw; the posterior should come either from a stanfit object or an array (I may want to mess around with the posterior before I simulate).

- some way to access the data from within the init function, i.e. like Ben pointed out; not so urgent, I am happy to live with the environment stuff I digged up in R.

- I saw you intend to parallelize things easily for users; here it would be great to keep things as flexible as possible (most people use some openmp, some MPI, and ...); concerning seeding I think it would be best to go with one stan seed which is the same for all chains, but different chain_ids; one more note: I keep reading that parallelization is not possible under windows which is not true, it is just different, i.e. you need to use "cl <- makeCluster(ncpu, type=ifelse(.Platform$OS.type == "windows", "PSOCK", "FORK"))"; but this PSOCK cluster needs to be handled with a bit of care (seeds, data exporting!); I use this with foreach which I find useful, but other will disagree here I guess

- consider to make the model chaching option configurable via the options interface from R so that users can set in their R profile if they like caching permanently on or not

- possibly consider to cache models in different compiled versions (fast/debug/NDEBUG) when they are requested in different flavors along the road

- I hope the current stan merge function stays, it is very useful as I run multiple chains on a cluster and each in a separate process which I merge at the end of the day

- Speeding up the monitor function would be great - I know you consider moving that bit into C++ to make it fast. If you could also write a function such that I can stick coda samples into it, that would even be better (sometimes I would like to do comparisons of Stan runs with JAGS/WinBUGS)

@ Bob: R is full of thousands of very convenient functions and I agree your closure type approach is programmatically much nicer (but the flow of my program does not go with it and after all it is just R - so who cares anyway).

Best,
Sebastian

> >> Stan's) notation.

> >> You have parameters theta = (alpha,beta) and data y and

> >> by doing something Gibbs-like in sampling p(alpha | beta, y)
> >> in Stan and p(beta | alpha, y) in some other program.
> >>

> >> it was part of our rejected DARPA probabilistic programming
> >> proposal.
> >>
> >> I think we'll be adding just about everything you'll need in
> >> the next version (more below).
> >>
> >> WARNING:  I think this is what you meant below about adaptation,
> >> but for everyone else's sake:  because beta now looks like "data" to
> >> Stan (even though it's a parameter of the bigger system), every time beta

> >>     a dynamically linkable library, but doesn't instantiate any instances
> >>     of the model

> >>   * create a model object with data: populate a compiled model with data,
> >>     creating a C++ class instance corresponding to the model using the shared object
> >>     code

> >> adaptation, so that you can
> >>
> >>   * extract (and then potentially save) current adaptation parameters
> >>
> >>   * start a sampler with given adaptation parameters
> >>

> >> forcing a very small step size, which can deal with different situations.

> >> you're just calling other functions that do the heavy lifting.  But
> >> you may find it prohibitive if you're in a tight loop doing a lot of
> >> computation using R.  But then if you have a good general technique
> >> prototyped in R, it's usually pretty straightforward to move it to
> >> something faster like C, C++, Fortran, or Java.
> >>
> >> - Bob
> >>
> >>
> >> On Jul 9, 2014, at 3:15 PM, Krzysztof Sakrejda <krzysztof...@gmail.com> wrote:

> >> >
> >> > Since you asked...

> >> >

> >> > - Working through R would be relatively slow but in my experience most of the wait time is due to autocorrelation caused by the model/data rather than the speed of the algorithm.
> >> >
> >> > Not my first time pitching this one but thought I'd give it another try...
> >> >
> >> > Krzysztof
> >> >
> >> >
> >> >
> >> > Sebastian's "trick" is exploiting Stan's dynamic scope to
> >> > read a global variable in the body of a function.  Perhaps not
> >> > the safest programming style, but then I'm not a huge fan of
> >> > this kind of scoping.
> >> >
> >> > But R is nothing if not flexible.  Maybe you'd be happier with
> >> > a functional programming solution --- take the data as an argument
> >> > to a "factory" function that creates the init function.  For example,
> >> >
> >> >   init_fun_factory <- function(stan_data) {
> >> >     return(function() { list(randomEffect=rnorm(stan_data$J,0,0.5)); }
> >> >   }
> >> >
> >> > and then call with
> >> >
> >> >   stan("mymodel.stan", data=stan_data, init=init_fun_factory(stan_data));
> >> >
> >> > Here's a simple example of how the idea works outside the context
> >> > of Stan:
> >> >
> >> >   > factory <- function(data) return(function() { return(data$alpha); })
> >> >
> >> >   > data <- list(alpha=10)
> >> >
> >> >   > alpha
> >> >   Error: object 'alpha' not found
> >> >
> >> >    > init_fun <- factory(data)
> >> >
> >> >    > init_fun()
> >> >    [1] 10
> >> >
> >> > You can also just use factory(data)() to get 10.
> >> >
> >> > Was there something you were suggesting we add to rstan?
> >> >
> >> > - Bob
> >> >
> >> >
> >> > On Jul 9, 2014, at 11:43 AM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:
> >> >
> >> > > Hi!
> >> > >
> >> > > I am regurlary handling models where I need to know during initialization the number of groups which are fitted in my hierachical model. This is needed to seed the random effects defined in the model for the individual units. For that to work out the init functions needs to figure some things out about the data which I solve right now like this
> >> > >
> >> > > attach(stan_data)
> >> > > stan("mymodel.stan", data=stan_data, init=myinitFunction)
> >> > > detach(stan_data)
> >> > >
> >> > > Assume now that stan_data$J <- 20 is the number of individual units over which random effects are defined. Then the init function should look like
> >> > >
> >> > > myinitFunction <- function() { list(randomEffect=rnorm(J,0,0.5)) }
> >> > >
> >> > > My trick with attach works, but I would certainly consider this as a hack. So if someone else finds this useful, I would like to request that the data is made available to the myinitFunction when this function is called.
> >> > >
> >> > > I hope this is not to confused - I am happy to work out a minimal example which even works.
> >> > >
> >> > > Best,
> >> > >
> >> > > Sebastian

messages.body_plain:
Hi!

One more thing: If possible, speed up the communication between R and Stan, i.e. I just had to rewrite a Stan model to expose fewer variables just because it took too long otherwise. I suspect that the issue is that Stan outputs all parameters while Rstan lets me select a subset and this subsetting is done on the R side. It seems to me that reading in large data chunks which come from Stan somehow takes a while (feels like stan is writing a csv file and rstan reads it in, which means rstan has to figure out the layout of the arrays).

Anything which speeds this stan<->R communication up and save me from copying my Stan models (with minor modifications then) around would be great.

Best,
Sebastian

On Wednesday, July 9, 2014 11:25:38 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> I don't see anything you're missing, so maybe Michael
> will chime in.

Ok, this is something I'm doing in an applied project so I would like to
hear if there are serious problems with it.

>
> I don't understand why Michael's talking about computing marginal
> distributions in closed form --- we just have Bayes's rule and compute
> everything up to a constant.  I think that'll work for your
> proposal.
>
> If we did limit models to DAGs a la BUGS, then there's more
> that we could infer from the graph structure, such as Markov
> blankets, which would make doing a proper per-variable
> Gibbs easy to implement.  The fact that we don't do that is
> why we don't have any discrete sampling.
>
> And just to be clear about our goals, we're not planning on building these
> Gibbs updates any time soon. And if you had to implement full Gibbs this way,
> as in trying to code up BUGS in Stan, it'd be too much copying to be efficient
> unless there were only a few blocks.

Yeah, a lot of copying.  I did a proof-of-concept a while ago which I'm pasting below.
Note that it currently does not work b/c I've changed the package code (and it requries
a library I have on github, which has also changed).  I am currently updating my examples
and I will link them here it in the next week or so to make it run-able.  For now it's an ugly mock-up...
but at least it makes my goals clear.  I think the ability to do a few big blocks will save me
and maybe others from writing NUTS by hand or writing the umpteenth version of slow code for doing an HLM.

library(Rux)
library(MASS)
library(rstan)

## From total marked population size (N), times of surveys (tos),
## survival probability (phi), and recapture probability (p),
## simulate times of ``births'', followed by the survival process
## (time of alive matrix, toaM), and the recapture process
## (time of recpature matrix, torM).  From these, calculate the
## list of times of recapture (tor) and the vector of times of
## death (tod).
tos <- 1:10
N <- 200
phi <- rep(.8,max(tos))
p <- 0.7
tbs <- rbinom(n=N, size=5, prob=.3)+1
toaM <- matrix(0,nrow=N, ncol=length(tos))
torM <- matrix(0,nrow=N, ncol=length(tos))

survive <- 0
die <- 0
recapture <- 0
miss <- 0

for ( i in 1:N ) {
  toaM[i,tbs[i]] <- 1
  torM[i,tbs[i]] <- 1
  for (j in (tbs[i]+1):max(tos) ) {
    toaM[i,j] <- toaM[i,j-1] *
      sample(x=c(0,1),size=1,replace=TRUE, prob=c(1-phi[j], phi[j]))
    if ((toaM[i,j] == 1) && (toaM[i,j-1] == 1)) survive <- survive + 1
    if ((toaM[i,j] == 0) && (toaM[i,j-1] == 1)) die <- die + 1

    torM[i,j] <- toaM[i,j] *
      sample(x=c(0,1),size=1,replace=TRUE, prob=c(1-p, p))
    if ((toaM[i,j] == 1) && (torM[i,j] == 1)) recapture <- recapture + 1
    if ((toaM[i,j] == 1) && (torM[i,j] == 0)) miss <- miss + 1

  }

}
tor <- apply(X=torM, MARGIN=1, FUN=function(x) {which(x==1)})
tod <- apply(X=toaM, MARGIN=1, FUN=function(x) {max(which(x==1))+1})

## Calculate realized survival and recapture probabilities.
true_phi <- survive/(survive + die)
true_p <-   recapture/(recapture + miss)

## Create matrices of (bad) initial values for the parameters of the
## survival (PHI) and recapture (P) processes.  These matrices are
## N x max(tos)*5 by default.
P <- matrix(data=0.6, nrow=N, ncol=max(tos)*5)
P[,(max(tos)+1):(max(tos)*5)] <- 0
PHI = 0.5

## Create a handle to the likelihood calculation and discrete slice
## sampler for time of death state.
o <- new("recapture_handle",
  times_of_surveys = tos,
  times_of_recaptures = tor,
  times_of_deaths = tod,
  known_deaths = rep(FALSE, N),
  PHI = PHI,
  P = P
)

## Calculate the initial likelihood, the time taken for this calculation
## should scale with N * K * 5.
ll_calculation_time <- system.time(expr=o$log_likelihood)

## Create vectors to hold output from MCMC.
N_it <- 1000
o_accept <- vector(mode="numeric", length=N_it)
o_PHI <- vector(mode="numeric", length=N_it)
o_P <- vector(mode="numeric", length=N_it)
o_lpd <- vector(mode="numeric", length=N_it)

## Stan model for simulating from PHI/P conditional on known
## birth, death, and recapture times for n tags.
stan_code <- '
  data {
    int<lower=0> n_tags;
    int<lower=0> n_occasions;
    int<lower=0> tb[n_tags];
    int<lower=0> td[n_tags];
    int<lower=0, upper=1> recaptures[n_tags, n_occasions];

  }

  // Declare parameters for the linear models.
  parameters {
    real beta;
    real gamma;
  }

  // Rubber meets the road for linear model specification.
  transformed parameters {
    real PHI_logit[n_tags, 5*n_occasions];
    real P_logit[n_tags, 5*n_occasions];
    for ( tag in 1:n_tags ) { // indexing covers PHI/P
      for ( t in tb[tag]:(td[tag]-1) ) {
        PHI_logit[tag,t] <- beta;
        P_logit[tag,t] <- gamma;
      }
    }
  }
 model {

    // Priors for linear model coefficients.
    beta ~ cauchy(0,2.5);
    gamma ~ cauchy(0,2.5);

    // Mark-recapture likelihood.
    for ( tag in 1:n_tags ) {
      for ( t in tb[tag]:(td[tag]-2) ) { // SURVIVES
        1 ~ bernoulli_logit(PHI_logit[tag,t]);
      }
      0 ~ bernoulli_logit(PHI_logit[tag,td[tag]-1]);  // DIES

      for ( t in (tb[tag]+1):min(n_occasions,td[tag]-1) ) {  // AVAILABLE
        recaptures[tag,t] ~ bernoulli_logit(P_logit[tag,t]);
      }
    }
  }

'

n_tags <- dim(o$recaptures)[1]
n_occ <- dim(o$recaptures)[2]
stan_fit <- NULL
stan_iter <- 200

stan_timing <- system.time({
for ( it in 1:N_it ) {
  print(it)
  ## Sample state:
  tds <- c(o$set_deaths(o$td))

  ## Sample PHI/P matrices:
  stan_fit <- stan(
    model_code=stan_code,
    data=list(
      n_tags = n_tags,
      n_occasions = n_occ,
      tb = tbs,
      td = tds,
      recaptures = o$recaptures
    ), fit=stan_fit,
    iter=stan_iter, chains=1, warmup=stan_iter/2,
    pars=c('beta','gamma')
  )

  ## Make matrices and re-assign them:
  stan_samples <- extract(stan_fit, permuted=TRUE)
  PHImat <- matrix(
    data=plogis(stan_samples$beta[stan_iter/2]),
    nrow=o$N, ncol=o$K*5, byrow=TRUE)
  Pmat <- matrix(
    data=plogis(stan_samples$gamma[stan_iter/2]),
    nrow=o$N, ncol=o$K*5, byrow=TRUE)
  Pmat[,(o$K+1):ncol(Pmat)] <- 0
  o$PHI <- PHImat
  o$P   <- Pmat

  ## Record for posterity
  o_PHI[it] = unique(c(o$PHI))
  o_P[it]   = max(unique(c(o$P)))
  o_lpd[it] = o$log_likelihood
}
})

plot(o_PHI, pch='*')
plot(o_lpd, pch='*')
plot(o_PHI, o_lpd, pch = '*')
plot(o_PHI, o_P, pch = '*')
abline(h=recapture/(recapture+miss))
abline(v=survive/(survive+die))

>
> - Bob
>
> On Jul 9, 2014, at 7:33 PM, Krzysztof Sakrejda <krzysztof...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> > On Wednesday, July 9, 2014 6:29:15 PM UTC-4, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> > I think everyone should temper their expectations until
> > (a) we limit Stan models to DAGs or (b) we find some
> > magical algorithm that can compute marginal distributions
> > in closed form.
> >
> > Following Bob's notation, from Stan's point of view the distribution
> > p(alpha|beta,y) is going to be p(alpha|data)... Stan can compute that
> > density given data = {beta,y} as well as sample from it.  I don't think
> > we need p(alpha|y) if the goal is to have this be part of a Gibbs step.
> >
> > ... what am I missing?
> >
> > Krzysztof
> >
> >
> > On Jul 9, 2014, at 10:57 PM, Krzysztof Sakrejda <krzysztof...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> >> Thank you for taking the time to rewrite and explain where things are at.
> >> This, combined with the optimization, is going to be amazing (even more
> >> amazing than Stan already is).
> >>
> >> Krzysztof
> >>
> >> On Wednesday, July 9, 2014 4:07:56 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> >> Let me rewrite your request following Andrew's (and hence
> >> Stan's) notation.
> >>
> >> You have parameters theta = (alpha,beta) and data y and
> >> you want to sample from a posterior p(alpha,beta | y)
> >> by doing something Gibbs-like in sampling p(alpha | beta, y)
> >> in Stan and p(beta | alpha, y) in some other program.
> >>
> >> Fair enough --- we'd love to make that easy to do.  In fact,
> >> it was part of our rejected DARPA probabilistic programming
> >> proposal.
> >>
> >> I think we'll be adding just about everything you'll need in
> >> the next version (more below).
> >>
> >> WARNING:  I think this is what you meant below about adaptation,
> >> but for everyone else's sake:  because beta now looks like "data" to
> >> Stan (even though it's a parameter of the bigger system), every time beta
> >> changes, it changes the posterior from which Stan is trying to sample.
> >> This is an issue because our adaptation assumes that we're
> >> only trying to adapt to a single posterior.
> >>
> >> In R, we are going to be breaking the stan() command down and exposing
> >> some more primitive operations:
> >>
> >>   * compiling a model:  translates model from Stan to C++ and compiles
> >>     a dynamically linkable library, but doesn't instantiate any instances
> >>     of the model
> >>
> >>   * create a model object with data: populate a compiled model with data,
> >>     creating a C++ class instance corresponding to the model using the shared object
> >>     code
> >>
> >> We also want to be able to specify all the inputs and outputs including
> >> adaptation, so that you can
> >>
> >>   * extract (and then potentially save) current adaptation parameters
> >>
> >>   * start a sampler with given adaptation parameters
> >>
> >> Most of the time in our algorithm is spent computing gradients.
> >> The faster that goes, the faster everything goes.  If the adaptation
> >> gets messed up, you'll have to intentionally slow everything down by
> >> forcing a very small step size, which can deal with different situations.
> >>
> >> The fact that interpreted R is snail slow isn't usually a problem if
> >> you're just calling other functions that do the heavy lifting.  But
> >> you may find it prohibitive if you're in a tight loop doing a lot of
> >> computation using R.  But then if you have a good general technique
> >> prototyped in R, it's usually pretty straightforward to move it to
> >> something faster like C, C++, Fortran, or Java.
> >>
> >> - Bob
> >>
> >>
> >> On Jul 9, 2014, at 3:15 PM, Krzysztof Sakrejda <krzysztof...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >>
> >> > On Wednesday, July 9, 2014 12:38:32 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> >> > We're about to undertake a major overhaul on the RStan interface,
> >> > so now is the time to get feature requests in!
> >> >
> >> > Since you asked...
> >> >
> >> > Feature request: I would like to be able to ask Stan to sample p(x|y,data) and use other code to sample p(y|x,data) to get samples from p(x,y|data). I think what is needed to make that happen is:
> >> >    1) make it easy to read/write data and read/write parameter values at any time from R without otherwise modifying the state/adaptation of the sampler.
> >> >    2) make it easy to read/write the sampler/optimizer tuning parameters from R without modifying the rest of the object, redoing adaptation, etc...
> >> >
> >> > Argument:
> >> > - Stan can do a lot but it can't do everything.
> >> > - R is frustrating at times but it's a good glue language for statistical analysis because everyone feels obliged to implement interfaces there.
> >> > - I acknowledge that it is sometimes necessary to re-do the adaptation but of the many ways you give users to shoot themselves in the foot this would not be the worst.
> >> > - Right now when I do an analysis I have to ask myself whether it's easier better to write my own code OR use Stan, I would like to be able to make that an "AND".
> >> > - This would provide a path for people outside of the Stan team to show that certain algorithms/functionality are relevant for Stan without writing Stan-compatible C++ code.
> >> > - Working through R would be relatively slow but in my experience most of the wait time is due to autocorrelation caused by the model/data rather than the speed of the algorithm.
> >> >
> >> > Not my first time pitching this one but thought I'd give it another try...
> >> >
> >> > Krzysztof
> >> >
> >> >
> >> >
> >> > Sebastian's "trick" is exploiting Stan's dynamic scope to
> >> > read a global variable in the body of a function.  Perhaps not
> >> > the safest programming style, but then I'm not a huge fan of
> >> > this kind of scoping.
> >> >
> >> > But R is nothing if not flexible.  Maybe you'd be happier with
> >> > a functional programming solution --- take the data as an argument
> >> > to a "factory" function that creates the init function.  For example,
> >> >
> >> >   init_fun_factory <- function(stan_data) {
> >> >     return(function() { list(randomEffect=rnorm(stan_data$J,0,0.5)); }
> >> >   }
> >> >
> >> > and then call with
> >> >
> >> >   stan("mymodel.stan", data=stan_data, init=init_fun_factory(stan_data));
> >> >
> >> > Here's a simple example of how the idea works outside the context
> >> > of Stan:
> >> >
> >> >   > factory <- function(data) return(function() { return(data$alpha); })
> >> >
> >> >   > data <- list(alpha=10)
> >> >
> >> >   > alpha
> >> >   Error: object 'alpha' not found
> >> >
> >> >    > init_fun <- factory(data)
> >> >
> >> >    > init_fun()
> >> >    [1] 10
> >> >
> >> > You can also just use factory(data)() to get 10.
> >> >
> >> > Was there something you were suggesting we add to rstan?
> >> >
> >> > - Bob
> >> >
> >> >
> >> > On Jul 9, 2014, at 11:43 AM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:
> >> >
> >> > > Hi!
> >> > >
> >> > > I am regurlary handling models where I need to know during initialization the number of groups which are fitted in my hierachical model. This is needed to seed the random effects defined in the model for the individual units. For that to work out the init functions needs to figure some things out about the data which I solve right now like this
> >> > >
> >> > > attach(stan_data)
> >> > > stan("mymodel.stan", data=stan_data, init=myinitFunction)
> >> > > detach(stan_data)
> >> > >
> >> > > Assume now that stan_data$J <- 20 is the number of individual units over which random effects are defined. Then the init function should look like
> >> > >
> >> > > myinitFunction <- function() { list(randomEffect=rnorm(J,0,0.5)) }
> >> > >
> >> > > My trick with attach works, but I would certainly consider this as a hack. So if someone else finds this useful, I would like to request that the data is made available to the myinitFunction when this function is called.
> >> > >
> >> > > I hope this is not to confused - I am happy to work out a minimal example which even works.
> >> > >
> >> > > Best,
> >> > >
> >> > > Sebastian
