messages.subject: The future of Dags in Stan
messages.subject_clean: The future of Dags in Stan
messages.body_plain:
We’re never gonna limit Stan models to Dags.  I think what we’re going to build sometimes is a wrapper for Stan where the user can supply a Dag and also say which nodes are observed, and then the wrapper will write the appropriate Stan model.

On Jul 10, 2014, at 5:25 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
> If we did limit models to DAGs a la BUGS, then there's more
> that we could infer from the graph structure, such as Markov
> blankets, which would make doing a proper per-variable
> Gibbs easy to implement.  The fact that we don't do that is
> why we don't have any discrete sampling.
>
>

> On Jul 9, 2014, at 7:33 PM, Krzysztof Sakrejda <krzysztof...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>> On Wednesday, July 9, 2014 6:29:15 PM UTC-4, Michael Betancourt wrote:
>> I think everyone should temper their expectations until
>> (a) we limit Stan models to DAGs or (b) we find some
>> magical algorithm that can compute marginal distributions
>> in closed form.
>>
>> Following Bob's notation, from Stan's point of view the distribution
>> p(alpha|beta,y) is going to be p(alpha|data)... Stan can compute that
>> density given data = {beta,y} as well as sample from it.  I don't think
>> we need p(alpha|y) if the goal is to have this be part of a Gibbs step.
>>
>> ... what am I missing?
>>
>> Krzysztof
>>
>>

>>
>>> Thank you for taking the time to rewrite and explain where things are at.

>>> amazing than Stan already is).

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] The future of DAGs in Stan
messages.body_plain:
Right --- we're not going to limit them everywhere.

I just meant that for the special case of directed acyclic
graphical models, we could exploit the graph structure.

The real trick in Andrew's proposal would be handling
missing data a la BUGS --- we'd need to break the parameters
apart into observed (data) and "missing" (parameters), but then
I don't know how the interfaces on the outside could work
without major overhauls.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] feature request for rstan
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] feature request for rstan
messages.body_plain:
Nothing is being written out to .csv format and
read back in.  That would be super slow.
Everything communicates directly in memory through Rcpp.

Restricting the number of parameters output more efficiently
from the C++ Stan side is on our to-do list.  But R should
already be able to do it pretty efficiently (in the sense
that the time should be negligible compared to computing
gradients each iteration).

I don't know where the hotspot in RStan is for this, but I'd
guess it's in reshaping everything to go into the fit
object.  One approach we could take would be to do more work
lazily --- I've been thinking about that for the new interfaces.

- Bob

On Jul 10, 2014, at 5:54 AM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi!
>
> One more thing: If possible, speed up the communication between R and Stan, i.e. I just had to rewrite a Stan model to expose fewer variables just because it took too long otherwise. I suspect that the issue is that Stan outputs all parameters while Rstan lets me select a subset and this subsetting is done on the R side. It seems to me that reading in large data chunks which come from Stan somehow takes a while (feels like stan is writing a csv file and rstan reads it in, which means rstan has to figure out the layout of the arrays).
>
> Anything which speeds this stan<->R communication up and save me from copying my Stan models (with minor modifications then) around would be great.
>
> Best,
> Sebastian
>
>
> On Thu, Jul 10, 2014 at 11:16 AM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi!
>
> Since you asked for features:
>
> - a facility to simulate from a posterior would be nice, i.e. currently I loop over each draw of a posterior and fire up stan for each draw; the posterior should come either from a stanfit object or an array (I may want to mess around with the posterior before I simulate).
>
> - some way to access the data from within the init function, i.e. like Ben pointed out; not so urgent, I am happy to live with the environment stuff I digged up in R.
>
> - I saw you intend to parallelize things easily for users; here it would be great to keep things as flexible as possible (most people use some openmp, some MPI, and ...); concerning seeding I think it would be best to go with one stan seed which is the same for all chains, but different chain_ids; one more note: I keep reading that parallelization is not possible under windows which is not true, it is just different, i.e. you need to use "cl <- makeCluster(ncpu, type=ifelse(.Platform$OS.type == "windows", "PSOCK", "FORK"))"; but this PSOCK cluster needs to be handled with a bit of care (seeds, data exporting!); I use this with foreach which I find useful, but other will disagree here I guess
>
> - consider to make the model chaching option configurable via the options interface from R so that users can set in their R profile if they like caching permanently on or not
>
> - possibly consider to cache models in different compiled versions (fast/debug/NDEBUG) when they are requested in different flavors along the road
>
> - I hope the current stan merge function stays, it is very useful as I run multiple chains on a cluster and each in a separate process which I merge at the end of the day
>
> - Speeding up the monitor function would be great - I know you consider moving that bit into C++ to make it fast. If you could also write a function such that I can stick coda samples into it, that would even be better (sometimes I would like to do comparisons of Stan runs with JAGS/WinBUGS)
>
> @ Bob: R is full of thousands of very convenient functions and I agree your closure type approach is programmatically much nicer (but the flow of my program does not go with it and after all it is just R - so who cares anyway).
>
> Best,
> Sebastian
>
>
> On Thu, Jul 10, 2014 at 5:25 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> I don't see anything you're missing, so maybe Michael
> will chime in.
>
> I don't understand why Michael's talking about computing marginal
> distributions in closed form --- we just have Bayes's rule and compute
> everything up to a constant.  I think that'll work for your
> proposal.
>
> If we did limit models to DAGs a la BUGS, then there's more
> that we could infer from the graph structure, such as Markov
> blankets, which would make doing a proper per-variable
> Gibbs easy to implement.  The fact that we don't do that is
> why we don't have any discrete sampling.
>
> And just to be clear about our goals, we're not planning on building these
> Gibbs updates any time soon. And if you had to implement full Gibbs this way,
> as in trying to code up BUGS in Stan, it'd be too much copying to be efficient
> unless there were only a few blocks.
>
> - Bob
>
> On Jul 9, 2014, at 7:33 PM, Krzysztof Sakrejda <krzysztof...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> > On Wednesday, July 9, 2014 6:29:15 PM UTC-4, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> > I think everyone should temper their expectations until
> > (a) we limit Stan models to DAGs or (b) we find some
> > magical algorithm that can compute marginal distributions
> > in closed form.
> >
> > Following Bob's notation, from Stan's point of view the distribution
> > p(alpha|beta,y) is going to be p(alpha|data)... Stan can compute that
> > density given data = {beta,y} as well as sample from it.  I don't think
> > we need p(alpha|y) if the goal is to have this be part of a Gibbs step.
> >
> > ... what am I missing?
> >
> > Krzysztof
> >
> >
> > On Jul 9, 2014, at 10:57 PM, Krzysztof Sakrejda <krzysztof...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> >> Thank you for taking the time to rewrite and explain where things are at.
> >> This, combined with the optimization, is going to be amazing (even more
> >> amazing than Stan already is).
> >>
> >> Krzysztof
> >>
> >> On Wednesday, July 9, 2014 4:07:56 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> >> Let me rewrite your request following Andrew's (and hence
> >> Stan's) notation.
> >>
> >> You have parameters theta = (alpha,beta) and data y and
> >> you want to sample from a posterior p(alpha,beta | y)
> >> by doing something Gibbs-like in sampling p(alpha | beta, y)
> >> in Stan and p(beta | alpha, y) in some other program.
> >>
> >> Fair enough --- we'd love to make that easy to do.  In fact,
> >> it was part of our rejected DARPA probabilistic programming
> >> proposal.
> >>
> >> I think we'll be adding just about everything you'll need in
> >> the next version (more below).
> >>
> >> WARNING:  I think this is what you meant below about adaptation,
> >> but for everyone else's sake:  because beta now looks like "data" to
> >> Stan (even though it's a parameter of the bigger system), every time beta
> >> changes, it changes the posterior from which Stan is trying to sample.
> >> This is an issue because our adaptation assumes that we're
> >> only trying to adapt to a single posterior.
> >>
> >> In R, we are going to be breaking the stan() command down and exposing
> >> some more primitive operations:
> >>
> >>   * compiling a model:  translates model from Stan to C++ and compiles
> >>     a dynamically linkable library, but doesn't instantiate any instances
> >>     of the model
> >>
> >>   * create a model object with data: populate a compiled model with data,
> >>     creating a C++ class instance corresponding to the model using the shared object
> >>     code
> >>
> >> We also want to be able to specify all the inputs and outputs including
> >> adaptation, so that you can
> >>
> >>   * extract (and then potentially save) current adaptation parameters
> >>
> >>   * start a sampler with given adaptation parameters
> >>
> >> Most of the time in our algorithm is spent computing gradients.
> >> The faster that goes, the faster everything goes.  If the adaptation
> >> gets messed up, you'll have to intentionally slow everything down by
> >> forcing a very small step size, which can deal with different situations.
> >>
> >> The fact that interpreted R is snail slow isn't usually a problem if
> >> you're just calling other functions that do the heavy lifting.  But
> >> you may find it prohibitive if you're in a tight loop doing a lot of
> >> computation using R.  But then if you have a good general technique
> >> prototyped in R, it's usually pretty straightforward to move it to
> >> something faster like C, C++, Fortran, or Java.
> >>
> >> - Bob
> >>
> >>
> >> On Jul 9, 2014, at 3:15 PM, Krzysztof Sakrejda <krzysztof...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >>
> >> > On Wednesday, July 9, 2014 12:38:32 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> >> > We're about to undertake a major overhaul on the RStan interface,
> >> > so now is the time to get feature requests in!
> >> >
> >> > Since you asked...
> >> >
> >> > Feature request: I would like to be able to ask Stan to sample p(x|y,data) and use other code to sample p(y|x,data) to get samples from p(x,y|data). I think what is needed to make that happen is:
> >> >    1) make it easy to read/write data and read/write parameter values at any time from R without otherwise modifying the state/adaptation of the sampler.
> >> >    2) make it easy to read/write the sampler/optimizer tuning parameters from R without modifying the rest of the object, redoing adaptation, etc...
> >> >
> >> > Argument:
> >> > - Stan can do a lot but it can't do everything.
> >> > - R is frustrating at times but it's a good glue language for statistical analysis because everyone feels obliged to implement interfaces there.
> >> > - I acknowledge that it is sometimes necessary to re-do the adaptation but of the many ways you give users to shoot themselves in the foot this would not be the worst.
> >> > - Right now when I do an analysis I have to ask myself whether it's easier better to write my own code OR use Stan, I would like to be able to make that an "AND".
> >> > - This would provide a path for people outside of the Stan team to show that certain algorithms/functionality are relevant for Stan without writing Stan-compatible C++ code.
> >> > - Working through R would be relatively slow but in my experience most of the wait time is due to autocorrelation caused by the model/data rather than the speed of the algorithm.
> >> >
> >> > Not my first time pitching this one but thought I'd give it another try...
> >> >
> >> > Krzysztof
> >> >
> >> >
> >> >
> >> > Sebastian's "trick" is exploiting Stan's dynamic scope to
> >> > read a global variable in the body of a function.  Perhaps not
> >> > the safest programming style, but then I'm not a huge fan of
> >> > this kind of scoping.
> >> >
> >> > But R is nothing if not flexible.  Maybe you'd be happier with
> >> > a functional programming solution --- take the data as an argument
> >> > to a "factory" function that creates the init function.  For example,
> >> >
> >> >   init_fun_factory <- function(stan_data) {
> >> >     return(function() { list(randomEffect=rnorm(stan_data$J,0,0.5)); }
> >> >   }
> >> >
> >> > and then call with
> >> >
> >> >   stan("mymodel.stan", data=stan_data, init=init_fun_factory(stan_data));
> >> >
> >> > Here's a simple example of how the idea works outside the context
> >> > of Stan:
> >> >
> >> >   > factory <- function(data) return(function() { return(data$alpha); })
> >> >
> >> >   > data <- list(alpha=10)
> >> >
> >> >   > alpha
> >> >   Error: object 'alpha' not found
> >> >
> >> >    > init_fun <- factory(data)
> >> >
> >> >    > init_fun()
> >> >    [1] 10
> >> >
> >> > You can also just use factory(data)() to get 10.
> >> >
> >> > Was there something you were suggesting we add to rstan?
> >> >
> >> > - Bob
> >> >
> >> >
> >> > On Jul 9, 2014, at 11:43 AM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:
> >> >
> >> > > Hi!
> >> > >
> >> > > I am regurlary handling models where I need to know during initialization the number of groups which are fitted in my hierachical model. This is needed to seed the random effects defined in the model for the individual units. For that to work out the init functions needs to figure some things out about the data which I solve right now like this
> >> > >
> >> > > attach(stan_data)
> >> > > stan("mymodel.stan", data=stan_data, init=myinitFunction)
> >> > > detach(stan_data)
> >> > >
> >> > > Assume now that stan_data$J <- 20 is the number of individual units over which random effects are defined. Then the init function should look like
> >> > >
> >> > > myinitFunction <- function() { list(randomEffect=rnorm(J,0,0.5)) }
> >> > >
> >> > > My trick with attach works, but I would certainly consider this as a hack. So if someone else finds this useful, I would like to request that the data is made available to the myinitFunction when this function is called.
> >> > >
> >> > > I hope this is not to confused - I am happy to work out a minimal example which even works.
> >> > >
> >> > > Best,
> >> > >
> >> > > Sebastian

messages.body_plain:
RStan saves the samples directly to an R vector.  So I don't think
there is much to be improved.  Also there is not reshaping for the final fit object, so there is no extra overload.

But if rstan is unexpected slow for a model with not many parameters, we should take a look and see if there are places that can be proved.  So please let us know such specific cases.

Jiqiang

> > > Krzysztof
> > >
> > >
> > > On Jul 9, 2014, at 10:57 PM, Krzysztof Sakrejda <krzysztof...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > >> Thank you for taking the time to rewrite and explain where things are at.

> > >>
> > >> Krzysztof
> > >>
> > >> On Wednesday, July 9, 2014 4:07:56 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > >> Let me rewrite your request following Andrew's (and hence
> > >> Stan's) notation.
> > >>
> > >> You have parameters theta = (alpha,beta) and data y and
> > >> you want to sample from a posterior p(alpha,beta | y)
> > >> by doing something Gibbs-like in sampling p(alpha | beta, y)
> > >> in Stan and p(beta | alpha, y) in some other program.
> > >>
> > >> Fair enough --- we'd love to make that easy to do.  In fact,
> > >> it was part of our rejected DARPA probabilistic programming
> > >> proposal.
> > >>
> > >> I think we'll be adding just about everything you'll need in
> > >> the next version (more below).
> > >>
> > >> WARNING:  I think this is what you meant below about adaptation,
> > >> but for everyone else's sake:  because beta now looks like "data" to
> > >> Stan (even though it's a parameter of the bigger system), every time beta
> > >> changes, it changes the posterior from which Stan is trying to sample.
> > >> This is an issue because our adaptation assumes that we're
> > >> only trying to adapt to a single posterior.
> > >>
> > >> In R, we are going to be breaking the stan() command down and exposing
> > >> some more primitive operations:
> > >>
> > >>   * compiling a model:  translates model from Stan to C++ and compiles
> > >>     a dynamically linkable library, but doesn't instantiate any instances
> > >>     of the model
> > >>
> > >>   * create a model object with data: populate a compiled model with data,
> > >>     creating a C++ class instance corresponding to the model using the shared object
> > >>     code
> > >>
> > >> We also want to be able to specify all the inputs and outputs including
> > >> adaptation, so that you can
> > >>
> > >>   * extract (and then potentially save) current adaptation parameters
> > >>
> > >>   * start a sampler with given adaptation parameters
> > >>
> > >> Most of the time in our algorithm is spent computing gradients.
> > >> The faster that goes, the faster everything goes.  If the adaptation
> > >> gets messed up, you'll have to intentionally slow everything down by
> > >> forcing a very small step size, which can deal with different situations.
> > >>
> > >> The fact that interpreted R is snail slow isn't usually a problem if
> > >> you're just calling other functions that do the heavy lifting.  But
> > >> you may find it prohibitive if you're in a tight loop doing a lot of
> > >> computation using R.  But then if you have a good general technique
> > >> prototyped in R, it's usually pretty straightforward to move it to
> > >> something faster like C, C++, Fortran, or Java.
> > >>
> > >> - Bob
> > >>
> > >>

> > >> >    1) make it easy to read/write data and read/write parameter values at any time from R without otherwise modifying the state/adaptation of the sampler.
> > >> >    2) make it easy to read/write the sampler/optimizer tuning parameters from R without modifying the rest of the object, redoing adaptation, etc...
> > >> >
> > >> > Argument:
> > >> > - Stan can do a lot but it can't do everything.
> > >> > - R is frustrating at times but it's a good glue language for statistical analysis because everyone feels obliged to implement interfaces there.
> > >> > - I acknowledge that it is sometimes necessary to re-do the adaptation but of the many ways you give users to shoot themselves in the foot this would not be the worst.
> > >> > - Right now when I do an analysis I have to ask myself whether it's easier better to write my own code OR use Stan, I would like to be able to make that an "AND".
> > >> > - This would provide a path for people outside of the Stan team to show that certain algorithms/functionality are relevant for Stan without writing Stan-compatible C++ code.
> > >> > - Working through R would be relatively slow but in my experience most of the wait time is due to autocorrelation caused by the model/data rather than the speed of the algorithm.
> > >> >
> > >> > Not my first time pitching this one but thought I'd give it another try...

> > >> > Krzysztof
> > >> >

> > >> >
> > >> > Sebastian's "trick" is exploiting Stan's dynamic scope to
> > >> > read a global variable in the body of a function.  Perhaps not
> > >> > the safest programming style, but then I'm not a huge fan of
> > >> > this kind of scoping.
> > >> >

> > >> > a functional programming solution --- take the data as an argument
> > >> > to a "factory" function that creates the init function.  For example,
> > >> >
> > >> >   init_fun_factory <- function(stan_data) {
> > >> >     return(function() { list(randomEffect=rnorm(stan_data$J,0,0.5)); }
> > >> >   }
> > >> >
> > >> > and then call with
> > >> >
> > >> >   stan("mymodel.stan", data=stan_data, init=init_fun_factory(stan_data));
> > >> >
> > >> > Here's a simple example of how the idea works outside the context
> > >> > of Stan:
> > >> >
> > >> >   > factory <- function(data) return(function() { return(data$alpha); })
> > >> >
> > >> >   > data <- list(alpha=10)
> > >> >
> > >> >   > alpha
> > >> >   Error: object 'alpha' not found
> > >> >
> > >> >    > init_fun <- factory(data)
> > >> >
> > >> >    > init_fun()
> > >> >    [1] 10
> > >> >
> > >> > You can also just use factory(data)() to get 10.
> > >> >
> > >> > Was there something you were suggesting we add to rstan?
> > >> >
> > >> > - Bob
> > >> >
> > >> >
> > >> > On Jul 9, 2014, at 11:43 AM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >> >
> > >> > > Hi!

> > >> > > I am regurlary handling models where I need to know during initialization the number of groups which are fitted in my hierachical model. This is needed to seed the random effects defined in the model for the individual units. For that to work out the init functions needs to figure some things out about the data which I solve right now like this
> > >> > >
> > >> > > attach(stan_data)
> > >> > > stan("mymodel.stan", data=stan_data, init=myinitFunction)
> > >> > > detach(stan_data)
> > >> > >
> > >> > > Assume now that stan_data$J <- 20 is the number of individual units over which random effects are defined. Then the init function should look like
> > >> > >
> > >> > > myinitFunction <- function() { list(randomEffect=rnorm(J,0,0.5)) }
> > >> > >
> > >> > > My trick with attach works, but I would certainly consider this as a hack. So if someone else finds this useful, I would like to request that the data is made available to the myinitFunction when this function is called.
> > >> > >
> > >> > > I hope this is not to confused - I am happy to work out a minimal example which even works.
> > >> > >
> > >> > > Best,

messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

The issue is:

no matches for function name="normal_log"
    arg 0 type=real[2]
    arg 1 type=int
    arg 2 type=real

For the left hand side of this expression:

alpha ~ normal(0,sigma_alpha);

you have alpha defined as:

real alpha[J,T];               // transparency for j,t - mean

If you want to use alpha as is, you'll need to replace "alpha ~ normal(0, sigma_alpha);" with:
    for (j in 1:J)
      for (t in 1:T)
        alpha[j, t] ~ normal(0, sigma_alpha);

or
    for (j in 1:J)
       alpha[j] ~ normal(0, sigma_alpha);

The second one uses the vectorized form for the left side.

So... the message is telling you that Stan doesn't have the normal distribution defined for a 2-d array of reals. We need to add better error messages, but that's how to interpret "arg 0 type=real[2]".

Daniel

> may work? 0 is considered as an integer whereas 0.0 as considered as real.
>
> The error massage is sufficient for this case. I guess it is difficult for non C++ people to understand... :(

If there's ever a place where 0.0 works but 0 doesn't,
that's a bug and we'd appreciate hearing about it.
C++ doesn't have this problem with non-templated
functions, because int can be promoted to double.  Ditto
for Java and C.  But in C++ templates, it's possible to
specialize so that there's a definition for double inputs
but not int inputs;  and if the templates can't resolve,
no go.

The problem here, as Daniel pointed out, is that the
normal_log function doesn't accept real[2] (i.e., 2D
array of real) arguments.

I want to replace the error output "real[2]" with
"real[,]" because that's what we're using in the function
syntax and I think it'll be clearer than just reporting the
number of arguments as we currently do:

> no matches for function name="normal_log"
>     arg 0 type=real[2]
>     arg 1 type=int
>     arg 2 type=real

- Bob

messages.subject: (r)stan slow with model generating data
messages.subject_clean: (r)stan slow with model generating data
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

I am using Stan to perform some simulations via the generated quantities block. I noticed that there is a severe performance hit if the output I request gets large. Attached is a minimal example which exemplifies the problem.

I am not sure if the issue is on the stan or rstan side. In any case, the more data I let stan generate, the longer the startup of Stan and the longer it takes to return the data to R. Of course, more data takes longer, but from watch the example yourself.

To give you a rough number: It takes more than 4 minutes to get 1e6 samples from a normal 0,1 from stan (the model is pre-compiled).

Best,
Sebastian

On Friday, July 11, 2014 10:33:28 AM UTC-4, Sebastian Weber wrote:
> Hi Ben!
>
> If I run as.array(fit), then I the sampler parameters are not part of the output (also the permuted argument seems broken):
>
> R3.0.2> aa <- as.array(f$fit, permuted=FALSE)
> Error in .local(object, ...) :
>   formal argument "permuted" matched by multiple actual arguments

The as.array() method hard-codes permuted=FALSE, so it generates an error if you try to pass it

> rstan:::as.array.stanfit
function (x, ...)
{
    if (x@mode != 0)
        return(numeric(0))
    out <- extract(x, permuted = FALSE, inc_warmup = FALSE, ...)
    return(out)
}
<environment: namespace:rstan>

but I see now that doesn't produce the stuff that you want.

> Moreover, I noticed that monitor does not like everything I give it:
> eight <- stan_demo("eight_schools", chains=1)
> print(eight)
> check_sampler(eight)
>
> The array is correctly formatted, but monitor in check_sampler gets confused for reasons I don't get.

In many cases, n_divergent is always zero and thus it throws an error when trying to inflate the variance. We'll fix that, but for now you could do

check_sampler <- function(fit, ...) {
  sp <- get_sampler_params(fit, inc_warmup=FALSE)
  spa <- do.call(abind, c(list(along=-1), sp))
  spa <- aperm(spa, c(2,1,3))

  spa <- spa[,,apply(spa, 3, sd) > 0, drop = FALSE]
  monitor(spa, warmup=0, ...)
}

Ben

It's not on our short-term schedule and we don't have
much of a long-term schedule.

This could actually be a nice standalone project.  It depends
on Stan, but nothing in Stan should need to be changed to
get it all going.  It'd be a wrapper.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: Problem setting up Hierarchical IRT model with 'student' and 'test' levels
messages.body_plain:
You can probably continue to vectorize.
I'm not sure what your data types are, though.

If alpha[j,t] is a scalar, then it might help to
transpose alpha and use alpha_t[t,j], at which

point you could write:

  for (t in 1:T)

    alpha_t[t] ~ normal(alpha_t[t-1], sigma_alpha);

You'd also be able to write just

   alpha_t[1] ~ normal(0, sigma_alpha);

Even better if you declare alpha_t as an array of vectors.
There's a chapter in the manual now on arrays versus
vectors and speed and where they are required.

This can be a really big speedup if J >> 1.

- Bob

On Jul 11, 2014, at 5:01 AM, Christopher Gandrud <christoph...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Thanks! This discussion has been really useful. It's really helping me convert my IRT models to Stan from Jags (so far I've definitely had the advertised convergence speed improvements).
>
> This worked perfectly:
>
> for (j in 1:J)
>     for (t in 1:T)
>         alpha[j,t] ~ normal(0, sigma_alpha);
>
> FYI for anyone else that might be interested: I've updated the priors slightly such that at time 1 alpha[j,t] ~ normal(0, sigma_alpha), but then for all t_1+n the previous year's alpha informs the prior for the following year, i.e.
>
> for (j in 1:J)
>     alpha[j,1] ~ normal(0, sigma_alpha);
> for (j in 1:J)
>     for (t in 2:T)
>         alpha[j,t] ~ normal(alpha[j,t-1], sigma_alpha);
>
> Any thoughts on further tweaks would be of course be welcome.
>
>

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] (r)stan slow with model generating data
messages.body_plain:
It's not going to be on the Stan C++ side because Stan just
iterates the sample independently in a streaming fashion (it's
implemented like an iterator underneath) and has no idea how
many draws it's going to be asked to make ahead of time.

If you're just simulating, you should turn off warmup if you
haven't already.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
On Jul 11, 2014, at 5:48 PM, Dora Zhou <zhou...@gmail.com> wrote:

> If my understanding of "increment_log_prob" function is right, we should be able to write the model block by specifying the log likelihood distribution log[ f(y|theta) ] in replace of the tilde version: y~ some defined distribution.

Correct --- as we try to make clear in the manual, the y ~ notation
is just a shorthand for increment_log_prob (and it also drops constants).

> It would be very helpful if the distribution is complex or not fully built in Stan.

That's the use case we give in the chapter on user-defined distributions :-)

>
> For my project, I have a likelihood which is a little bit complicated. R code is as follows:
>
> ff1 <- function(Y.fail,Kamp.fail,Y.cen,Kamp.cen,beta) {
> b0 <-beta[1]
> b1 <-beta[2]
> s <-exp(beta[3])
> mu <-exp(beta[4])
> ss<-exp(beta[5])
> int=function(ii){
> b=function(b){
> u=b0+b1*log(Kamp.fail[ii]-b)
> Z1=dnorm(Y.fail[ii],mean=u,sd=s)*dweibull(b,scale=mu,shape=ss)
> return(Z1)
> }
> return(integrate(b,lower = 0, upper =Kamp.fail[ii],stop.on.error=F)$value)
> }
> int.cen=function(ii){
> b=function(b){
> u=b0+b1*log(Kamp.cen[ii]-b)
> Z1=pnorm(Y.cen[ii],mean=u,sd=s)*dweibull(b,scale=mu,shape=ss)
> return(Z1)
> }
> return(1-integrate(b,lower = 0, upper =Kamp.cen[ii],stop.on.error=F)$value)
> }
>
> log.l=sum(log(vapply(X=1:N.fail,int,FUN.VALUE=0)))+sum(log(vapply(X=1:N.cen,int.cen,FUN.VALUE=0)))
> return(-log.l)
> }
>
> It has "sum" function and "integrate" function.

Stan has a sum() function, but not integrate().

> Since Stan doesn't "integrate" function at this point, I can use other code ( by summing up hundreds of small pieces) to realize it.

Now that gets complicated to code.  The main issue is whether
Stan's automatically calculated derivatives will do the right
thing.

> I found that in User Manual 2.3, section 15, page 107, we can create user-defined functions, and put the function as a separate block in Stan code.
>
> My question is, can I define a function which returns the log likelihood log[ f(y|theta) ], and then put it into the model block as increment_log_prob( log[ f(y|theta) ] )  ?

Yes.  You can also define your own densities and use
them with ~.  The manual has examples.

Warning:  we're still working out some kinks in the functions
and they don't recompile in R yet and there are some issues
with namespaces and voids and things being cleaned up.

> How can I put the user_defined function into the model block?

It'll work just like a built-in function.

> As a simple example:
>
> functions {
> real user_defined(real mu, real<lower=0> sigma, real x) {
> y <- -log(sigma)- square(x-mu)/(2*square(sigma));
> return y;
> }
> }
> ...
> model {
> increment_log_prob(user_defined(mu, sigma, x));  // I don't think it works, but want to know how to do it
> }
>
> I don't think it works, but want to know how to use the user defined function. Do we have examples that include user defined questions?

Yes, the above will work.

There aren't examples yet with user-defined functions.

If you had declared "user_defined" as "user_defined_log" then
you could've written the model as:

  mu ~ user_defined(sigma,x);

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] The future of DAGs in Stan
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] The future of DAGs in Stan
messages.body_plain:
Cool.  We totally have to check that out.

For functionality:

1.  Basically, the whole BUGS/JAGS language.  Ideally,
something that would translate models in both of those
languages!

2.  Something that would take in the data for the model,
figure out which values are "missing" and create a model
where the missing data are considered parameters and then
glue everything back together.  I'm not even sure how
BUGS does this in terms of returns, since the missing data
can be part of bigger structures (at least in some cases).

3.  Something that could compute the Markov blanket for
discrete parameters so that we could do discrete sampling
with Gibbs.  This is a wide-open research area in terms of
how this will interact with HMC and how adaptation would work.

4.  Whatever Andrew wants for model comparison, data simulation
and posterior predictive checks. Looks like you're a long way
down that road already.

For compatibility:

1. We want everything we build for Stan to work in
CmdStan and PyStan as well as RStan.  So we couldn't
have dependencies to R or anything else that's not
BSD-compatibly licensed (specifically, no GPL).

- Bob

P.S.  We're also interested in something similar for the
R expression language --- I know you've worked on that before,
too.  We're working on implementing uncertainty estimation for
MLE and also doing marginal maximum likelihood.  There are still
some issues in how we take uncertainty back from the unconstrained
parameters to the constrained --- the best idea so far is to
use the normal approximation to generate samples around the mode
then transform back to the constrained space.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Can't install Rstan 2.3 [Cygwin/Rtools issues]
messages.body_plain:
Yes, that's how it should look, with Rtools\bin before cyginwin64\bin.

That's been the problem before with users with Cygwin installed
on Windows.

There are instructions for compiling RStan under Cygwin in the
CmdStan manual (those need to move to the RStan doc):

  https://github.com/stan-dev/cmdstan/releases/download/v2.3.0/cmdstan-guide-2.3.0.pdf

These are for 64-bit R and 64-bit Cygwin
==================================================================

	• Kill all Cygwin bash shells and shut down R.

	• After installing R and Rtools, make sure that R and Rtools are in the PATH environment variable. My R installation directory was c:\Program Files\R\R-3.0.1 and my Rtools installation directory was c:\Rtools, so I added the following to the end of my user PATH variable:

• C:\Program Files\R\R-3.0.1\bin\x64
• C:\Rtools\bin
• C:\Rtools\gcc-4.6.3\bin

	• Now there could be a conflict between Cygwin and Rtools when running a bash shell under Cygwin, so I added the following lines to my .bash_profile file to remove any PATH directory referencing Rtools:

     > TMP=`echo $PATH | /usr/bin/tr ':' '\n'                      \
                       | /usr/bin/egrep -iv '^/cygdrive/c/Rtools/' \

| tr '\n' ':'`

     > PATH=${TMP%:}

(Note that the backslash characters signal that the line continues after a return.) This was only necessary to allow me to continue using Cygwin.

	• Apparently there is something in Rcpp or inline or rstan that doesn’t like UNC paths. My home directory was \\server\users\kevinv and apparently this caused my local R library directory to be \server\users\kevinv\R as verified by .libPaths() from the R command prompt.

I fixed this by copying the entire directory tree rooted at \server\users\kevinv\R over to a local directory on my worksta- tion, C:\Users\KevinV\R, then adding the user environment variable R_LIBS_USER=C:\Users\KevinV\R. I shut down R and restarted it.

	• At this point the instructions given for installing Rstan finally worked.

==========================end outtake===============================

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] confusion on categorical distribution [explanation of expression type system]
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] confusion on categorical distribution [explanation of expression type system]
messages.body_plain:
Short Answer:

  The types of expressions, function arguments, and right-hand
  sides of assignments do not involve constraints.

  This is just a general feature of the language, and nothing to
  do with the categorical distribution.  It's discussed at length
  in the manual, but I'd like to make it clearer for you and everyone
  else if it's confusing.

Long Answer (with embedded Stan syntax tutorial presented computer
science style):

An EXPRESSION is something that has a value, like "1.2" or
"log(x)" or "x[i] * beta".

A STATEMENT is something that can be executed, like an assignment
statement or a log-prob increment statement.  Statements can
be primitive, as in a simple assignment statement "x <- 3;" or they
can be made up of other statements, as in
"for (n in 1:N) y[n] ~ normal(mu,sigma)".

Each expression in Stan has a unique type that does not change as
the program is run --- that is, Stan is STATICALLY TYPED (compile time)
rather than DYNAMICALLY TYPED (run time).

Now here's the key to your question.

  STAN'S EXPRESSION TYPES DO NOT INVOLVE CONSTRAINTS

An expression type can be a basic type:

  primitive:  int, real

  matrix:     matrix, vector, row_vector

or it can be an array type built out of another expression
type,

  array:      T[], where T is any expression type

Note that the way I wrote these without sizes is not accidental,
because as well as not involving constraints,

  EXPRESSION TYPES DO NOT INVOLVE SIZES.

That is, if I declare a variable as matrix[M,N], the sizes M and N are
not part of the expression type.  Sizes are determined only after data
is read in.  For example, the data can determine the value of M and N
in the matrix declaration above.

Now here's how the type of an expression is calculated.

The types of LITERALS, such as "1" and "10.378e-3" are
determined by whether they have a period or "e" or not ("13"
is an int, whereas "1e-3" and "1.3" are real).

The types of VARIABLES are determined by their DECLARATIONS,
but IGNORING CONSTRAINTS AND SIZES.  For example, a variable declared
as "real mu;"  has the expression type real, as does
a variable declared as "real<lower=0> sigma;".  An array
declared as "real x[N];" has type real[].  The fact that it
is an array is part of its type.
A variable declared with "matrix[M,N] A;" has type matrix,
as does a variable declared as "cov_matrix[K] Sigma;".

The types of other expressions, such as those built
from functions, "exp(sigma_raw)", arithmetic operators ("2 * beta"),
or indexing ("x[i]"), are determined by the rules of the language
(more on that below).

Each function specifies what is known as a SIGNATURE, which
is the type of its arguments and the type of its result.  Some
functions are OVERLOADED so that they have more than one signature.
For example, the exp() function has four signatures in Stan:

   real exp(real);
   vector exp(vector);
   row_vector exp(row_vector);
   real[] exp(row_vector[]);

The signatures for each function are listed in the index.
This allows us to validate argument types at compile time and
also determine what the type of any function application is (it
is illegal to have two functions with the same argument types
and different result types).

Stan is not like BUGS, which I believe restricts some arguments
to be variables rather than general expressions (I don't think
JAGS has this restriction anywhere).  In Stan, the argument
to a function or the right-hand side of an assignment can always
be any expression of the appropriate expression type.  The function
will validate that its argument is appropriate and essentially
return -infinity and print a warning message if its fed an argument whose value
violates the requirements on function arguments (technically it's
raising an exception at the C++ which is caught by an optimizer
or sampler).

Constraints are used for only two purposes:

  1.  Defining the transform (and associated Jacobian) from
      the constrained parameter to unconstrained.

  2.  Providing error checking and validation.
      a.  As each data variable is read in, its constraint is validated.
      b.  At the end of the transformed data, transformed parameters and
          generated quantities block, the constraint is validated for
          each variable declared in that block.

One of the reasons for this design is to allow intermediate
values for constrained types that do not satisfy the constraint.
As in:

   cov_matrix[K] Sigma; // at this point, no value at all
   for (m in 1:K)
     for (n in 1:K)
       Sigma[m,n] <- sigma[m] * sigma[n] * Omega[m,n];

During the loop, Sigma does not remain symmetric and positive definite.
That's why we only validate constraints at the end of blocks.

Sooooo, how do you think I should try to make this all clearer?  It's
explained in pretty much the above terms in the section on
expressions and assignment and functions in the language reference
for the manual.

A big issue in refactoring the manual, which we want to do soon,
is pulling more of these descriptions of how the language works out
of the language reference section and describing them with less
technical language and lots of examples.

One issue I see is that most probability functions we have require
a constrained argument, even normal(mu,sigma), which requires
a sigma with a lower bound of 0.  Nothing anywhere in Stan requires
an argument to a function (or the right-hand side of an assignment)
to be a variable of constrained type.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Welcome to the club of users bothered by that message.

Yes, the constraint says lower=0, but the problem is
that we're dealing with limited-precision (64-bit
double precision, to be specific) floating point numbers,
and they don't behave like continuous quantities.

The transform we use is exp() to map the unconstrained
parameters back to positive parameters.  If x < -800 or so,
exp(x) = 0.  It underflows to 0 use more precise terminology.
To illustrate in R, consider:

> log(exp(-800))
[1] -Inf

Hmm.  Shouldn't that be -800?  No, because exp(-800) underflows to 0
and log(0) is -Inf.

Have you been following the umpteen discussions on these
messages we've had?  Most recently last week?

Do you have an opinion as to what we should do about the messages?
The behavior's pretty much built into floating point unless we change
the transform we use.

The current plan (in my mind at least) is to remove any hint of
the words "error" or "warning" and point users to a longer discussion
in the manual of what's going on with floating point and ill-conditioned
posteriors.

As to making the non-centered parameterization (formerly known as
the matt trick) built in, maybe we could define a density directly for
it and save the user doing anything at all.  I'll have to think about it,
and while waiting for lunch is perhaps not the best time for that...

- Bob

On Jul 12, 2014, at 6:40 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

> Short Answer:
>
>  The types of expressions, function arguments, and right-hand
>  sides of assignments do not involve constraints.
>
>  This is just a general feature of the language, and nothing to
>  do with the categorical distribution.  It's discussed at length
>  in the manual, but I'd like to make it clearer for you and everyone
>  else if it's confusing.
>
> Long Answer (with embedded Stan syntax tutorial presented computer
> science style):
>
> An EXPRESSION is something that has a value, like "1.2" or
> "log(x)" or "x[i] * beta".
>
> A STATEMENT is something that can be executed, like an assignment
> statement or a log-prob increment statement.  Statements can
> be primitive, as in a simple assignment statement "x <- 3;" or they
> can be made up of other statements, as in
> "for (n in 1:N) y[n] ~ normal(mu,sigma)".
>
> Each expression in Stan has a unique type that does not change as
> the program is run --- that is, Stan is STATICALLY TYPED (compile time)
> rather than DYNAMICALLY TYPED (run time).
>
> Now here's the key to your question.
>
>  STAN'S EXPRESSION TYPES DO NOT INVOLVE CONSTRAINTS
>
> An expression type can be a basic type:
>
>  primitive:  int, real
>
>  matrix:     matrix, vector, row_vector
>
> or it can be an array type built out of another expression
> type,
>
>  array:      T[], where T is any expression type
>
> Note that the way I wrote these without sizes is not accidental,
> because as well as not involving constraints,
>
>  EXPRESSION TYPES DO NOT INVOLVE SIZES.
>
> That is, if I declare a variable as matrix[M,N], the sizes M and N are
> not part of the expression type.  Sizes are determined only after data
> is read in.  For example, the data can determine the value of M and N
> in the matrix declaration above.
>
> Now here's how the type of an expression is calculated.
>
> The types of LITERALS, such as "1" and "10.378e-3" are
> determined by whether they have a period or "e" or not ("13"
> is an int, whereas "1e-3" and "1.3" are real).
>
> The types of VARIABLES are determined by their DECLARATIONS,
> but IGNORING CONSTRAINTS AND SIZES.  For example, a variable declared
> as "real mu;"  has the expression type real, as does
> a variable declared as "real<lower=0> sigma;".  An array
> declared as "real x[N];" has type real[].  The fact that it
> is an array is part of its type.
> A variable declared with "matrix[M,N] A;" has type matrix,
> as does a variable declared as "cov_matrix[K] Sigma;".
>
> The types of other expressions, such as those built
> from functions, "exp(sigma_raw)", arithmetic operators ("2 * beta"),
> or indexing ("x[i]"), are determined by the rules of the language
> (more on that below).
>
> Each function specifies what is known as a SIGNATURE, which
> is the type of its arguments and the type of its result.  Some
> functions are OVERLOADED so that they have more than one signature.
> For example, the exp() function has four signatures in Stan:
>
>   real exp(real);
>   vector exp(vector);
>   row_vector exp(row_vector);
>   real[] exp(row_vector[]);
>
> The signatures for each function are listed in the index.
> This allows us to validate argument types at compile time and
> also determine what the type of any function application is (it
> is illegal to have two functions with the same argument types
> and different result types).
>
> Stan is not like BUGS, which I believe restricts some arguments
> to be variables rather than general expressions (I don't think
> JAGS has this restriction anywhere).  In Stan, the argument
> to a function or the right-hand side of an assignment can always
> be any expression of the appropriate expression type.  The function
> will validate that its argument is appropriate and essentially
> return -infinity and print a warning message if its fed an argument whose value
> violates the requirements on function arguments (technically it's
> raising an exception at the C++ which is caught by an optimizer
> or sampler).
>
> Constraints are used for only two purposes:
>
>  1.  Defining the transform (and associated Jacobian) from
>      the constrained parameter to unconstrained.
>
>  2.  Providing error checking and validation.
>      a.  As each data variable is read in, its constraint is validated.
>      b.  At the end of the transformed data, transformed parameters and
>          generated quantities block, the constraint is validated for
>          each variable declared in that block.
>
> One of the reasons for this design is to allow intermediate
> values for constrained types that do not satisfy the constraint.
> As in:
>
>   cov_matrix[K] Sigma; // at this point, no value at all
>   for (m in 1:K)
>     for (n in 1:K)
>       Sigma[m,n] <- sigma[m] * sigma[n] * Omega[m,n];
>
> During the loop, Sigma does not remain symmetric and positive definite.
> That's why we only validate constraints at the end of blocks.
>
> Sooooo, how do you think I should try to make this all clearer?  It's
> explained in pretty much the above terms in the section on
> expressions and assignment and functions in the language reference
> for the manual.
>
> A big issue in refactoring the manual, which we want to do soon,
> is pulling more of these descriptions of how the language works out
> of the language reference section and describing them with less
> technical language and lots of examples.
>
> One issue I see is that most probability functions we have require
> a constrained argument, even normal(mu,sigma), which requires
> a sigma with a lower bound of 0.  Nothing anywhere in Stan requires
> an argument to a function (or the right-hand side of an assignment)
> to be a variable of constrained type.
>
> - Bob
>
>
> On Jul 12, 2014, at 5:48 AM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>
>> Hi, I was confused.  In the description of the categorical distribution (model, page 278, it says that theta is a simplex.  But in the example on page 29-30, theta is a vector  that just happens to sum to 1 (that is, it's not a "simplex" variable type).  I ask because I'm using the categorical distribution but was struggling to get its input into a "simplex" form.  So I think we need to fix the description of the categorical distribution in the model to make clear that it does not require a simplex variable type.
>>

messages.body_plain:
It's really simple!

Most programming languages work this way, so there
are only a few details that differentiate Stan from
say, C++, in terms of how types work.

One thing I didn't go into was promotion, which lets
you assign an int to a real.  I'd like to make this fully
covariant for containers.  What that means is that if you can
assign the elements of one container to the elements of the other,
then you can assign the container.  That would let you everywhere
assign an int array to a real array, use an int array as an
argument to normal, and so on.  And similarly for argument
passing, because argument passing is really just a kind of
assignment.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Stan crashing R or Python?
messages.body_plain:
Have you noticed at what point the crashes happen?  During
model compilation, during sampling, or after sampling's done?

I take it you're using the the script from Sebastian to try to
reuse compiled Stan programs?  Across R sessions?  I have no idea
what assumptions that technique is making, but it's a big difference
between how you're using Stan and everyone other than Sebastian is
using it.

I run everything from script files.  It's the only way
I can keep track of what I've done and have any hope of
reproducing it later.

Really, R should be restarted all the time because people
and packages tend to use global variables which linger and
can make scripts non-standalone if they're run assuming
some context that isn't there when R starts.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
The key points are:

  * every variable needs to be defined before if is used
  * data, transformed data, parameters, and transformed parameters
    variables are automatically defined before the model block
    is executed

We need to rename "sampling statement" to something more like
"distribution log probability increment statement" to make it
a bit clearer that it doesn't literally do sampling of the left-hand
side variable from the right-hand side distribution.

Having said that, I prefer the style where the priors come before
the likelihood if your model's programmed in terms of priors and
likelihood.

- Bob

On Friday, July 11, 2014 5:42:08 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> It looks like that R function does multiple integrals and
> uses QUADPACK under the hood.  Just today, someone was suggesting
> porting QUADPACK to Eigen (we use Eigen for linear algebra
> in Stan).
>

Bob, I don't know if it matters, but `integrate <http://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-patched/library/stats/html/integrate.html>` in R does one-dimensional integration), and it is based on QUADPACK. The only package I know of that does multivariate integration of some sort is `cubature <http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/cubature/index.html>` (by Steve Johnson of NLOPT fame) and that uses bespoke C routines, I think.

Avi

messages.subject: Initialization problems (possibly due to indexing?)
messages.subject_clean: Initialization problems (possibly due to indexing?)
messages.body_plain:
Hi dear Stan Developers and users,

Thank you for writing such an excellent software! Apart from being fast, it's usually a pleasure to debug (not a statement I tend to write often)
I am currently trying to implement a hierarchical model to estimate parameters for test kinetics from repeated measurement data. I've managed to write it up so that it compiles, and managed to get a previous
version running and more-or-less converging. Because of missing some observations, I've now had to change from using a wide format, with one column per observation, to a long format, with one row per observation,and therefore had to include an indexing vector to keep track of which individual a particular observation is from.
When trying to run this model, I'm getting the error

"Error : Rejecting user-specified initialization because of vanishing density.
error occurred during calling the sampler; sampling not done"

>From looking over the mailing list archives, this problem seems similar to that reported by Fil Krynecki https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/stan-users/Rejecting$20user-specified$20initialization/stan-users/QnxFhV9RViE/8APcQn51HBQJ , but there's no solution in that thread.

 I've attached the moderately complex model file. The error is the same whether using init="random", init="0", or using the following initial conditions:

my.inits<-list(
  theta2IgLogmu=log(matrix(rep(c(Xstar=0.15,D=100,a=0.01,S=0.05),each=3),nrow=3)),
  theta1IgLogmu=log(aperm(array(rep(matrix(rep(c(Xstar=0.15,D=100,a=0.01,S=0.05),each=3),nrow=3),
                       N),dim=c(3,4,N)),c(3,1,2))),
  igCorr=aperm(array(rep(diag(4)+(1-diag(4))*0.0001,3),dim=c(4,4,3)),c(3,2,1)),
  igTau=array(rep(rep(1,4),3),dim=c(3,4)),
  omegaCorr=diag(3)+(1-diag(3))*0.0001,
  tau=rep(1,3)*1.5
  )

These conditions seems reasonably close to the real values when comparing to the data.
Any insight and/or suggestion in further bug tracking would be much appreciated!

Best regards,
Gustaf Rydevik

messages.subject: Comparison Operators in Stan do not take a vector, but only integers?
messages.subject_clean: Comparison Operators in Stan do not take a vector, but only integers?
messages.body_plain:
Dear Stan experts

I am trying to vectorize a non-linear Bayesian continuous(!) change point model using an indicator function for a linear spline, but it seems the "Comparison Operators" in Stan do not take a vector, (but only integers/reals):

In my model, y is the outcome, x1 are time points, tau are change points, all are vectors (continuous), beta is a scalar to be estimated:

y~ normal ( intercept...
   + ( (x1 <= tau ) * ( beta  * x1 ) )
                                                 ^-- here

DIAGNOSTIC(S) FROM PARSER:
binary infix operator < with functional interpretation logical_lte requires arguments or primitive type (int or real), found left type=vector, right arg type=vector; no matches for function name="logical_lte"

Is there a smart way around this, please?

Thank you very much.
Michael

messages.body_plain:
Robert,

I am thinking about what you mentioned, but I have not verified it.  What rstan does is creating a list of vectors at the beginning of sampling.  The length of the list is the number of parameters and the length of the vector is the total iterations that would be saved.  I got a stack overflow for large number of parameters.  Issue https://github.com/stan-dev/rstan/issues/76 might be due to this as well.

Jiqiang

messages.subject: Re: Initialization problems (possibly due to indexing?)
messages.subject_clean: Initialization problems (possibly due to indexing?)
messages.body_plain:
And a follow-up:
As I was generating some example data to go with this post, I discovered that I had a data point of zero, which generated the error.
Removing the data point solved the problem! My apologies for taking up unnecessary space.
As a comment/suggestion: Is it possible to have boundaries as <lower>0> (or something similar),
as opposed to <lower=0>? That would have caught this error a bit earlier, and it seems like boundary values are in general discouraged anyway.

Best regards,
Gustaf

On Monday, July 14, 2014 3:05:00 PM UTC+1, Gustaf Rydevik wrote:
> Hi dear Stan Developers and users,
>
> Thank you for writing such an excellent software! Apart from being fast, it's usually a pleasure to debug (not a statement I tend to write often)
> I am currently trying to implement a hierarchical model to estimate parameters for test kinetics from repeated measurement data. I've managed to write it up so that it compiles, and managed to get a previous
> version running and more-or-less converging. Because of missing some observations, I've now had to change from using a wide format, with one column per observation, to a long format, with one row per observation,and therefore had to include an indexing vector to keep track of which individual a particular observation is from.
> When trying to run this model, I'm getting the error
>
> "Error : Rejecting user-specified initialization because of vanishing density.
> error occurred during calling the sampler; sampling not done"
>
> From looking over the mailing list archives, this problem seems similar to that reported by Fil Krynecki https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/stan-users/Rejecting$20user-specified$20initialization/stan-users/QnxFhV9RViE/8APcQn51HBQJ , but there's no solution in that thread.
>
>  I've attached the moderately complex model file. The error is the same whether using init="random", init="0", or using the following initial conditions:
>
> my.inits<-list(
>   theta2IgLogmu=log(matrix(rep(c(Xstar=0.15,D=100,a=0.01,S=0.05),each=3),nrow=3)),
>   theta1IgLogmu=log(aperm(array(rep(matrix(rep(c(Xstar=0.15,D=100,a=0.01,S=0.05),each=3),nrow=3),
>                        N),dim=c(3,4,N)),c(3,1,2))),
>   igCorr=aperm(array(rep(diag(4)+(1-diag(4))*0.0001,3),dim=c(4,4,3)),c(3,2,1)),
>   igTau=array(rep(rep(1,4),3),dim=c(3,4)),
>   omegaCorr=diag(3)+(1-diag(3))*0.0001,
>   tau=rep(1,3)*1.5
>   )
>
> These conditions seems reasonably close to the real values when comparing to the data.
> Any insight and/or suggestion in further bug tracking would be much appreciated!
>
> Best regards,
> Gustaf Rydevik

Each data structure has a dimensionality, for instance, both of

  matrix[M,N] a;

  vector[N] a[M];

define an (M x N) structure.  To use Daniel's suggestion, you need
to read the data in transposed.

To just transpose in the model, all you need to replace the declaration

  real alpha[J,T];

with

  matrix[J,T] alpha;

and then define:

  transformed data {
    matrix[T,J] alpha_t;
    alpha_t <- alpha';
  }

even more efficient would be:

  transformed data {
    vector[J] alpha_t[T];

    for (t in 1:T)

      alpha_t[t] <- col(alpha,t);
  }

Then just use alpha_t in the code as suggested earlier.

But I wouldn't worry about any of this if the model's fast
enough without it.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
We're trying to make debugging even better.  I'm going to
take a pass at the parser error messages to try to clean
them up so they're more in user-facing notation and provide
a bit more information when the parser doesn't see the symbol
it's expecting to see.

For constrained continuous values, the bounds are usually
exclusive in practice because of the transforms involved.
We need to make that clearer in the manual for the transforms
and the distributions.

Basically, any time a boundary value for a transform produces an
infinite value, things will break.  This is actually what we
want with

  real<lower=0> sigma;

because we can't make sense of

  y ~ normal(mu,0);

(Yes, we could treat it as a discrete distribution with all its mass
on mu, but that won't work in either HMC or L-BFGS.)

- Bob

On Jul 14, 2014, at 10:12 AM, Michael Andreae <mhan...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Dear Stan experts
>
> I am trying to vectorize a non-linear Bayesian continuous(!) change point model using an indicator function for a linear spline, but it seems the "Comparison Operators" in Stan do not take a vector, (but only integers/reals):
>
> In my model, y is the outcome, x1 are time points, tau are change points, all are vectors (continuous), beta is a scalar to be estimated:
>
> y~ normal ( intercept...
>    + ( (x1 <= tau ) * ( beta  * x1 ) )
>                                                  ^-- here
>
> DIAGNOSTIC(S) FROM PARSER:
> binary infix operator < with functional interpretation logical_lte requires arguments or primitive type (int or real), found left type=vector, right arg type=vector; no matches for function name="logical_lte"
>
> Is there a smart way around this, please?

If by smart way around, you mean a vectorized version of <=, then I'm
afraid the answer is no.  No reason in principle not to vectorize these,
but we haven't gotten around to it.

So what you need to do is define the intercept in a loop, assign
it to an vector mu, and then call y ~ normal(mu, ...);  That'll be
faster than calling y[n] ~ normal(...[n]..., ); in the loop.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi Michael,

A more general point that you might find useful to consider regarding change point models in Stan. Recently, there has been a discussion <https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/QlgX00f6JG8/ZmNUg7rvZEsJ> on the stan user list about change point models and I think the following were the main conclusions:
If the change point is a parameter to be estimated (tau in your case), the derivative of the posterior will be discontinuous wherever tau == [any value of x1 in the data]. This will break the Hamiltonian dynamics and the algorithm will degenerate to a random walk, driven by the random momentum of the Hamiltonian particle. Hamiltonian MC requires the posterior and its first derivative to be continuous everywhere to be able to simulate draws from the posterior.
Prior issue can be theoretically overcome by marginalizing over all possible values of the change point, using a mixture model (see manual for example). So if the data are X = (x1, x2, x3, x4, ...), marginalize over [x1 < tau < x2], [x2 < tau < x3],[x3 < tau < x4], ... Unfortunately, as Michael Betancourt pointed out, the posterior for this model will be multimodal (unless you have relatively precise information about were the change point is), and will prove hard to sample from.
Alternatively, Emmanuel Charpentier proposed a continuous approximation of the step function x1 <= tau, e.g. by means of a logistic function (which has a derivative). However, the issue here is that although the first derivative of the posterior is now always continuous, its curvature will still be relatively extreme wherever tau == [any value of x1 in the data]. This may cause HMC to only sample a region most proximal to a mode of the posterior, and not explore the whole posterior appropriate (i.e. the Hamiltonian particle would need a lot of random momentum to be able to climb the steep curvature around tau == [any value of x1 in the data]).

I'm sure that all the people involved in the aforementioned discussion would be very interested to hear about your experiences with your change point model!

Best,

Luc

On Jul 14, 2014, at 4:41 PM, Luc Coffeng <lucco...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi Michael,
>
> A more general point that you might find useful to consider regarding change point models in Stan. Recently, there has been a discussion on the stan user list about change point models and I think the following were the main conclusions:
> 	• If the change point is a parameter to be estimated (tau in your case), the derivative of the posterior will be discontinuous wherever tau == [any value of x1 in the data]. This will break the Hamiltonian dynamics and the algorithm will degenerate to a random walk, driven by the random momentum of the Hamiltonian particle. Hamiltonian MC requires the posterior and its first derivative to be continuous everywhere to be able to simulate draws from the posterior.
> 	• Prior issue can be theoretically overcome by marginalizing over all possible values of the change point, using a mixture model (see manual for example). So if the data are X = (x1, x2, x3, x4, ...), marginalize over [x1 < tau < x2], [x2 < tau < x3],[x3 < tau < x4], ... Unfortunately, as Michael Betancourt pointed out, the posterior for this model will be multimodal (unless you have relatively precise information about were the change point is), and will prove hard to sample from.
> 	• Alternatively, Emmanuel Charpentier proposed a continuous approximation of the step function x1 <= tau, e.g. by means of a logistic function (which has a derivative). However, the issue here is that although the first derivative of the posterior is now always continuous, its curvature will still be relatively extreme  wherever tau == [any value of x1 in the data]. This may cause HMC to only sample a region most proximal to a mode of the posterior, and not explore the whole posterior appropriate (i.e. the Hamiltonian particle would need a lot of random momentum to be able to climb the steep curvature around tau == [any value of x1 in the data]).
> I'm sure that all the people involved in the aforementioned discussion would be very interested to hear about your experiences with your change point model!
>
> Best,
>
>
> Luc

messages.body_plain:
I'm afraid that model's not going to be directly translatable
to Stan, because

  * categorical outcomes are integers

  * Stan does not allow integer parameters

The only way to work around the restriction on integer parameters
is to marginalize them out as described in the mixture model chapter
of the manual.

The upside is that the models run much faster with the integer
parameters marginalized out than they do sampling in JAGS/BUGS.

Also unlike in BUGS, you don't need to define intermediate
values, and you definitely don't want to define them as parameters.
Defining theta as a parameter is inconsistent with this assignment:

> theta[n,t] <- if_else(n==L[t], 1, 0);

Variables can only be assigned to in the blocks in which they
are defined.  But presumably you don't care about theta itself.

So what you need to do is define the log density of p(x) in the
model.

So for your model, all you need to do is remove L and theta
from the parameters declaration (leaving only x) and
calculate p(x[,t] | sigma, pdist) in the inner loop here:

> for (t in 1:T){
>         L[t] ~ categorical(pdist);
>         for (n in 1:N){
>             theta[n,t] <- if_else(n==L[t], 1, 0);
>             x[n,t] ~ normal( theta[n,t], Sigma );
>         }
>     }

I think this will do it in an arithmetically stable way (see
the manual for simpler examples and an explanation of log_sum_exp
and increment_log_prob):

for (t in 1:T) {

  vector[N] temp;
  temp <- rep_vector(0, N);  // fill temp with zeros

  for (n in 1:N) {

    for (n2 in 1:N) {
      temp[n] <- temp[n] + categorical_log(n, pdist)
                         + normal_log(x[n2,t], n2 == n, Sigma);
    }
  }
  // temp[n] =def= log p(x[,t] | Sigma, pdist)
  increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(temp));
}

Note that (n2 == n) is equal to 1 if they're equal and 0 if
they're not, so you don't need the if_else.  And this completely
bypasses the need to define theta.

So the marginalized loop is just calculating:

   log p(x[,t] | Sigma, pdist)

   =  log SUM_n  p(x[,t], L[t] == n | Sigma, pdist)

   =  log SUM_n  p(L[t] == n | pdist) * PROD_n p(x[n,t] | L[t])

At least that's my best guess for the marginalization.

I don't understand the model and am just doing the brute
force marginalization.   I was very confused by the multiple uses
of N here --- does L have the same number of outcomes as theta
and x's first dimension?

- Bob

> Thanks for the reply. I'll work through your suggestion.
>
> There was a typo, so L was a vector of length T, but it's not the biggest problem.
>

> On each of T trials, a biased N-sided dice is rolled where the bias is given by the simplex (pdist). This then determines the mean (via theta) of a normally distributed variable. So the idea was to have observations centred on theta, which is determined by L.

But the mean is just 0 or 1, right?  I still don't quite
get the point of the model, but then I don't have a very
broad experience in modeling.

Maybe someone else could chime in on the model or suggest
alternatives.

> Presumably if I can't use the L output of Categorical as a parameter, I should be able to use this integer output as an array index to look up values in a pre-defined matrix which I can then use as parameters?

The problem is that there isn't an output per se.

A statement like "a ~ foo(b)" just increments the log probability
for the model, it doesn't literally sample a from the foo(b) distribution.
(And by the way, neither does JAGS --- JAGS and BUGS both use the graphical model
structure to compute the Markov blanket of each node, then does
conjugate or non-conjugate Gibbs based on the structure of that blanket.)

> I've tried to implement this with an ultra minimal example, but it doesn't work. Maybe the differences between STAN and JAGS are greater than I thought, but I would have expected this model would sample values of L, but I still can't get it to parse.

Let me emphasize again that the categorical distribution
takes an integer outcome and integers cannot be parameters
in Stan.  So the following isn't legal because the type of
L[t] is real, but categorical wants it to be int.

In Stan, the only way to fit a model that has integer
parameters it to marginalize out the integer parameters to
produce a model that's purely continuous.

This can't be done in all cases, but I think the sketch
I gave you earlier should work for this case.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I cooked up some code for a toy example.

Because Michael said he was using a linear spline, I assumed that the two linear splines should intersect exactly over the change point (i.e. the function is continous at the change point, although the first derivative is not), even though the code in the Michael's error message seems to suggest otherwise. So I'm assuming you want a linear spline that is continuous over the change point. Under this assumption, for any two values of X in the data, there are infinitely many positions between these two x's where the spline knot may be. Using the mixture approach in the Stan manual, it's impossible to marginalize over all these values (at least, I'm not sure how to). So I propose an adaptation.

Specify the change point itself as a latent unknown variable cp_x with unknown mean mu_cp and standard deviation sigma_cp, and then for M mixture components (for each consecutive pair of x's in the data) specify a parameter for the position of a potential change point cp_x[m] between the consecutive two values of x, such that:

cp_x[m] ~ normal(mu_cg, sigma_cg) T[x1, x2];  // x1 and x2 are two consecutive observed values of x

Finally, weight each mixture component representing the interval (x1,x2) by the normal CDF(x2, mu_cp, sigma_cp) - CDF(x1, mu_cp, sigma_cp).

The attached r-script simulates data based on the aforementioned assumption of a continuous regression line (but discontinuous derivative) at the change point. I didn't constrain the support for the change point for each mixture component as the support varies per mixture component, and defining the support would mean creating separate parameters for each mixture component and losing the ability to loop through the components of a vector or array. Bad form! As a result, the model will not initialize if you don't supply it with initial values. In a version of stan before 2.3.0, you would probably see lots and lots of metropolis rejections being spewed out because the support is not defined for cp_x.

As it turns out, the model is currently rather ineffecient (N_eff < 30 when producing 2500 samples in about 1-4 minutes with 40 data points and 21 mixture components, depending on what mode the sampler is). The posterior for the point estimate of the changing point is rather multimodal, though I found that on several occasions, the model actually sampled from a mode very close to the parameter values that were used in the data-generating process. Still, I don't really understand why the sampling of the parameters for the regression line of each mixture component is so horrible...

-Luc

messages.subject_clean: toy example contingency table sampling
messages.body_plain:
Dear dev team and stan users,

Please see attached a toy example for sampling contingency tables with known row and column margins in Stan. The model requires a prior for the distribution of counts within each row (can be anything as long as it's a simplex). The model produces the estimated probability of observations being in a certain cell of the table. The application of this particular model was to redistribute the prevalence of anemia due to difference causes (the row totals) to three severity levels for which we know the total prevalence in the population (the column totals), and given expert priors about the severity distribution of anemia due to each cause (within row distribution).

Best,

Luc

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Can stan be used for a fast replacement of linear/nonlinear regression?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Can stan be used for a fast replacement of linear/nonlinear regression?
messages.body_plain:
Hi David,

The quick answer is that Stan isn't designed to solve any one specific model, it's designed to be able to work with a very general class of models.  For specific models, like this one, packages which focus on solving such models are very likely to work faster.  The power of Stan comes when you want to start making changes to this model to better suite your data, e.g., a student_t model, non-linear transforms of the parameters, hierarchical models, etc.

This particular model may be hard for Stan because of the way constraints are handled using a log transform.  This makes it effectively impossible for beta to ever be zero.  If the data strongly supports that, the optimizer could end up spending a long time trying to get close to zero.

Now, that said, we would like to make Stan as competitive as possible even with these simple models for which there may be specialized approaches.  So, can you send along any scripts, data, initialization, etc that you were using for this so that we can look into it?  Also any printed output from your Stan run would be helpful.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.subject: What is a good default prior for a scale parameter?
messages.subject_clean: What is a good default prior for a scale parameter?
messages.body_plain:
What is a good default prior for a scale parameter?  I think we can have different levels of defaults.

0.  Noninformative priors

Simplest is just uniform on (0, infinity).  That’s our default default and it seems fine to me, although it can have problems if the number of observations is small.

Another option is uniform on log(sigma) but this has the problem of failing for hierarchical models.  This does reduce to the standard result for linear regression so in some sense we need to consider it for “backward compatibility” with conventional Bayesian inference, but really I feel that this prior is more trouble than it’s worth.

For point estimation with hierarchical models, we recommend gamma(2,1/A) for some large value of A (or, most simply, gamma(2,0)); this is discussed at exhausting length in our recent Psychometrika paper.  This prior keeps the point estimate away from 0 which is a practical necessity in many applications of hierarchical models.

1.  Weakly informative priors

If number of observations (or, in a hierarchical model, the number of groups) is small, then we’ll want to control the estimation of the scale parameter at the high end.  One choice that I’ve recommended in the past (most notably, in my 2006 Bayesian Analysis paper) is half-Cauchy with peak at 0 and scale A, where A is some large value.  A=10 would not be a bad choice, I think.  Of course it’s easy to imagine a situation where the user would need a much larger scale (for example, in a model where the data have not been normalized), but in that case it is the user’s responsibility to set a larger value.

I could even imagine some sort of diagnostic, where if the posterior estimate of the scale parameter is comparable to or higher than the prior scale, that we issue a warning, something like:  “Attention:  estimate of parameter sigma_y is high compared to the prior distribution.  Check the scale of your model and, if necessary, rescale your data or increase the upper scale of your prior distribution.”

For point estimation, we could go with gamma(2,1/A), with A set to some default value such as 10.

2.  Informative priors

A lot depends on what sort of information is available.  But one way to frame this is in terms of hierarchical models.  Suppose we have a model with many scale parameters:  sigma1, sigma2, sigma3, etc.  By default we’ll want to give them a common prior with unknown hyperparameters.  And then if more info is available it could be natural to set things up as a regression model on log(sigma) with predictors at the level of the variance component.  This suggests a lognormal model:  log(sigma_j) ~ normal(mu,tau), and then we need priors on mu and tau.

What sort of informative priors on mu, tau would be good here?  I’m not sure, but the point is that we can also use this model when we have only one variance component, in which case we have a model that is set up as a mixture-of-lognormals.  That said, once we’ve set it up we probably would want to avoid the mixture formulation as it could make the computation run slower.

OK, another question:  what’s a good default prior for a covariance matrix?  We have various uniform-like options, also for point estimation there’s the Wishart (_not_ inverse-Wishart) which we recommend in our forthcoming JEBS paper.
