messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] What is a good default prior for a scale parameter?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] What is a good default prior for a scale parameter?
messages.body_plain:
On Jul 15, 2014, at 8:41 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

> > Simplest is just uniform on (0, infinity).  That's our default default and it seems fine to me, although it can have problems if the number of observations is small.
>
> Our default default is improper?  I'm so confused.  I
> thought you'd said you wanted to see priors in our examples.
> So I should just go through and remove priors everywhere
> in the manual?

No, I just mean that the default default, if no prior is specified, is uniform.

> > Another option is uniform on log(sigma) but this has the problem of failing for hierarchical models.  This does reduce to the standard result for linear regression so in some sense we need to consider it for "backward compatibility" with conventional Bayesian inference, but really I feel that this prior is more trouble than it's worth
>
> That’s improper uniform on the unconstrained scale.

Yes but it is my impression that we are generally specifying our models on the scale of the named parameters.

> It's equal to the standard presumably because it undoes
> the Jacobian in the constraint <lower=0> on sigma.

Yup.

> > For point estimation with hierarchical models, we recommend gamma(2,1/A) for some large value of A (or, most simply, gamma(2,0)); this is discussed at exhausting length in our recent Psychometrika paper.  This prior keeps the point estimate away from 0 which is a practical necessity in many applications of hierarchical models.
>
> OK --- this we should include.
>
> > 1.  Weakly informative priors
> >
> > If number of observations (or, in a hierarchical model, the number of groups) is small, then we'll want to control the estimation of the scale parameter at the high end.  One choice that I've recommended in the past (most notably, in my 2006 Bayesian Analysis paper) is half-Cauchy with peak at 0 and scale A, where A is some large value.  A=10 would not be a bad choice, I think.  Of course it's easy to imagine a situation where the user would need a much larger scale (for example, in a model where the data have not been normalized), but in that case it is the user's responsibility to set a larger value.
>
> OK, that'll work.  So not a uniform prior here?

Uniform is a type of noninformative prior but for weakly informative we need a bit more.

> > I could even imagine some sort of diagnostic, where if the posterior estimate of the scale parameter is comparable to or higher than the prior scale, that we issue a warning, something like:  "Attention:  estimate of parameter sigma_y is high compared to the prior distribution.  Check the scale of your model and, if necessary, rescale your data or increase the upper scale of your prior distribution."
>
> That'd have to be something that has access to all the samples
> rather than something done online.

Yup.

> Judging from all of Ben's work, I don't think the Wisharts make
> a lot of sense.  I think they got a lot of use in BUGS/JAGS because
> those systems could only handle conjugate priors for multivariate
> quantities.

No, Bugs etc. use _inverse_-Wisharts.  What I’m talking about here is plain old Wishart, which when given the appropriate scale parameter keeps the point estimate away from the non-positive-definite boundary, something that a uniform prior doesn’t do.  Again it’s the difference between a prior for point estimation vs a prior for rull Bayes.

Hi Bob,

Hm, I see your point.

I've experimented with binomial-binomial models in a setting where observations can be misclassified, so there are unobserved true values and observed values that are a function of the true values and the specificity (% true negative detected) and sensitivity (% true positive detected) of some test that determines positiveness. Because there are many sums of false and true positives that can lead to the observed values (and sums of true and false negatives that can lead to observed negatives), it is significantly more complicated to marginalize over all possible combinations, but the concept of marginalizing over all possible sums is similar to the current example (I think). Anyway, I found that a stan model based on marginalization behaved exactly the same as a simple model with: y ~ binomial(N, p_true * sensitivity + (1-p_true) * (1-specificity), including the uncertainty estimates. I tried to find the code this morning so that I could post it here, but couldn't find it (and had to head out to the office). Will post it later if I can find it.

Best,
Luc

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Can stan be used for a fast replacement of linear/nonlinear regression?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Can stan be used for a fast replacement of linear/nonlinear regression?
messages.body_plain:
Andrew,

NNLS is definitely using a specialized algorithm for non-negatively constrained linear least squares.  See http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-negative_least_squares#Algorithms

There are definitely things we can do about it.  Simple linear bound constraints (i.e., lb <= x <= ub) are actually pretty easy to handle in optimization algorithms.  The issue is the plumbing necessary to take a model and represent the constraints that way instead of how we're currently doing it with non-linear transforms.  That might be worth doing as it would also allow us to play with other ways of sampling in the presence of such constraints.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.body_plain:
Yup.  For HMC-stan it makes sense to work on the unconstrained scale.  (We’ve also talked on occasion about implementing bouncing for constrained parameters, but maybe that makes the algorithm too messy.)  But for point estimation, boundary estimates come up a lot.  Sometimes we go to some trouble to avoid boundary estimates (as with our boundary-avoiding priors for group-level variance parameters), other times boundary estimates are considered a plus (for example, lasso).  So, indeed, maybe we should think about implementing constrained optimization in Stan.  Perhaps, for example, the Stan program could be altered by including a tag for each parameter that we want to enforce will _not_ be transformed.
A

There are two models, which may be part of the confusion.

In the model with explicit sorting, the prior for y_raw is
normal(0,1), but the prior for y isn't i.i.d. normal, as
there is sorting involved.

In the ordered vector model, the prior is not i.i.d. because
of the sorting constraint.

In both cases you get a kind of dependence in the prior for y.
In the y_raw case, the y_raw values are generated i.i.d., but
then sorted to get what you want.

of the Stan dev team and many of our users, which is why I was
asking for help in the first place.  So I may still be misunderstanding
something fundamental here myself.  I certainly can't connect
why the two models give the same behavior theoretically.

messages.body_plain:
All the information is already in the model in the form of constraints on variables, so tagging isn't really required.  The key is making the information explicitly available to the optimizer or sampler (if desired) instead of always automatically transforming things into an unconstrained space.  This is basically the same plumbing that would be needed if someone wanted to implement bouncing for constrained parameters.

I guess tags could be useful if someone wanted to explicitly request something be transformed to an unconstrained scale for some reason or if they explicitly wanted boundary values included/excluded.

On Tue, Jul 15, 2014 at 4:19 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
> Yup.  For HMC-stan it makes sense to work on the unconstrained scale.  (We’ve also talked on occasion about implementing bouncing for constrained parameters, but maybe that makes the algorithm too messy.)  But for point estimation, boundary estimates come up a lot.  Sometimes we go to some trouble to avoid boundary estimates (as with our boundary-avoiding priors for group-level variance parameters), other times boundary estimates are considered a plus (for example, lasso).  So, indeed, maybe we should think about implementing constrained optimization in Stan.  Perhaps, for example, the Stan program could be altered by including a tag for each parameter that we want to enforce will _not_ be transformed.

The issue is the plumbing necessary to take a model and represent the constraints that way instead of how we're currently doing it with non-linear transforms. messages.subject: Re: change point models?
messages.subject_clean: change point models?
messages.body_plain:
Update: (thanks to a hint by Dr. Goodrich, with most credit to Jonah Sol Gabry):

Is this a way around the discontinuous derivative issue?

Problem: Observational cohort shows an reduction in a disease outcome y after initiation of treatment:

tau, the single change point where this change occurs, is CONTINUOUS
y, the outcomes is measured k =5 times at irregular intervals x, for each subject n=100
data are in long format, we use a inv-wishart as prior for the beta intercept, beta pre slope and beta post change point slope.
Preliminary model below.

model{

  for (i in 1:n) {
          y [i] ~ normal(beta[1]*100,sigma);                               //intercept

     for (j in 2:k) {

       if (x [ i + (n* (j-1)) ] <= tau )                            //pre tau point
          y [i + (n* (j-1))] ~ normal (y[i]
                                      +beta [2] * ( x [i + (n* (j-1))] - x[i] ),
                                      sigma);

       else                                                         //post tau point
          y [i + (n* (j-1))] ~ normal( y[i]
                                       +( beta [2] * (tau - x[i]) )
                                       +( beta [3] * (x [i + (n* (j-1))] - tau)),
                                       sigma);
     }
  }

beta ~ multi_normal(means, SIGMA);
means ~ normal(0, 1000);
SIGMA ~ inv_wishart(3.0,W);

On Wednesday, July 2, 2014 3:34:08 PM UTC-4, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> Hi all.  I generally don’t like change point models because it’s my impression that real life does not usually have sudden changes—and when sudden changes exist, we usually know when they happen.
>
> But, setting those qualms aside, the model seems well-enough specified.  I see the potential HMC problem, though, as there is a discontinuous derivative.  One way to handle this would be to allow the change to be continuous, which in some way is an application of the folk theorem in that I expect actual changes really are continuous.
>
> Beyond this, we (Stan-dev, that is) might want to think more generally about how to patch models that have bits of discontinuity so they work ok in HMC.  Maybe we can map to some latent continuous model?
>
> A
>
> > Has anybody fitted a change point model in Stan, please?
> >
> > We are interested to fit a change point (broken stick) model in RStan to model longitudinal continuous outcomes measured about three to ten times (at baseline and follow-ups) for each of about hundreds of subjects (i.e. patients in a clinical trial); (So this is different from a time series on a single outcome for a single unit of observation, say a NYSE stock.). The timing of the outcome observations is different for each individual (the patients come in for appointments at different, irregularly), as are the slopes before and after the change point, the intercept and the actual change point itself.
> >
> > The model:
> >
> > y[i,k] = beta[pre, i] * (t[i, k] – tau[i]) * I(t[i, k] < tau[i]) + beta[intercept, i]+ beta[post, i] * (t[i,k] – tau[i]) * I(t[i,k] > tau[i]) + epsilon[i,j]
> >
> > where the error term epsilon [i,k] ~MVN (0, Sigma), iid;
> >
> > y[i,j,t] is the continuous outcome of the ith subject at the kth observation at time t[i,k]; beta[pre,i] is the random slope for each subject before,  beta[post,i] is the random slope for each subject after the subject specific change point tau. We think a reasonable prior for beta may be ~MVN, iid, but the slopes and intercept are certainly not iid.
> >
> > I( t[i,k] > tau[i]) is the indicator function used to define a linear spline: (t[i, k] – tau[i]) * I(t[i, k] < tau[i]) = t[i,k] - tau[k]  iff t[i,k] < tau[i] ; 0 otherwise;
> >
> > tau [i] is the random change point (to be estimated for each subject i); tau [i] is the time of the ‘kink’ in the spline measured before say a diagnosis of dementia.;
> >
> > See for example attached: Hall CB, Ying J, Kuo L, Sliwinski M, Buschke H, Katz M, Lipton RB. Estimation of bivariate measurements having different change points, with application to cognitive ageing. Stat Med. 2001 Dec 30;20(24):3695-714. PubMed PMID: 11782027.
> >
> > We are interested to learn from similar models other users may have fitted or know about or to share related functions, now possible in Rstan.
> >
> > Thank you.
> >
> > Michael Andreae
>
>

messages.subject: Bayesian factor analysis
messages.subject_clean: Bayesian factor analysis
messages.body_plain:
My coauthor and I are working on a governance indicators projects, and we plan to use Bayesian factor analysis to aggregate a bunch of different measures. We'd also like to use informative priors to reflect our extra-data information about the relationship between observable and latent variables.

In some detail: we have many dozens variables that measure various aspects of government capacity for a large number of countries. And we have hunches regarding the different dimensions (regulatory capacity, service delivery capacity) that these variables measure. So for instance, we might have school test scores and immunization rates, that we consider measures of service delivery; environmental regulation and business regulation, that we consider measures of regulatory capacity; and so on.

What we'd like to do is fit a factor analysis model with multiple dimensions, and encode our substantive hunches regarding which measures belong to which dimension in the priors for the discrimination parameters. But at the same time, we'd want the model to be flexible enough to allow for a given variable to load on a dimension other than the "natural" one we'd expect it to load. This is particularly important when there's some ambiguity regarding exactly what aspect of government capacity a given variable is measuring. So for instance, it is unclear whether revenue collection is more like a "service delivery" or more like regulation; and the same for clean air, and a bunch of other measures.

What I've been doing is setting the prior for the discrimination parameter of a given variable on its "natural" dimension to be centered at 1 and with a relatively small standard deviation, while the discrimination on the other dimension(s) is given a prior centered at 0 and with larger standard deviation.

So we estimate something in the form

 y[i] ~ dnorm (mu.y[i], tau.y[i])

mu.y[i] <- mu.0 + b[source[i],1]*theta[country[i],1] + b[source[i],2]*theta[country[i],2]+a[source[i]]

where y are the observed variables (in "long" format, so that multiple measures for a given country are stacked as successive observations in y; also, the variables are standardized so that they are all approximately on the same scale)

the theta are the latent variables (in this case, theta[ j, 1] and theta[j, 2] are the values of the latent variable for country j respectively on dimension 1 and 2)

a[k] is the "difficulty" for observable variable k

and b the discriminations, so that b[k, l] is the discrimination parameter for observable variable k on latent dimension l. In the example, l can be either 1 or 2.

The prior for b[k,1] is centered at one, with sd_low, if our hunch is that variable k belongs to dimension 1, and centered at 0, with sd_high, otherwise; and the same happens for the second dimension obviously.

Models like this seem to have a lot of issues with convergence, when estimated in JAGS and WinBUGS, especially if I do not set sd_high to be also quite small, and also if there are more (e.g. four) latent dimensions. Which makes me suspect that there's a problem with the model itself. It would be great if any of you here had any suggestion regarding how to design a model that allows for multiple latent dimensions while also encoding these hunches regarding which dimension a given variable belongs. [And yes, we are migrating to Stan...]

thanks
Piero

messages.subject: multinomial probit choice models
messages.subject_clean: multinomial probit choice models
messages.body_plain:
I am currently working on conducting Bayesian analysis for multinomial probit models in discrete choice models. The attached paper proposed a MCMC sampler for multinomial probit choice models, using latent variables via data augmentation. I have tried it and it worked, but it exhibits high autocorrelation, because the latent variables and the regression coefficients are sampled separately.

So I want to see if Stan would work for this type of model. Is there anyone who has done a multinomial probit model with Stan before?

Thanks,
Amy

On Wednesday, July 16, 2014 10:13:46 AM UTC-4, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> Hi, as Bob would say it’s probably best to model the outcome probabilities directly rather than use latent variables.  See Section "5.6. Ordered Logistic and Probit Regression” in the Stan manual.

As economists would say, the multivariate probit likelihood function for the outcome probabilities entails integrating the multivariate normal PDF, which Stan does not support and would be brutal on the autodiff if we did.

Doing it with latent variables in Stan is tedious and may not be any better than a Gibbs sampler, although an LKJ prior will probably work better than a scaled inverse-Wishart. The attached is probably wrong in some of the details but at least parses.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Just so you don't think I'm ignoring the message, the short
answer is "no", I don't have any suggestions, but then I don't
even know what "loading" means in this context.

Feel free to send along an implementation for comments.

Is the problem one chain stabilizing or multiple chains arriving
at the same estimates?

One thing I can say is that in Stan, unlike in BUGS or JAGS,
you need to assign a variable a value before using it.  The
statements are executed in order.

Have you tried fitting simulated data to see if the sampler
can recover parameters known to generate the observed data.
You can run into sampling problems with misspecified models.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: change point models?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: change point models?
messages.body_plain:
You only provided the model part of the Stan program.  It
really helps to understand the parameter and data definitions,
too.

We have alternative recommendations for priors on covariance
matrices, but that's a second-order detail.

I'm also not clear on why beta[1] is multiplied by 100 on the
first line.

And wouldn't it be easier to use 2D arrays than fiddling indexes?
The latter's very error prone, at least when I'm coding.

- Bob

On Jul 15, 2014, at 4:53 PM, Michael Andreae <mhan...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Update: (thanks to a hint by Dr. Goodrich, with most credit to Jonah Sol Gabry):
>
> Is this a way around the discontinuous derivative issue?
>
> Problem: Observational cohort shows an reduction in a disease outcome y after initiation of treatment:
>
> tau, the single change point where this change occurs, is CONTINUOUS
> y, the outcomes is measured k =5 times at irregular intervals x, for each subject n=100
> data are in long format, we use a inv-wishart as prior for the beta intercept, beta pre slope and beta post change point slope.
> Preliminary model below.
>
> model{
>
>   for (i in 1:n) {
>           y [i] ~ normal(beta[1]*100,sigma);                               //intercept
>
>      for (j in 2:k) {
>
>        if (x [ i + (n* (j-1)) ] <= tau )                            //pre tau point
>           y [i + (n* (j-1))] ~ normal (y[i]
>                                       +beta [2] * ( x [i + (n* (j-1))] - x[i] ),
>                                       sigma);
>
>        else                                                         //post tau point
>           y [i + (n* (j-1))] ~ normal( y[i]
>                                        +( beta [2] * (tau - x[i]) )
>                                        +( beta [3] * (x [i + (n* (j-1))] - tau)),
>                                        sigma);
>      }
>   }
>
> beta ~ multi_normal(means, SIGMA);
> means ~ normal(0, 1000);
> SIGMA ~ inv_wishart(3.0,W);
>
> On Wednesday, July 2, 2014 3:34:08 PM UTC-4, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> Hi all.  I generally don’t like change point models because it’s my impression that real life does not usually have sudden changes—and when sudden changes exist, we usually know when they happen.
>
> But, setting those qualms aside, the model seems well-enough specified.  I see the potential HMC problem, though, as there is a discontinuous derivative.  One way to handle this would be to allow the change to be continuous, which in some way is an application of the folk theorem in that I expect actual changes really are continuous.
>
> Beyond this, we (Stan-dev, that is) might want to think more generally about how to patch models that have bits of discontinuity so they work ok in HMC.  Maybe we can map to some latent continuous model?
>
> A
>
> > Has anybody fitted a change point model in Stan, please?
> >
> > We are interested to fit a change point (broken stick) model in RStan to model longitudinal continuous outcomes measured about three to ten times (at baseline and follow-ups) for each of about hundreds of subjects (i.e. patients in a clinical trial); (So this is different from a time series on a single outcome for a single unit of observation, say a NYSE stock.). The timing of the outcome observations is different for each individual (the patients come in for appointments at different, irregularly), as are the slopes before and after the change point, the intercept and the actual change point itself.
> >
> > The model:
> >
> > y[i,k] = beta[pre, i] * (t[i, k] – tau[i]) * I(t[i, k] < tau[i]) + beta[intercept, i]+ beta[post, i] * (t[i,k] – tau[i]) * I(t[i,k] > tau[i]) + epsilon[i,j]
> >
> > where the error term epsilon [i,k] ~MVN (0, Sigma), iid;
> >
> > y[i,j,t] is the continuous outcome of the ith subject at the kth observation at time t[i,k]; beta[pre,i] is the random slope for each subject before,  beta[post,i] is the random slope for each subject after the subject specific change point tau. We think a reasonable prior for beta may be ~MVN, iid, but the slopes and intercept are certainly not iid.
> >
> > I( t[i,k] > tau[i]) is the indicator function used to define a linear spline: (t[i, k] – tau[i]) * I(t[i, k] < tau[i]) = t[i,k] - tau[k]  iff t[i,k] < tau[i] ; 0 otherwise;
> >
> > tau [i] is the random change point (to be estimated for each subject i); tau [i] is the time of the ‘kink’ in the spline measured before say a diagnosis of dementia.;
> >
> > See for example attached: Hall CB, Ying J, Kuo L, Sliwinski M, Buschke H, Katz M, Lipton RB. Estimation of bivariate measurements having different change points, with application to cognitive ageing. Stat Med. 2001 Dec 30;20(24):3695-714. PubMed PMID: 11782027.
> >
> > We are interested to learn from similar models other users may have fitted or know about or to share related functions, now possible in Rstan.
> >
> > Thank you.
> >

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Help with first model, please.
messages.body_plain:
On Jul 15, 2014, at 5:53 AM, Ben Vincent <drben...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Ok, thanks for your reply, much appreciated. You've answered the core of my question, and I'll see if I can make progress reformulating without the Categorical, following your suggestion.
>
> It would still be great to hear from someone if the approach I was using in JAGS is just not applicable here.
>
> The aim is to model how well a person can localise a signal item amongst noise items, over T trials. All observations are noisy, but the signal has a higher mean value (1) than the noise (0). The general approach is to use the same JAGS model twice.
> - The first stage generates some simulated data P(D,x|p,sigma) of locations of the signal (D; sorry this was previously referred to as L) and what noisy observations were made (x), given a prior over the location of the signal and a specific level of observation noise (sigma).
> - The second step is to use this simulated data to see how well true signal locations can be inferred from the noisy observations P(D|x,p,sigma),  given the noisy observations x, the prior over signal location and the observation noise.
> - In a third step, outside of JAGS, converts this inferred distribution over D to a best guess (the MAP value) and then compares it to the true vector of signal locations generates in step 1 to calculate the percent correct localisation of the signal.

We recommend always doing this step of simulating data
according to the model with known parameters and making sure
those parameters can then be estimated from the data.

Why would you want a posterior mode (aka "MAP", but Andrew hates
that term for some reason) rather than a posterior mean?   The
posterior mean has the least expected square error (and a posterior
median has the least expected absolute error).  There's no such
decision theoretic interpretation for the MAP.

Also, the typical set (high mass volume of the posterior) doesn't
even contain the max in some cases --- Beta(0.5,0.5) is a good
example to get the general idea of what's going on.

And if you do only want a posterior mode, you might be able to
use Stan's optimization directly rather than MCMC (would depend
on whether there is a maximum likelihood estimate over all parameters
or whether you want a marginal makimum likelihood, which we
should also be supporting in the future).

> JAGS model
>
> model{
>   for (t in 1:T){
>     D[t] ~ dcat(pdist)
>     for (n in 1:N){
>       theta[n,t] <- ifelse(n==D[t],1,0)
>       x[n,t] ~ dnorm(theta[n,t] , 1/variance)
>     }
>   }
> }
>
>
> I get that theta is an irrelevant intermediate variable here, but I just have it because it is used and affected by other variables in more complex variations of the model.

Stan lets you declare local variables.  It's just a matter
of whether you want to save it or not.  If you want to save it,
declare it as a transformed parameter.  If you want to just use,
declare it as a local variable in the model block.

And you don't need the ifelse in Stan (and probably in JAGS); you
can just write:

  theta[n,t] <- n == D[t];

The == operator returns 1 if the expressions are equal and 0 otherwise.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] hierarchical models
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] hierarchical models
messages.body_plain:
It can be hard to fit groups with few members, and 3 is
difficult.  It's not impossible, but you'll need reasonable
priors.

Otherwise, the basic idea of grouping parameters in a hierarchical
model is exchangeability (given the inputs for modeling).

As to assuming a mean of 0 at the top of the hierarchy, you
probably want a fairly diffuse standard deviation.  And
that should be chosen given what you know about the problem.
Things like whether the predictors standardized.

There's also a major techncial problem for Stan
with the model as formulated.

For the sampler to work effectively, all parameters should
have support at any point that satisfies their constraint.

In the attached model, a variable is declared as

   vector[J] beta_raw; // standard covariate coefficients

without constraints and then given a constrained density:

   beta_raw[1] ~ uniform(-5, 5);

It would probably make sense to have a more meaningful prior
than uniform.

- Bob

On Jul 16, 2014, at 4:14 PM, Ross Boylan <ro...@biostat.ucsf.edu> wrote:

> I estimated a bunch of hierarchical models, and am looking for feedback
> about whether the models are appropriate.  I have some doubts.
>
> The stan code is below, but the key point is that each batch of
> coefficients had a prior with mean 0 and and estimated variance.  Call
> two such distribution F and G.  Let b1, b2, ... be coefficients for
> covariants x1, x2, ... (there were about 10) and let b1A, b1B, and b1C
> be coefficients for x1 a categorical covariate takes values A, B, or C
> respectively (exactly 3 levels).  So
> b1A ~ F
> b1B ~ F
> b2A ~ F.
> The coefficients without interaction were in a separate batch, so
> b1 ~ G
> b2 ~ G.
>
> I believe the usual procedure would be
> b1A, b1B, b1C ~ F(m1, s1)
> b2A, b2B, b2C ~ F(m2, s2)
> with no separate b1 and b2 coefficient, and the m's and s's (means and
> standard deviations) in turn coming from other distributions.
>
> I think the b1 and b2 coefficients in my formulation are equivalent to
> m1 and m2, so the difference there is merely formal.
>
> However, my batching scheme is equivalent to s1=s2.  It didn't seem a
> good idea to try fitting the standard deviation when each group had only
> 3 members.  It was often challenging to fit the models I did; adding
> more parameters seemed pushing my luck.
>
> Finally, I'm a bit concerned that since at the highest hiearchical level
> (or do I mean shallowest?  the most meta level, the distribution of the
> b1, b2, ... coefficients) I simply assumed a mean of 0, the estimates
> may be unduly small.  They might also be too small if the estimated
> variance parameters are too small, e.g., if there were notable
> differences in the interaction term for only 1 variable, the batching of
> those interactions with all the others would lead to a small sigma.
>
> So, does the procedure I followed seem reasonable?  If not, what other
> models would be advisable?
>
> Here's a representative model:
> data {
>   int<lower=0> N; // number of respondents (~400)
>   int<lower=0> J;  //number of covariates (~10, not counting clusters)
>   int<lower=0> NSD;  // number of classes of beta for sd (~3 classes)
>   int<lower=1,upper=NSD> SDClass[J];  // beta[j, k] has sigma_beta[SDClass[j]]
>   int<lower=0> NCLUSTER;  //number of seeds (~200)
>   int iCluster[N]; // cluster id
>   matrix[N, J] x;  // covariates
>   int<lower=1,upper=15> nDetail[N];  // outcome
> }
> parameters {
>    vector[J] beta_raw; // standard covariate coefficients
>    vector[NCLUSTER] alpha_raw; // cluster effects
>    real<lower=0> sigma;
>    real<lower=0> sigma_beta[NSD];
> }
> transformed parameters {
>    vector[J] beta;
>    vector[NCLUSTER] alpha;
>    for(ir in 1:J) {
>       beta[ir] <- beta_raw[ir]*sigma_beta[SDClass[ir]];
>    }
>    alpha <- alpha_raw*sigma;
> }
> model {
>    vector[N] beta_x;
>    sigma ~ cauchy(0, 5);
>    sigma_beta ~ cauchy(0, 5);
>    beta_raw[1] ~ uniform(-5, 5);
>    for (j in 2:J) {
>      beta_raw[j] ~ normal(0, 1);
>    }
>    alpha_raw ~ normal(0, 1);
>    for (n in 1:N) {
>        beta_x[n] <- (x[n] * beta)+alpha[iCluster[n]];
>      //truncated poisson can't be vectorized
>      // and is not available in log form
>      nDetail[n] ~ poisson(exp(beta_x[n])) T[1, 15];
>    }
> }
>
> Some of the models were more complex, including multinomial model with 5
> outcome categories and a model with 2 nested levels of clustering.  The
> more complex models had considerably more observations, about 2000.
>
> Thanks for any advice.
> Ross Boylan

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: change point models?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: change point models?
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

Well, not really a change-point model, but something very similar are so-called Emax models in PK/PD. The hill function can be written in terms of the log-concentration like

hill(conc) = inv_logit(h * (lconc - lEC50) )

here the "l" denotes log. I experienced some issues in Stan when fitting this type of model with h larger than 1. I suppose the derivatives can become quite steep in that case. So if such a function could be stabilized by providing a specialized function, that would be great. The behavior would be such that with h >> 1 the function essentially becomes the step function.

Best,
Sebastian

> >
> > Is this a way around the discontinuous derivative issue?
> >
> > Problem: Observational cohort shows an reduction in a disease outcome y after initiation of treatment:
> >
> > tau, the single change point where this change occurs, is CONTINUOUS
> > y, the outcomes is measured k =5 times at irregular intervals x, for each subject n=100
> > data are in long format, we use a inv-wishart as prior for the beta intercept, beta pre slope and beta post change point slope.

> >   for (i in 1:n) {

> >
> >      for (j in 2:k) {
> >
> >        if (x [ i + (n* (j-1)) ] <= tau )                            //pre tau point
> >           y [i + (n* (j-1))] ~ normal (y[i]
> >                                       +beta [2] * ( x [i + (n* (j-1))] - x[i] ),
> >                                       sigma);
> >
> >        else                                                         //post tau point
> >           y [i + (n* (j-1))] ~ normal( y[i]
> >                                        +( beta [2] * (tau - x[i]) )
> >                                        +( beta [3] * (x [i + (n* (j-1))] - tau)),
> >                                        sigma);
> >      }
> >   }
> >
> > beta ~ multi_normal(means, SIGMA);
> > means ~ normal(0, 1000);
> > SIGMA ~ inv_wishart(3.0,W);
> >
> > On Wednesday, July 2, 2014 3:34:08 PM UTC-4, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> > Hi all.  I generally don’t like change point models because it’s my impression that real life does not usually have sudden changes—and when sudden changes exist, we usually know when they happen.
> >
> > But, setting those qualms aside, the model seems well-enough specified.  I see the potential HMC problem, though, as there is a discontinuous derivative.  One way to handle this would be to allow the change to be continuous, which in some way is an application of the folk theorem in that I expect actual changes really are continuous.
> >
> > Beyond this, we (Stan-dev, that is) might want to think more generally about how to patch models that have bits of discontinuity so they work ok in HMC.  Maybe we can map to some latent continuous model?
> >
> > A
> >
> > > Has anybody fitted a change point model in Stan, please?
> > >
> > > We are interested to fit a change point (broken stick) model in RStan to model longitudinal continuous outcomes measured about three to ten times (at baseline and follow-ups) for each of about hundreds of subjects (i.e. patients in a clinical trial); (So this is different from a time series on a single outcome for a single unit of observation, say a NYSE stock.). The timing of the outcome observations is different for each individual (the patients come in for appointments at different, irregularly), as are the slopes before and after the change point, the intercept and the actual change point itself.
> > >
> > > The model:
> > >
> > > y[i,k] = beta[pre, i] * (t[i, k] – tau[i]) * I(t[i, k] < tau[i]) + beta[intercept, i]+ beta[post, i] * (t[i,k] – tau[i]) * I(t[i,k] > tau[i]) + epsilon[i,j]
> > >
> > > where the error term epsilon [i,k] ~MVN (0, Sigma), iid;
> > >
> > > y[i,j,t] is the continuous outcome of the ith subject at the kth observation at time t[i,k]; beta[pre,i] is the random slope for each subject before,  beta[post,i] is the random slope for each subject after the subject specific change point tau. We think a reasonable prior for beta may be ~MVN, iid, but the slopes and intercept are certainly not iid.
> > >
> > > I( t[i,k] > tau[i]) is the indicator function used to define a linear spline: (t[i, k] – tau[i]) * I(t[i, k] < tau[i]) = t[i,k] - tau[k]  iff t[i,k] < tau[i] ; 0 otherwise;
> > >
> > > tau [i] is the random change point (to be estimated for each subject i); tau [i] is the time of the ‘kink’ in the spline measured before say a diagnosis of dementia.;
> > >
> > > See for example attached: Hall CB, Ying J, Kuo L, Sliwinski M, Buschke H, Katz M, Lipton RB. Estimation of bivariate measurements having different change points, with application to cognitive ageing. Stat Med. 2001 Dec 30;20(24):3695-714. PubMed PMID: 11782027.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Can stan be used for a fast replacement of linear/nonlinear regression?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Can stan be used for a fast replacement of linear/nonlinear regression?
messages.body_plain:
Hi David.  We just discussed this problem in the Stan meeting and Bob came up with a clever solution which would allow Stan to optimize on the original scale.  The trick is simply to not specify the bound on beta but instead to put the constraint into the model.  Something like this:

data {
  int<lower=0> N; // number of data items
  int<lower=0> K; // number of predictors
  matrix[N,K] x; // predictor matrix
  vector[N] y; // outcome vector

  real<lower=0> A; //set A to be really large to make a hard constraint of beta to be positive
}
parameters {
  vector[K] beta; // coefficients for predictors

  real<lower=0> sigma; // error scale
}
model {

  for (k in 1:K)
    increment_log_prob(log_inv_logit(A*b[k]))

  y ~ normal(x * beta, sigma); // likelihood
}

Ummm, maybe I’m bumbling the details here, but the idea is that you run it and specify some large positive value of A, which has the effect of enforcing positivity on the estimate of the coefficients b[k].

This is a hack (presumably it would make more sense for Stan to automatically increase A while it’s running) but it might be worth a try.  If the problem with the original run was that Stan was taking forever to get to the boundary, this could help things.
A

For specific models, like this one, packages which focus on solving such models are very likely to work faster. That said, for simple inequality constraints, there are easier and more efficient approaches.

Anyway, until we actually see the data/output from David's model it's impossible to know if this is what's actually going on or not.

messages.subject: discrete parameters in Stan
messages.subject_clean: discrete parameters in Stan
messages.body_plain:
I also wanted to briefly respond to David’s comment, “Also, seems you should extend Stan to deal with discrete parameters — usually this is simple using vanilla Metropolis-Hastings or Gibbs mixed in with your HMC."

We are planning at some point to extend Stan to discrete parameters using slice sampling.  One reason we haven’t done this is that it requires some tinkering with the language itself:
1.  Stan needs to be “told” to treat discrete variables differently
2.  We need to specify the log-posterior in some way so that, when updating the discrete variables, Stan doesn’t have to compute the entire log posterior at each step.

These are doable (if necessary, we can do step 2 above in a clunky but effective way requiring some duplication of code).  We haven’t done it yet, partly because of our usual resource constraints (notably, Bob and Daniel’s time!) and partly because most of the discrete-parameter applications we’ve seen so far are finite mixture models which can be better solved by marginalizing out in the model (as described in the Stan manual).  To this end we’re also planning at some time to introduce a general mixture() distribution which will allow these models to be specified more easily and directly by users.

A

On Jul 17, 2014, at 10:35 PM, David Dunson <dun...@duke.edu> wrote:

> sure -- I wonder perhaps if Stan can deal with the non-discrete mixture approach we proposed in the enclosed manuscript (to appear Biometrika).  This model is really quite simple - Gaussian process regression in a latent variable & can be trivially applied to nonparametric modeling of a random effect distribution with no discrete parameters.  Seems Stan should be good with it?  Also, seems you should extend Stan to deal with discrete parameters -- usually this is simple using vanilla Metropolis-Hastings or Gibbs mixed in with your HMC.
>
> David
>
> <biometrika revision5.pdf>
>
> On Jul 17, 2014, at 12:14 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>
> > I defer to David when it comes to this sort of model, so maybe the DP mixture is just fine.
> >
> > Regarding Stan and HMC:  just about all existing methods (with the possible exception of the new idea of thermodynamic sampling that Mike Betancourt is working on) have problems with multimodal posteriors.  I don’t know that HMC is worse than Gibbs and Metropolis here.  The thing that HMC (and Stan) can’t handle is inference for discrete parameters.  Maybe you could do the DP mixture without discrete parameters by having a fixed number of mixture components (maybe 3 or 4) and going from there.
> >
> > I’ll post this discussion the stan-users list if youall don’t object.
> > A
> >
> > On Jul 17, 2014, at 5:04 PM, David Dunson <dun...@duke.edu> wrote:
> >
> > > Hi Andrew,
> > >
> > > I'd disagree - I think the DP mixture is really actually very simple & effectively behaves like a finite mixture.  In fact, one way to implement a good approximation to a DP mixture is to define a finite mixture with a symmetric Dirichlet prior for the mixture weights having parameters \alpha/k with k a fixed number of mixture components treated as an upper bound on the number of components needed.  This type of prior will have the effect of zeroing out the extra unnecessary components & converges to a DP as k increases.  It's a simple Gibbs sampler to implement but I don't know anything about Stan -- seemingly Hamiltonian Monte Carlo is poor for multimodal and mixture models so may fail.  Some details on such things in BDA3.
> > >
> > > David
> > >

> > > >
> > > > On Jul 17, 2014, at 7:42 AM, Avi Feller <avi.f...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > >
> > > > > Hi Andy and David,
> > > > >
> > > > > Thanks for the response.
> > > > >
> > > > > We've definitely thought about a mixture prior here---my guess at the "true" distribution of effects is that it's unimodal, with some heavy tails and possibly some skew. A mixture model with a small number of components could pick up some of this. While not the ideal solution, you're right that we could fit it in Stan, which is a definite plus. On the negative side, since we don't have any good prior information on mixture means (like what you did in the 1990 paper), I'm a bit wary of the mixture modeling approach here. Hence, thinking about DP priors.
> > > > >
> > > > > All that said, you're probably right that the DP prior is overkill. But figured it was worth asking!
> > > > >
> > > > > Great to get your thoughts, as always.
> > > > >
> > > > > - Avi

> > > > >
> > > > > On Wed, Jul 16, 2014 at 1:36 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
> > > > > > Hi, Avi.  I have an annoying habit of kicking all nonparametric questions to my coauthors…  In any case, I’m cc-ing David Dunson here.  David:  what do you think?
> > > > > > My general impression is that I like DP priors in some settings but it seems to me a bit of overkill to try to use them for modeling a batch of varying coefficients.  What about something simpler like a mixture model (as in my 1990 paper with King)?  That would also have the advantage of being easily fittable in Stan.
> > > > > > A

> > > > > >
> > > > > > On Jul 15, 2014, at 7:54 AM, Avi Feller <avi.f...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > >
> > > > > > > Hi Andy,
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > I hope that you're doing well---it's been ages since we last spoke.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > I'm writing in the hope that you'll offer some useful advice on a multilevel modeling problem before I get myself in too deep. The data come from a large evaluation of Head Start, in which 3 and 4 year-old children on a wait list were randomly offered slots in Head Start, with randomization conducted separately across roughly 350 separate Head Start centers. It is of substantive interest to estimate both center-specific treatment effects and the overall distribution of those effects. Moreover, these centers are very small (many with only 2 kids who qualify for the evaluation), so partially pooling is essential.
> > > > > > >
> > > > > > > Thanks to Stan, we've been able to construct reasonable estimates of the center-specific effects using Normal and t distributions for the center-level variation (the "random effect," though I know you hate that term); the estimates are close to each other, though it seems useful to allow for heavy tails.

> > > > > > > After some prodding from our collaborators, we've recently started looking to DP priors for the center-level effects, especially after seeing these <http://www.stat.ufl.edu/archived/casella/Papers/AOS731.pdf> papers <http://www.stat.ufl.edu/archived/casella/Papers/jasaA07046.pdf> from Casella and co-authors. My questions:
> > > > > > > What do you think of Dirichlet Process priors for something like this? I'm sure you've written about this (beyond BDA3), but I couldn't find much. I'm inclined to be very positive toward them, but I'm still new to this.
> > > > > > > What do you think about trying to hack my way through this in Stan? I've loved having Stan for the rest of this project (in fact, I don't think the project would have been possible without Stan!), but I know that there's no pretty way to pull off a Dirichlet Process prior in Stan at the moment. Hence, before I abandon Stan for this part of the project, I figured it was worth asking.
> > > > > > > Thanks, as always, for the help. And I'll be sending the current Head Start paper your way at some point soon.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: change point models?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: change point models?
messages.body_plain:
As discussed elsewhere on the Stan user list <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/stan-users/change$20point/stan-users/QlgX00f6JG8/ZmNUg7rvZEsJ>, functions with step-like behaviour cause ridges in the posterior (like you say, areas where the gradient is extreme), which are problematic as they may confine the Hamiltonian particle to an area around the posterior mode (or one of the modes), unless the random momentum is just exactly right (not too big to overshoot and prevent efficient sampling, not too small to get stuck around the (or a particular) mode). Correct me if I'm wrong, but the random momentum is calibrated to an optimal values during adaptation, but this is probably optimized such that the sampler explores the area around the mode efficiently, and not the whole posterior. As a result, the sampler will poorly explore tails of the posterior. I remember the Stan dev team pointing out that Stan's samplers work best with posteriors with a curvature close to a normal distribution. Maybe therefore, Stan is currently not very good at fitting non-linear models. Hopefully, Riehmannian HMC will make it possible to better explore extremely curved posteriors (what's the planning for that?). Until that's available, I'm considering using some brute-force methods such as Bayesian melding and incremental mixed importance sampling (IMIS; there's an R package) to fit non-linear models as an alternative to Stan.

Best,
Luc

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: change point models?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: change point models?
messages.body_plain:
Adapatation does a global estimation of the mass matrix (diagonal
by default).  It only uses the second half of the adaptation iterations
to do this, so if the sampler has converged, it will do this in the
high-mass volume of the posterior, aka the typical set, which is
not necessarily very close (especially in high dimensions) to the mode.

For the "step-like" function Sebastian's talking about, if the
multiplier (like an IRT discrimation value) isn't too high, then
the derivatives will still be stable.  You could put a prior on
that multiplier to give it effectively step-like behavior, but
still be stably differentiable, I would think.  Just be sure to
use the log_inv_logit variant for arithmetic stability on the log scale.

I'm not sure what you mean by fitting non-linear models.
Often the posteriors, which is the curvature that matters, can
be normal even when the models don't look particularly normal.
But as Luc says, if there's very high curvature, the Hamiltonian
dynamics simulator (aka the leapfrog integrator) will struggle
and need small step sizes (and hence more time).

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
You probably always want to use NUTS rather than estimating
an optimal number of leapfrog steps, because it's not necessarily
the same for every position and random momentum.

You can fix the step size.

But the easiest thing to do is just set a higher target acceptance
rate for adaptation (the delta parameter), which forces a smaller
step size to ensure a higher acceptance rate.

Michael's been recommending validation runs that crank down the
acceptance rate target substantially to make sure runs with higher
acceptance rates are doing the right things in the tails or other hard
to read parts of the posterior.

- Bob

> > > But, setting those qualms aside, the model seems well-enough specified.  I see the potential HMC problem, though, as there is a discontinuous derivative.  One way to handle this would be to allow the change to be continuous, which in some way is an application of the folk theorem in that I expect actual changes really are continuous.
> > >
> > > Beyond this, we (Stan-dev, that is) might want to think more generally about how to patch models that have bits of discontinuity so they work ok in HMC.  Maybe we can map to some latent continuous model?
> > >
> > > A
> > >
> > > > Has anybody fitted a change point model in Stan, please?
> > > >
> > > > We are interested to fit a change point (broken stick) model in RStan to model longitudinal continuous outcomes measured about three to ten times (at baseline and follow-ups) for each of about hundreds of subjects (i.e. patients in a clinical trial); (So this is different from a time series on a single outcome for a single unit of observation, say a NYSE stock.). The timing of the outcome observations is different for each individual (the patients come in for appointments at different, irregularly), as are the slopes before and after the change point, the intercept and the actual change point itself.
> > > >
> > > > The model:
> > > >
> > > > y[i,k] = beta[pre, i] * (t[i, k] – tau[i]) * I(t[i, k] < tau[i]) + beta[intercept, i]+ beta[post, i] * (t[i,k] – tau[i]) * I(t[i,k] > tau[i]) + epsilon[i,j]
> > > >
> > > > where the error term epsilon [i,k] ~MVN (0, Sigma), iid;
> > > >
> > > > y[i,j,t] is the continuous outcome of the ith subject at the kth observation at time t[i,k]; beta[pre,i] is the random slope for each subject before,  beta[post,i] is the random slope for each subject after the subject specific change point tau. We think a reasonable prior for beta may be ~MVN, iid, but the slopes and intercept are certainly not iid.
> > > >
> > > > I( t[i,k] > tau[i]) is the indicator function used to define a linear spline: (t[i, k] – tau[i]) * I(t[i, k] < tau[i]) = t[i,k] - tau[k]  iff t[i,k] < tau[i] ; 0 otherwise;
> > > >
> > > > tau [i] is the random change point (to be estimated for each subject i); tau [i] is the time of the ‘kink’ in the spline measured before say a diagnosis of dementia.;
> > > >
> > > > See for example attached: Hall CB, Ying J, Kuo L, Sliwinski M, Buschke H, Katz M, Lipton RB. Estimation of bivariate measurements having different change points, with application to cognitive ageing. Stat Med. 2001 Dec 30;20(24):3695-714. PubMed PMID: 11782027.
> > > >
> > > > We are interested to learn from similar models other users may have fitted or know about or to share related functions, now possible in Rstan.
> > > >
> > > > Thank you.

messages.body_plain:
Right — if you’re worried that the adaptation is not finding a small enough step size
then you can rerun with a larger target acceptance probability, or turn off adaptation
altogether and run with a constant step size.  The ultimate issue here is one of
spatially-varying curvature — the integrator needs to have a step size adapted to the
largest curvatures and when there are huge variations this inevitably leads to
inefficient samples in regions of low curvature.

As Bob noted, _always_ run a second chain with a larger target acceptance
probability to be sure that you didn’t miss anything.  And make sure you look at
the n_divergent statistic!  If that’s non-zero you’re already having problems.

If you’re already seeing problems there’s not much you can do.  In fact, such a
pathological model will be hard to fit using almost _any_ algorithm.  Importance
sampling is going to fail just as hard because the hard edges mean that the
importance weights are concentrated on a very small filament that will be hard to
hit with unguided samples.

RHMC will definitely help here, but it won’t be a complete panacea.  I’ve really
bought into the folk theorem in the last year — these kinds of pathological models
typically indicate that the model isn’t quite what you want it to be, either in
terms of the actual specification or it’s explicit parameterization.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] change point models?
messages.body_plain:
> Hmm... RHMC sounds like it is going to solve many problems, but this beast is also very costly computational wise. Is it possible to run RHMC on a sub-space of the parameters space and use HMC for the rest?

Anytime you try to partition parameters you’re going to face a huge drop is performance and
this would be no different.  There are various approximate RHMC implementations that can
be much faster if the pathologies are limited (see the SoftAbs paper), but in the end the kinds
of pathologies we’re talking about increase exponentially with dimension, N, and the N^{3}
cost of RHMC isn’t that bad in comparison.

On Friday, July 18, 2014 11:43:38 AM UTC-4, Amy Shi wrote:
>
> Many thanks, Ben, for the Stan code. It seems that you took difference against the chosen alternative. However, the order of alternatives in a choice set matters. The usual practice is to take difference against a particular alternative, either the first or the last one, so the resulting error difference covariance matrix makes sense. I don't know how to interpret the covariance matrix of the error difference in your set-up.

You could do it that way too. The main motivation for defining a reference category is to obtain identification for maximum likelihood; otherwise you could add a constant to all the raw utilities and not affect the utility differences or the observed choices. That way would be harder in Stan I think because you would have to constrain one utility difference to be positive and the rest negative. The way I did it, the utilities are unconstrained except for one positive difference, and the translation indeterminacy is broken by the standard normal priors on all the coefficients.

>  I have been trying to sample the latent utility variables and the regression coefficients at the same time using HMC. But there is one constraint: the utility for the chosen alternative should be the largest. I am trying to use the "bounce-off-the-walls" technique suggested in section 5.5.1.5 in Neal (2011), but don't know if it will work. Stan uses variable transformation to handle constraints. How should I transfer the latent utilities to avoid constraints?

As Michael mentioned, Stan doesn't have a bouncing sampler to enforce that constraint that utility is highest for the chosen alternative. That is why the model block is so convoluted. Basically, the bump parameter is constrained to be positive and can be interpreted as the difference in utility between the best and second-best alternatives. Then, there is a marginal multivariate normal density for the utility of unchosen alternatives. Finally, there is a truncated univariate normal for the utility of the best alternative conditional on the utility of the unchosen alternatives. So, if you multiply that marginal density and that conditional density together, I think you have the likelihood function implied by the MNP model.

But I didn't actually test it.

Ben

messages.subject: Not needing to recompile a stan model in R
messages.subject_clean: Not needing to recompile a stan model in R
messages.body_plain:
You can use the stan_run() function; just cut and paste this:

stan_run <- function(stanModel, ...) {
  if(class(stanModel) == "stanfit") {
    stanExe <- stanModel
  } else {
    stanModel.rda <- gsub("stan$", "rda", stanModel)
    if(!file.exists(stanModel.rda) || file.info <http://file.info>(stanModel.rda)$mtime < file.info <http://file.info>(stanModel)$mtime) {
      cat("Model",stanModel,"needs recompilation.\n")
      args <- modifyList(list(...), list(file=stanModel, iter=0, warmup=0, chains=0))
      stanExe <- do.call(stan, args)
      saveRDS(stanExe, file=stanModel.rda)
    } else {
      cat("Loading cached stan model", stanModel, ".\n")
      stanExe = readRDS(stanModel.rda)
    }
  }
  # This bit with the seed is for debugging purposes; once we figure out why Stan is crashing R we can remove it.
  seed <- sample.int <http://sample.int>(.Machine$integer.max, 1)
  write (paste (stanModel, seed), file="stan_seed.txt")
  stan(fit=stanExe, seed=seed, …)
}

An example of the use of this function is here:
http://andrewgelman.com/2014/07/13/stan-analyzes-world-cup-data/
Basically, you use it like you’d use stan() and it automatically only recompiles the model when needed.

We’re planning to have this behavior automatically in rstan3, but for now you can use stan_run()

messages.subject: GRM model consulation
messages.subject_clean: GRM model consulation
messages.body_plain:
Hello All,

First off, thank you to everyone who's contributed to this list.  Searching through the questions and answers has helped me solve a number of problems with this model.

The model I'm working on (a version and simulated data are attached) is a graded response IRT model, where the difficulty parameter is decomposed into two components: an item component and a person component.  The person component would theoretically encompass response styles.  I am hoping to capture response style by having respondents answer items with regard to themselves, as well as a vignette (or three, in this case).  Response styles should remain constant across self-report, vignettes, and items.

The model shows poor convergence across parameters.  Rhat is large for most parameters, n_effs can be 2, and the chains wander about.  The problem seems to be caused by difficulties estimating the person difficulties (bi), because RStan frequently warns that the category cutpoints are not appropriately ordered.  The model will converge without bi, or if bi_scale is given a very tight prior.  My hunch is that there is a better way to parameterize bi.  The category cutpoints (bj) can be declared as ordered vectors, but the person parameters can't, so the sum of bi and bj is not always ordered.  The prior on bi_scale (uniform(0,3*N)) should keep bi in about the right range, given the distance between category cutpoints, but that doesn't seem to be enough.

I'd really appreciate your thoughts.  Thanks again to all the list contributors.

Katherine

Hmm, it looks like you’re scaling each cutpoint separately, which would seem like it would leave the vector bi[] not being ordered in at least some cases. Shouldn’t you be multiplying by a single value (or a single value per item, at least)?

Also, I think that’s not the best way to fix a value for bj[1,2]. Better to construct bj in the transformed parameters block, which would require a bit of reorganization of the code, but would allow you to simply assign 0 to bj[1,2]. You’d do something like declare parameters:

ordered[K-1] bj_raw[J-1];
real<upper=0> bj_init_a;
real<lower=0> bj_init_b;

Then in the transformed parameters, declare vector[K-1] bj[J], and:

bj[1,1]<-bj_init_a; bj[1,2]<-0; bj[1,3]<-bj_init_b;
for (j in 2:J) {
bj[j]<-bj_raw[j-1];
}

and put the necessary priors on all the declared parameters (bj_raw, bj_init_a, bj_init_b).

Hope that helps.

Josh

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: change point models?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: change point models?
messages.body_plain:
But Stan only needs log probability, never linear probabilities.
The more you can do things on the log scale, the more stable it
tends to be.

- Bob

On Jul 18, 2014, at 3:52 AM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi Bob!
>
> It certainly makes sense to calculate the log_inv_logit with respect to smooth derivatives - but at some point in time I simply have to back transform it with exp and here I am a bit confused, i.e. at what point should I do that?
>
> I mean the hill function does not live in the log-space, but I need it on the natural scale at some point in time in order to formulate the likelihood.
>
> Best,
> Sebastian
>
> On Friday, July 18, 2014 4:48:55 AM UTC+2, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Adapatation does a global estimation of the mass matrix (diagonal
> by default).  It only uses the second half of the adaptation iterations
> to do this, so if the sampler has converged, it will do this in the
> high-mass volume of the posterior, aka the typical set, which is
> not necessarily very close (especially in high dimensions) to the mode.
>
> For the "step-like" function Sebastian's talking about, if the
> multiplier (like an IRT discrimation value) isn't too high, then
> the derivatives will still be stable.  You could put a prior on
> that multiplier to give it effectively step-like behavior, but
> still be stably differentiable, I would think.  Just be sure to
> use the log_inv_logit variant for arithmetic stability on the log scale.
>
> I'm not sure what you mean by fitting non-linear models.
> Often the posteriors, which is the curvature that matters, can
> be normal even when the models don't look particularly normal.
> But as Luc says, if there's very high curvature, the Hamiltonian
> dynamics simulator (aka the leapfrog integrator) will struggle
> and need small step sizes (and hence more time).
>
> - Bob
>
> On Jul 17, 2014, at 8:07 PM, Luc Coffeng <lucco...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> > As discussed elsewhere on the Stan user list, functions with step-like behaviour cause ridges in the posterior (like you say, areas where the gradient is extreme), which are problematic as they may confine the Hamiltonian particle to an area around the posterior mode (or one of the modes), unless the random momentum is just exactly right (not too big to overshoot and prevent efficient sampling, not too small to get stuck around the (or a particular) mode). Correct me if I'm wrong, but the random momentum is calibrated to an optimal values during adaptation, but this is probably optimized such that the sampler explores the area around the mode efficiently, and not the whole posterior. As a result, the sampler will poorly explore tails of the posterior. I remember the Stan dev team pointing out that Stan's samplers work best with posteriors with a curvature close to a normal distribution. Maybe therefore, Stan is currently not very good at fitting non-linear models. Hopefully, Riehmannian HMC will make it possible to better explore extremely curved posteriors (what's the planning for that?). Until that's available, I'm considering using some brute-force methods such as Bayesian melding and incremental mixed importance sampling (IMIS; there's an R package) to fit non-linear models as an alternative to Stan.
> >
> > Best,
> > Luc
> >
> > On Thursday, 17 July 2014 13:08:21 UTC-7, Sebastian Weber wrote:
> > Hi!
> >
> > Well, not really a change-point model, but something very similar are so-called Emax models in PK/PD. The hill function can be written in terms of the log-concentration like
> >
> > hill(conc) = inv_logit(h * (lconc - lEC50) )
> >
> > here the "l" denotes log. I experienced some issues in Stan when fitting this type of model with h larger than 1. I suppose the derivatives can become quite steep in that case. So if such a function could be stabilized by providing a specialized function, that would be great. The behavior would be such that with h >> 1 the function essentially becomes the step function.
> >
> > Best,
> > Sebastian
> >
> > On Wednesday, July 16, 2014 7:58:20 PM UTC+2, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > You only provided the model part of the Stan program.  It
> > really helps to understand the parameter and data definitions,
> > too.
> >
> > We have alternative recommendations for priors on covariance
> > matrices, but that's a second-order detail.
> >
> > I'm also not clear on why beta[1] is multiplied by 100 on the
> > first line.
> >
> > And wouldn't it be easier to use 2D arrays than fiddling indexes?
> > The latter's very error prone, at least when I'm coding.
> >
> > - Bob
> >
> > On Jul 15, 2014, at 4:53 PM, Michael Andreae <mhan...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > > Update: (thanks to a hint by Dr. Goodrich, with most credit to Jonah Sol Gabry):
> > >
> > > Is this a way around the discontinuous derivative issue?
> > >
> > > Problem: Observational cohort shows an reduction in a disease outcome y after initiation of treatment:
> > >
> > > tau, the single change point where this change occurs, is CONTINUOUS
> > > y, the outcomes is measured k =5 times at irregular intervals x, for each subject n=100
> > > data are in long format, we use a inv-wishart as prior for the beta intercept, beta pre slope and beta post change point slope.
> > > Preliminary model below.
> > >
> > > model{
> > >
> > >   for (i in 1:n) {
> > >           y [i] ~ normal(beta[1]*100,sigma);                               //intercept
> > >
> > >      for (j in 2:k) {
> > >
> > >        if (x [ i + (n* (j-1)) ] <= tau )                            //pre tau point
> > >           y [i + (n* (j-1))] ~ normal (y[i]
> > >                                       +beta [2] * ( x [i + (n* (j-1))] - x[i] ),
> > >                                       sigma);
> > >
> > >        else                                                         //post tau point
> > >           y [i + (n* (j-1))] ~ normal( y[i]
> > >                                        +( beta [2] * (tau - x[i]) )
> > >                                        +( beta [3] * (x [i + (n* (j-1))] - tau)),
> > >                                        sigma);
> > >      }
> > >   }
> > >
> > > beta ~ multi_normal(means, SIGMA);
> > > means ~ normal(0, 1000);
> > > SIGMA ~ inv_wishart(3.0,W);
> > >
> > > On Wednesday, July 2, 2014 3:34:08 PM UTC-4, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> > > Hi all.  I generally don’t like change point models because it’s my impression that real life does not usually have sudden changes—and when sudden changes exist, we usually know when they happen.
> > >
> > > But, setting those qualms aside, the model seems well-enough specified.  I see the potential HMC problem, though, as there is a discontinuous derivative.  One way to handle this would be to allow the change to be continuous, which in some way is an application of the folk theorem in that I expect actual changes really are continuous.
> > >
> > > Beyond this, we (Stan-dev, that is) might want to think more generally about how to patch models that have bits of discontinuity so they work ok in HMC.  Maybe we can map to some latent continuous model?
> > >
> > > A
> > >
> > > > Has anybody fitted a change point model in Stan, please?
> > > >
> > > > We are interested to fit a change point (broken stick) model in RStan to model longitudinal continuous outcomes measured about three to ten times (at baseline and follow-ups) for each of about hundreds of subjects (i.e. patients in a clinical trial); (So this is different from a time series on a single outcome for a single unit of observation, say a NYSE stock.). The timing of the outcome observations is different for each individual (the patients come in for appointments at different, irregularly), as are the slopes before and after the change point, the intercept and the actual change point itself.
> > > >
> > > > The model:
> > > >
> > > > y[i,k] = beta[pre, i] * (t[i, k] – tau[i]) * I(t[i, k] < tau[i]) + beta[intercept, i]+ beta[post, i] * (t[i,k] – tau[i]) * I(t[i,k] > tau[i]) + epsilon[i,j]
> > > >
> > > > where the error term epsilon [i,k] ~MVN (0, Sigma), iid;
> > > >
> > > > y[i,j,t] is the continuous outcome of the ith subject at the kth observation at time t[i,k]; beta[pre,i] is the random slope for each subject before,  beta[post,i] is the random slope for each subject after the subject specific change point tau. We think a reasonable prior for beta may be ~MVN, iid, but the slopes and intercept are certainly not iid.
> > > >
> > > > I( t[i,k] > tau[i]) is the indicator function used to define a linear spline: (t[i, k] – tau[i]) * I(t[i, k] < tau[i]) = t[i,k] - tau[k]  iff t[i,k] < tau[i] ; 0 otherwise;
> > > >
> > > > tau [i] is the random change point (to be estimated for each subject i); tau [i] is the time of the ‘kink’ in the spline measured before say a diagnosis of dementia.;
> > > >
> > > > See for example attached: Hall CB, Ying J, Kuo L, Sliwinski M, Buschke H, Katz M, Lipton RB. Estimation of bivariate measurements having different change points, with application to cognitive ageing. Stat Med. 2001 Dec 30;20(24):3695-714. PubMed PMID: 11782027.
> > > >
> > > > We are interested to learn from similar models other users may have fitted or know about or to share related functions, now possible in Rstan.
> > > >
> > > > Thank you.
> > > >
> > > > Michael Andreae
> > >

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] GRM model consulation
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] GRM model consulation
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the suggestions.  Using only one scale parameter helped.  In this model (attached), the priors on bi_raw and bi_scale are constrained so that bi + bj will be appropriately ordered.  The item cutpoints are declared and fixed as per your suggestion.  With those changes, STAN is producing fewer errors (just one or two per warm up period per chain).

The traces look better than before, but still aren't mixing well (a few from bi are attached).  Rhats are still high, from 1.3 to 20.  However, the bi estimates themselves are generally in the right range.  At least, they tend to be of the same sign as the simulated values.

Another possible hiccup is in the response data.  Some simulated respondents never use certain response categories, due to response style.  It would be very difficult to estimate the third threshold (bi[,3]) for someone who never uses the highest response category.  Simulating more extreme vignettes helps, but in the real world there are often respondents with this sort of response data.  It may call for a ragged array.

On Fri, Jul 18, 2014 at 7:43 PM, Joshua Rosenau <josh.r...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hmm, it looks like you’re scaling each cutpoint separately, which would seem like it would leave the vector bi[] not being ordered in at least some cases. Shouldn’t you be multiplying by a single value (or a single value per item, at least)?
>
> Also, I think that’s not the best way to fix a value for bj[1,2]. Better to construct bj in the transformed parameters block, which would require a bit of reorganization of the code, but would allow you to simply assign 0 to bj[1,2]. You’d do something like declare parameters:
>
> ordered[K-1] bj_raw[J-1];
> real<upper=0> bj_init_a;
> real<lower=0> bj_init_b;
>
> Then in the transformed parameters, declare vector[K-1] bj[J], and:
>
> bj[1,1]<-bj_init_a; bj[1,2]<-0; bj[1,3]<-bj_init_b;
> for (j in 2:J) {
> bj[j]<-bj_raw[j-1];
> }
>
> and put the necessary priors on all the declared parameters (bj_raw, bj_init_a, bj_init_b).
>
> Hope that helps.
>
> Josh
>
> On Jul 18, 2014, at 4:27 PM, Katherine Grace Jonas <katherine....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> > Hello All,
> >
> > First off, thank you to everyone who's contributed to this list.  Searching through the questions and answers has helped me solve a number of problems with this model.
> >
> > The model I'm working on (a version and simulated data are attached) is a graded response IRT model, where the difficulty parameter is decomposed into two components: an item component and a person component.  The person component would theoretically encompass response styles.  I am hoping to capture response style by having respondents answer items with regard to themselves, as well as a vignette (or three, in this case).  Response styles should remain constant across self-report, vignettes, and items.
> >
> > The model shows poor convergence across parameters.  Rhat is large for most parameters, n_effs can be 2, and the chains wander about.  The problem seems to be caused by difficulties estimating the person difficulties (bi), because RStan frequently warns that the category cutpoints are not appropriately ordered.  The model will converge without bi, or if bi_scale is given a very tight prior.  My hunch is that there is a better way to parameterize bi.  The category cutpoints (bj) can be declared as ordered vectors, but the person parameters can't, so the sum of bi and bj is not always ordered.  The prior on bi_scale (uniform(0,3*N)) should keep bi in about the right range, given the distance between category cutpoints, but that doesn't seem to be enough.
> >
> > I'd really appreciate your thoughts.  Thanks again to all the list contributors.
> >
> > Katherine
> >

messages.body_plain:
The reason we're hounding you is that we need to diagnose
the problem if RStan is crashing R so that we can fix the
problem --- right now, we have nothing to go on.

As far as we know, nobody else is having the same kind of
problem.  If you are reading this and are seeing calls to RStan
crash R please let us know, especially if you can provide some
output, or even better, a reproducible example.

Did this happen when you (Andrew) were working with the borrowed
machine, too?  That would probably rule out a hardware problem.

I know you've said it's hard to reproduce and that you don't
have an R script that will crash Stan when run from a fresh
start of R.  That's what makes me think it must be some kind of
statefulness in R itself or your hardware.

As Ben points out, it'd be really helpful if you could
switch to using the terminal version of R for the time
being, then if R crashes, send us the full output that's
printed out by the terminal.

The tedious thing to do would be to keep a *complete* record
of everything you run from the start.  Just keep appending it
to a script in a file somewhere, so that we can run the whole
thing.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
You could still script it, but it'd be a pain.   But
if Stan is really crashing on you all the time as you
say, it shouldn't be that much work.  And even if
the below steps are too hard, maybe you could use the terminal,
since you said it crashed as much there as in RStudio.
Then at least we'd have some clue to go on from the stack
trace.

Your (a) is no problem --- you just need to set a seed
in both R and Stan so the pseudo-random behavior is
reproducible.

Your (b) is harder.  You need to create a snapshot of each
of your edited versions, and swap them in at the appropriate
time.  Otherwise, it wouldn't be an exact
dupe and wouldn't catch issues, say, with dynamically linking
models of the same name.

Just think of these steps as being the software equivalent of model
checking.  It's a huge pain compared to just running a model, but
necessary if you want to diagnose problems.  And diagnosing problems
is the only way to fix them.

You could, of course, solve your problem by restarting R before
each command and re-running the script from scratch, but we want
to fix the underlying problem, assuming there still is one.

- Bob

Thanks for searching the manual, but there's no way
to do that built in yet.

I added a note to our manual issue to clarify the
legal lvalues in a table.

At some point, we'll extend the matrix indexing and
assignment operations to make the R assignment you
want to do legal (either with the syntax as written
or using col() and block() operations --- but I'd
rather do it in full generality).  There's nothing
fundamentally difficult about doing this --- it's just
a matter of getting the coding time to do it.

If it's any help, you can assign rows using syntax

  m[j] <- rv;

where m is a matrix and rv is a row vector.

We'll also be adding the R equivalent of rbind and
cbind if that's what you really want.  But not for 2.4.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi Guys,

Thanks a lot for the interesting discussion, and sorry for the delay. I have prepared a minimal example you can download here <https://docs.google.com/file/d/0B8NMC3DDTeQQOUs5TXF0dnRLZGc/edit?pli=1>, which compares nnls with a nonnegative constrained stan optimization problem.

I tried to make the stan problem as simple as possible, and went with maximum likelihood estimation (squared_error <- dot_self(y - x * beta)) with a simple nonnegative constraint on beta (<lower=0>).

Here are the main problems:
Stan is a few orders slower than nnls.
Stan solutions do not seem correct:  fitted values look nothing like y, while nnls fitted values seem to be a right solution.
Stan is inconsistent: fitted values vary wildly an widely with every run. The answers are very different each time, and so are the processing times.
The above problems almost disappear when the stan problem is unconstrained.

Andrew: I have tried your suggestion, unfortunately it did not work. What you suggested is basically a heavily penalized unconstrained regularized linear regression. This is intrusive to the fitted values, and changes their shape (even with dot_self() version).

messages.body_plain:
Hi David,

Thanks for following up!  For a convex problem like this Stan should definitely be getting to the right answer, even if it might be slower than nnls.  I don't have time today but I'll take a look tomorrow and see what's going on.

Cheers,
Marcus

>
> I tried to make the stan problem as simple as possible, and went with maximum likelihood estimation (squared_error <- dot_self(y - x * beta)) with a simple nonnegative constraint on beta (<lower=0>).

> Stan is a few orders slower than nnls.
> Stan solutions do not seem correct:  fitted values look nothing like y, while nnls fitted values seem to be a right solution.

>
