messages.body_plain:
I have a Stan model that crashes RStudio using RStan. A friend got it to work using CmdStan, so I gave up trying to get it to work in R. I'm at a conference right now, but when I get back home, I will see if I can reproduce the crash using R from the terminal. If so, I'll send the crash message.

Noah Silbert

On Monday, July 21, 2014 1:35:21 AM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> You could still script it, but it'd be a pain.   But
> if Stan is really crashing on you all the time as you
> say, it shouldn't be that much work.  And even if
> the below steps are too hard, maybe you could use the terminal,
> since you said it crashed as much there as in RStudio.
> Then at least we'd have some clue to go on from the stack
> trace.
>
> Your (a) is no problem --- you just need to set a seed
> in both R and Stan so the pseudo-random behavior is
> reproducible.
>
> Your (b) is harder.  You need to create a snapshot of each
> of your edited versions, and swap them in at the appropriate
> time.  Otherwise, it wouldn't be an exact
> dupe and wouldn't catch issues, say, with dynamically linking
> models of the same name.
>
> Just think of these steps as being the software equivalent of model
> checking.  It's a huge pain compared to just running a model, but
> necessary if you want to diagnose problems.  And diagnosing problems
> is the only way to fix them.
>
> You could, of course, solve your problem by restarting R before
> each command and re-running the script from scratch, but we want
> to fix the underlying problem, assuming there still is one.
>
> - Bob
>
>
> On Jul 20, 2014, at 5:00 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>
> > Bob
> > The difficulty of keeping a complete record is that (a) I do a lot of things using random numbers, and (b) I overwrite things.  For example, if I have a stan model foo.stan and I find a typo in it, I just change foo.stan, I don't create a new file name each time I fix the model.  Also, the crashing is intermittent and right now in fact I'm not able to reproduce it.  But I'll let you know next time it happens.
> > A
> >
> > On Jul 20, 2014, at 10:37 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> >
> >> The reason we're hounding you is that we need to diagnose
> >> the problem if RStan is crashing R so that we can fix the
> >> problem --- right now, we have nothing to go on.
> >>
> >> As far as we know, nobody else is having the same kind of
> >> problem.  If you are reading this and are seeing calls to RStan
> >> crash R please let us know, especially if you can provide some
> >> output, or even better, a reproducible example.
> >>
> >> Did this happen when you (Andrew) were working with the borrowed
> >> machine, too?  That would probably rule out a hardware problem.
> >>
> >> I know you've said it's hard to reproduce and that you don't
> >> have an R script that will crash Stan when run from a fresh
> >> start of R.  That's what makes me think it must be some kind of
> >> statefulness in R itself or your hardware.
> >>
> >> As Ben points out, it'd be really helpful if you could
> >> switch to using the terminal version of R for the time
> >> being, then if R crashes, send us the full output that's
> >> printed out by the terminal.
> >>
> >> The tedious thing to do would be to keep a *complete* record
> >> of everything you run from the start.  Just keep appending it
> >> to a script in a file somewhere, so that we can run the whole
> >> thing.
> >>
> >> - Bob
> >>

> >>
> >>> Hi, just to be clear:  I've said all along that the problem is hard for me to reproduce, that I'm working on tracking it down, and I'll let you know when I can reproduce it.  I'm not asking you to diagnose anything.

> >>>
> >>>

> >>>
> >>>> Given that you haven't given us any way to diagnose

> >>>>
> >>>> Could you start using the terminal version so you get

> >>>> - Bob

> >>>>>>> stanExe <- stanModel

> >>>>>>> }

messages.body_plain:
Dear Stan Team,

You guys did great work! A question rises during my play with Stan. Hope you could help me with that.

Q1. In Page 6 of Stan-2.3.0 Reference, you mentioned that "If the prior is uniform, the posterior mode corresponds to the maximum likelihood estimate (MLE) of the parameters". If I want to get MLE of parameters in parameter block in Stan, in model block I should not give those parameters any prior, right? But when I tried comparing results between Stan and SAS (or NONMEM), the MLEs are quite different. Were the estimates by Stan with non-informative prior (priors not specified) really MLEs? I also saw examples of giving weak priors that make the R_hat much better. Do the results with weak priors differs a lot from MLEs?

Q2. If I want to put random effects in the model, then the results run by "optimize" is no longer the MLEs, right? Then I can only use "sample" and take the mean for random effects?

Your answers really help. Thank you so much!

Bests,
Fei

>
> Even if you get that "error" message, I believe you should still get point estimates, but they might be a bit inaccurate.

They are very inaccurate, the fitted values are many orders larger than what they should be.

>
> I would do init="0" in your case iff you use the square() parameterization rather than the fabs() one.

init='0' always gives that error, leaving all betas as 0.

>
> By 3 seconds, do you mean total wall time or just from the time it starts optimizing to when it terminates? RStan is not super efficient at passing data back and forth so that might be noticeable for large scale optimization problems.

Yes, I use system.time(optimizing(...)). I do not think it's rstan to blame, a plain vanilla unconstrained linear regression takes 0.05 seconds with < 3 iterations.

With 3 seconds, it takes about 2,000 iterations to converge, which is not a good sign. I wouldn't mind the 3 seconds timing, but my original problem is a large scale one:

y = x_1 * beta_1
y = x_2 * beta_2
...
y = x_n * beta_n

, where I am trying to get point estimations from many different sets of x_i, for a given y, with n being about 1e6. This is already very slow with looping R's nnls, and I was hoping that I could convert it to one single integrated problem in stan, rather than solving n separate optimizations, with the hope of achieving some speed. At the moment, I'm struggling with matching stan with nnls for n = 1.

>
> Ben

Fei:
1. Stan gives mle (or, if there’s a prior, penalized mle) if you run it in optimize mode, but not if you run it in sampling mode.  Sampling mode is the default.  If you run stan in optimize mode with no piror and the point estimate is not a (local) maximum of the likelihood, there is a problem.
2.  Nonmem also gives marginal mle which is something different.  We’re planning to put marginal mle in Stan but it’s not there yet.

messages.subject: Default priors
messages.subject_clean: Default priors
messages.body_plain:
Hmm, let me make some recommendations:

First, the general ladder of priors:
1.  Noninformative
2.  Weakly informative
3.  Informative

A noninformative prior is typically uniform; it’s what we get when no prior is specified at all (which is why I’ve called it a “default default”).

A weakly informative prior will typically have a scale set to some value larger than 1, on the assumption that the data have been scaled so that parameters should not be much more than 1 in absolute value.  Even after rescaling, though, parameters often _can_ be much less than 1, for example .01 or .001 or even closer to 0).  For this reason, our weakly informative priors typically put a (soft) constraint on the parameter at the high end but not at the low end.  This is why a weakly informative prior can often be specified using just one hyperparameter.  This hyperparameter could have a default value of 10, but for some classes of models that we understand well, we might recommend a smaller value for the default scale, for example 2.5 for logistic regression coefficients.

An informative prior will typically have two hyperparameters, which can be conceptualized as a prior estimate and uncertainty, or as a lower and upper prior bound.

And there are various intermediate steps.  For example, we can be moderately informative, using some subject-matter knowledge to (soft)-constrain a prior distribution but without trying to fully include all prior knowledge.  This can make sense in settings where default weakly informative priors don’t regularize enough, but where we don’t want to put in the effort to fully quantify our prior information.

I’ve struggled for years to put all this in a theoretical framework, and I’m still struggling.  Still, I think what I’m saying is reasonable.

Also, the side note that in some settings we might want boundary-avoiding priors for point estimation (for example, to keep hierarchical variance parameters away from 0) while in other settings we might be happy for point estimates to be on the boundary or to hit some special value (for example, in lasso regression where it is considered desirable to get coefficient estimates of 0).

There’s also this attached paper by Sander Greenland who recommends the log-F family of priors, which he says has better properties than the Cauchy which I’ve been recommending.  He may well be right; I’d never thought that hard about the functional form but I agree that Cauchy is pretty extreme for most applications.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Default priors
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Default priors
messages.body_plain:
For what it’s worth, I like to classify priors by the different criteria
used to chose them.

The “non informative” priors are all dependent on the chosen parameterization (one
of the reasons why we keep getting confused between the Stan default being uniform
on the constrained or uniform on the unconstrained scale).  Essentially you’re choosing
a distinguished parameterization as somehow identifying the right sense of ignorance.

Weakly informative priors set a scale to the problem, identifying “small” and “big” but
being relatively ignorant beyond that.  These are nice because they provide a means
of actually converting domain knowledge into mathematical constructions.

Informative priors, as Andrew notes, add structure beyond the choice of scale.

messages.subject: Using stan as an MCMC kernel within a bigger algorithm
messages.subject_clean: Using stan as an MCMC kernel within a bigger algorithm
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to everyone involved for a very polished piece of software!  Got up and running very quickly (and without a background in bugs!).

I have a question about the viability of using Stan as an implementation of HMC/NUTS for an MCMC kernel - but used in combination with other MCMC kernels that I would like to write myself.

There are a few interesting applications such as:

* a way to handle discrete parameters (i.e. do that bit outside Stan) - although sounds like this will be solved shortly anyway...

* infinite dimensional models.

* applying kernels to annealed distributions e.g. annealed importance sampling

* explicitly using tricks like this: http://andrewgelman.com/2011/10/19/an-interweaving-transformation-strategy-for-boosting-mcmc-efficiency/

My guess is that while this is non-trivial - it can be done by "simply" writing R or python wrappers for a bunch of underlying functions.  Any thoughts?  Is this a common request (sorry if I missed it).

Cheers,
David

If the recomputed lp__ depends on the continuous unknown y, then HMC would need to know the derivative of that with respect to y. And that would basically entail working out the derivative analytically and writing custom C++. Moreover, Stan currently has a really hard distinction between known data (that never changes) and unknown parameters (that it updates). So, there is not a mechanism by which you can pass "data" that is really an unknown that gets updated some other way.

Ben

> My hope was primarily to deal with models changing dimension and with discrete latent variables...   but I put in a couple of other suggestions ...  (I agree the annealing bit is particularly questionable)...  On the other hand Mark Girolami actually recommends interweaving here: http://www.dcs.gla.ac.uk/publications/PAPERS/9382/tech_rep_lgms.pdf .  Iain Murray argues running HMC on the full posterior for latent variable Gaussian process hierarchical  models doesn't work so well - but I must admit I don't understand why.
>
> It is fairly common that a published algorithm uses HMC as a kernel in combination with standard Metropolis-Hastings or Gibbs kernels...  it would be surprising if this were _never_ a good idea....   It would really be wonderful to be able to use Stan to make the HMC part easier...  but it looks like that is at least not easy right now...  although I am still a little puzzled as to why...
>
> Thanks again, for the feed back and for Stan!

Well, if it matters at all I work for Mark, so I'm not coming from an orthogonal direction!

Firstly, the big issue here is sampling jointly or sampling conditionally.  Sampling conditionally is always going to bring in problems when the target measure has large correlations, i.e. any realistic problem.  HMC appears to use a Gibbs step to sample the auxiliary momenta, but technically that sampling is doing something else.  Ignoring the technical details, HMC is making a joint update of all the model parameters which is what is important.

This leaves two issues: hierarchical modes are hard and discrete models are harder.

We review hierarchical models thoroughly in http://arxiv.org/abs/1312.0906, in particular we address why Euclidean HMC can run into problems.  A common approach that people take, starting with Radford Neal way back when he was first introducing HMC into stats, is to sample from the hyperparameters conditional on the local parameters,
but this inevitably leads to large autocorrelations because of the strong dependencies between the hyperparameters and the local parameters.  What you'd really want to do is sample from the marginal distribution of the hyperparameters, but computing that distribution is a tremendously difficult task.  Pseudomarginal methods are trying to solve this, but they are hard to make general and can run into their own pathologies.  As noted in the paper, Riemannian HMC solves many of these problems by construction, and it's coming soon to Stan.  At the moment your best bet is to find a good non-centered parameterization.

Everyone wants discrete parameters but everyone also needs to understand the underlying problems.  Without the nice structure of a continuous measure, it's very, very hard to construct an efficient sampler.  Moreover, if you split your parameters into continuous and discrete then you're doing conditional updates, which will be slow as discussed above.  We've seen lots of success when the discrete parameters can be marginalized out to give a fully continuous model amenable to HMC.  This includes discrete latent models, provided there aren't too many possible states.

You can certainly use Stan as a sampling API and stick it into a bigger sampler, but without addressing the fundamental problems with discrete variables and conditional updates you're only going to be able to go so far.

On Jul 22, 2014, at 1:27 AM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:

> For what it's worth, I like to classify priors by the different criteria
> used to chose them.
>
> The "non informative" priors are all dependent on the chosen parameterization (one
> of the reasons why we keep getting confused between the Stan default being uniform
> on the constrained or uniform on the unconstrained scale).  Essentially you're choosing
> a distinguished parameterization as somehow identifying the right sense of ignorance.
>
> Weakly informative priors set a scale to the problem, identifying "small" and "big" but
> being relatively ignorant beyond that.  These are nice because they provide a means
> of actually converting domain knowledge into mathematical constructions.
>
> Informative priors, as Andrew notes, add structure beyond the choice of scale.
>
>
> On Jul 21, 2014, at 11:45 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>
> > Hmm, let me make some recommendations:
> >
> > First, the general ladder of priors:
> > 1.  Noninformative
> > 2.  Weakly informative
> > 3.  Informative
> >
> > A noninformative prior is typically uniform; it's what we get when no prior is specified at all (which is why I've called it a "default default").
> >
> > A weakly informative prior will typically have a scale set to some value larger than 1, on the assumption that the data have been scaled so that parameters should not be much more than 1 in absolute value.  Even after rescaling, though, parameters often _can_ be much less than 1, for example .01 or .001 or even closer to 0).  For this reason, our weakly informative priors typically put a (soft) constraint on the parameter at the high end but not at the low end.  This is why a weakly informative prior can often be specified using just one hyperparameter.  This hyperparameter could have a default value of 10, but for some classes of models that we understand well, we might recommend a smaller value for the default scale, for example 2.5 for logistic regression coefficients.
> >
> > An informative prior will typically have two hyperparameters, which can be conceptualized as a prior estimate and uncertainty, or as a lower and upper prior bound.
> >
> > And there are various intermediate steps.  For example, we can be moderately informative, using some subject-matter knowledge to (soft)-constrain a prior distribution but without trying to fully include all prior knowledge.  This can make sense in settings where default weakly informative priors don't regularize enough, but where we don't want to put in the effort to fully quantify our prior information.
> >
> > I've struggled for years to put all this in a theoretical framework, and I'm still struggling.  Still, I think what I'm saying is reasonable.
> >
> > Also, the side note that in some settings we might want boundary-avoiding priors for point estimation (for example, to keep hierarchical variance parameters away from 0) while in other settings we might be happy for point estimates to be on the boundary or to hit some special value (for example, in lasso regression where it is considered desirable to get coefficient estimates of 0).
> >
> > There's also this attached paper by Sander Greenland who recommends the log-F family of priors, which he says has better properties than the Cauchy which I've been recommending.  He may well be right; I'd never thought that hard about the functional form but I agree that Cauchy is pretty extreme for most applications.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Using stan as an MCMC kernel within a bigger algorithm
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Using stan as an MCMC kernel within a bigger algorithm
messages.body_plain:
I'm not a stan user, but I have implemented NUTS together with other samplers, particularly DREAM (and RWM). The reason is two-fold - DREAM can handle, at least to some degree, discrete parameters and multi-modal situations. Secondly, when DREAM works well, it works well, and can be faster than NUTS. So I mix randomly DREAM and NUTS, in concept NUTS is used to generate a good population, and then DREAM is used to sample and difference from that population. This is all done randomly at each step and for each chain.

This also avoids one of the main pitfalls of DREAM, IMHO, that heuristic tricks have to be used to make it go outside of the hyperplane defined by the chains at the current step. The inclusion of NUTS means that those tricks are no longer needed.

In addition, I examine the acceptance rate for DREAM, and vary the proportion of time spent in DREAM according to how close the acceptance rate is to the theoretical value for normal distributions. I use dual averaging for the DREAM step (i.e. the scaled difference).

Remarkably, the dual averaging generated a step size almost identical to the theoretical value for a normal test problem. Well, I'm always surprised when theory meets practice.

So, long story short, I found value in mixing samplers. It's the same when you mix optimisation algorithms, they all have different good and bad behaviours, and a mixture is more robust.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Can stan be used for a fast replacement of linear/nonlinear regression?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Can stan be used for a fast replacement of linear/nonlinear regression?
messages.body_plain:
Hi David,

So I took a look at what was going on with this case and I've found a few things

- The optimal solution (from nnls) is very sparse, i.e., all but maybe a dozen coefficients are zero.  This solution is going to be very hard (if not impossible) for Stan to reach using the parameterization (using lower=0) that you used in the basic model.  This is because in the unconstrained domain, a parameter needs to effectively get to infinity for it to be zero.  Worse though is that it is definitely possible for it to converge to bad solution due to numerical issues.  This happens when the unconstrained parameter x becomes sufficiently negative that exp(x) underflows and is numerically zero.  The problem is that then the derivative wrt x becomes zero and this parameter will *never* change again.  So, if the optimizer over shoots for a parameter, it can get stuck in a bad place.  Worse, this can't be easily diagnosed because it's gradient will appear to be zero!

To summarize for users:  If you are optimizing and expect your solution to end up on a constraint boundary, *do not* use Stan's "lower=" or "upper=" constraints.  They will almost certainly result in failures and it's likely that it there will be no obvious indication that it's failed.

For stan-dev:  It would be really nice if we could handle simple bound constraints directly in the optimizer.  One more thing to put on the (ever-growing) todo list...  Also, it may be worth checking for underflow in exp() and throwing an exception.  I hate to do it because it's going to potentially really hurt performance, but issues like this seem to pop up more than I'd like.

- Using a squared or fabs parameterization avoids this issue for the most part.  You can't use init=0 in this case because the gradients are all zero there, but otherwise it will work better.  However for it to have a chance of working, you need to normalize your data a bit.  Right now the scale on the data is huge which is blowing out the gradients and making it difficult for the optimizer to make initial progress.  You should normalize your data to have a std dev of 1.  Note that this can even be done in the transformed data block of the Stan model to make it easier.

- This model is sufficiently large that you'll want to use LBFGS instead of BFGS.  On my machine LBFGS is about 40 times faster for your data.  As an added bonus, because LBFGS is often better at adapting to curvature changes, it actually gets to a better optimum for me.

- Also, be aware of the convergence criteria.  They are set to values which are reasonable but certainly may need to be adjusted for different problems.  If the optimizer is stopping but not at the right solution, consider adjusting (or turning off) some of the convergence tests.  E.G., for your data and model I found turning off the relative convergence tests to be useful.  See also normalizing your data.

- The model could be made a bit faster by using squared_distance() instead of dot_self().  (Not a huge speedup, but it will help a little bit.)

Play around a bit with normalizing your data, using the squared() parameterization and LBFGS and let us know how it goes.

Cheers,
Marcus

I hate to do it because it's going to potentially really hurt performance, but issues like this seem to pop up more than I'd like.
> > >
> > > - Using a squared or fabs parameterization avoids this issue for the most part.  You can't use init=0 in this case because the gradients are all zero there, but otherwise it will work better.  However for it to have a chance of working, you need to normalize your data a bit.  Right now the scale on the data is huge which is blowing out the gradients and making it difficult for the optimizer to make initial progress.  You should normalize your data to have a std dev of 1.  Note that this can even be done in the transformed data block of the Stan model to make it easier.
> > >
> > > - This model is sufficiently large that you'll want to use LBFGS instead of BFGS.  On my machine LBFGS is about 40 times faster for your data.  As an added bonus, because LBFGS is often better at adapting to curvature changes, it actually gets to a better optimum for me.
> > >
> > > - Also, be aware of the convergence criteria.  They are set to values which are reasonable but certainly may need to be adjusted for different problems.  If the optimizer is stopping but not at the right solution, consider adjusting (or turning off) some of the convergence tests.  E.G., for your data and model I found turning off the relative convergence tests to be useful.  See also normalizing your data.
> > >
> > > - The model could be made a bit faster by using squared_distance() instead of dot_self().  (Not a huge speedup, but it will help a little bit.)

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Using stan as an MCMC kernel within a bigger algorithm
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Using stan as an MCMC kernel within a bigger algorithm
messages.body_plain:
The technical problem right now in plugging samples back into
Stan is that there's not an easy way to pull the adapted mass matrix out
and then plug it back in.  We'll be making that easier going forward,
probably as part of Stan 3, which is not on the near term horizon yet,
but we're working on design.

- Bob

On Jul 22, 2014, at 7:27 AM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:

>
> My hope was primarily to deal with models changing dimension and with discrete latent variables...   but I put in a couple of other suggestions ...  (I agree the annealing bit is particularly questionable)...  On the other hand Mark Girolami actually recommends interweaving here: http://www.dcs.gla.ac.uk/publications/PAPERS/9382/tech_rep_lgms.pdf .  Iain Murray argues running HMC on the full posterior for latent variable Gaussian process hierarchical  models doesn't work so well - but I must admit I don't understand why.
>
> It is fairly common that a published algorithm uses HMC as a kernel in combination with standard Metropolis-Hastings or Gibbs kernels...  it would be surprising if this were _never_ a good idea....   It would really be wonderful to be able to use Stan to make the HMC part easier...  but it looks like that is at least not easy right now...  although I am still a little puzzled as to why...
>
> Thanks again, for the feed back and for Stan!
>
> Well, if it matters at all I work for Mark, so I'm not coming from an orthogonal direction!
>
> Firstly, the big issue here is sampling jointly or sampling conditionally.  Sampling conditionally is always going to bring in problems when the target measure has large correlations, i.e. any realistic problem.  HMC appears to use a Gibbs step to sample the auxiliary momenta, but technically that sampling is doing something else.  Ignoring the technical details, HMC is making a joint update of all the model parameters which is what is important.
>
> This leaves two issues: hierarchical modes are hard and discrete models are harder.
>
> We review hierarchical models thoroughly in http://arxiv.org/abs/1312.0906, in particular we address why Euclidean HMC can run into problems.  A common approach that people take, starting with Radford Neal way back when he was first introducing HMC into stats, is to sample from the hyperparameters conditional on the local parameters,
> but this inevitably leads to large autocorrelations because of the strong dependencies between the hyperparameters and the local parameters.  What you'd really want to do is sample from the marginal distribution of the hyperparameters, but computing that distribution is a tremendously difficult task.  Pseudomarginal methods are trying to solve this, but they are hard to make general and can run into their own pathologies.  As noted in the paper, Riemannian HMC solves many of these problems by construction, and it's coming soon to Stan.  At the moment your best bet is to find a good non-centered parameterization.
>
> Everyone wants discrete parameters but everyone also needs to understand the underlying problems.  Without the nice structure of a continuous measure, it's very, very hard to construct an efficient sampler.  Moreover, if you split your parameters into continuous and discrete then you're doing conditional updates, which will be slow as discussed above.  We've seen lots of success when the discrete parameters can be marginalized out to give a fully continuous model amenable to HMC.  This includes discrete latent models, provided there aren't too many possible states.
>
> You can certainly use Stan as a sampling API and stick it into a bigger sampler, but without addressing the fundamental problems with discrete variables and conditional updates you're only going to be able to go so far.
>
>

messages.body_plain:
How do you deal with the interleaving when DREAM assumes an ensemble
and HMC/NUTS don't?  And just to be clear here, DREAM isn't a random
walk algorithm in the same way as Metropolis and Gibbs are.

We're working on some ensemble samplers now, starting with the Goodman-Weare
versions, but we'll probably also implement differential evolution (which in my
understanding is like DREAM w/o the detailed-balance violating heuristics).

- Bob

On Jul 22, 2014, at 2:27 PM, Nigel Goodwin <goo...@essence-property.com> wrote:

> I'm not a stan user, but I have implemented NUTS together with other samplers, particularly DREAM (and RWM). The reason is two-fold - DREAM can handle, at least to some degree, discrete parameters and multi-modal situations. Secondly, when DREAM works well, it works well, and can be faster than NUTS. So I mix randomly DREAM and NUTS, in concept NUTS is used to generate a good population, and then DREAM is used to sample and difference from that population. This is all done randomly at each step and for each chain.
>
> This also avoids one of the main pitfalls of DREAM, IMHO, that heuristic tricks have to be used to make it go outside of the hyperplane defined by the chains at the current step. The inclusion of NUTS means that those tricks are no longer needed.
>
> In addition, I examine the acceptance rate for DREAM, and vary the proportion of time spent in DREAM according to how close the acceptance rate is to the theoretical value for normal distributions. I use dual averaging for the DREAM step (i.e. the scaled difference).
>
> Remarkably, the dual averaging generated a step size almost identical to the theoretical value for a normal test problem. Well, I'm always surprised when theory meets practice.
>
> So, long story short, I found value in mixing samplers. It's the same when you mix optimisation algorithms, they all have different good and bad behaviours, and a mixture is more robust.
>
>
> On Tuesday, 22 July 2014 14:40:05 UTC+1, david...@gmail.com wrote:
>
> Random walk on the hyperparameters isn't going to do anyone any good.  Certainly in the worst case HMC reduces to a random walk, so why not just use it in the first place?
>
>
> I believe its the overhead of HMC.  On a per iteration basis I agree random walk Metropolis has no advantage - but random walk Metropolis will iterate faster...  but see the conclusion of Filippone rather than have me paraphrase...
>
>  Of course any algorithm will work well in some circumstances, but we're (okay, maybe I should just speak for myself) interested in algorithms that work well with great generality,
> and Gibbs is not going to be that algorithm, especially for modern applied problems.
>
>
> I take your point completely - but would still like to be able to use Gibbs/single component Metropolis for problems that I don't know how to do anything else with - and for which there is some sort of track record of at least moderate performance....
>
> I really look forward to modifications to rstan that make this possible.  Thanks again for your advice and pointers!
>
> Cheers,
> David

On Jul 22, 2014, at 10:01 AM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:

> +1
> On Jul 22, 2014, at 1:27 AM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>> For what it's worth, I like to classify priors by the different criteria
>> used to chose them.
>>
>> The "non informative" priors are all dependent on the chosen parameterization (one
>> of the reasons why we keep getting confused between the Stan default being uniform
>> on the constrained or uniform on the unconstrained scale).  Essentially you're choosing
>> a distinguished parameterization as somehow identifying the right sense of ignorance.
>>
>> Weakly informative priors set a scale to the problem, identifying "small" and "big" but
>> being relatively ignorant beyond that.  These are nice because they provide a means
>> of actually converting domain knowledge into mathematical constructions.
>>
>> Informative priors, as Andrew notes, add structure beyond the choice of scale.
>>
>>
>> On Jul 21, 2014, at 11:45 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>>
>>> Hmm, let me make some recommendations:
>>>
>>> First, the general ladder of priors:
>>> 1.  Noninformative
>>> 2.  Weakly informative
>>> 3.  Informative
>>>
>>> A noninformative prior is typically uniform; it's what we get when no prior is specified at all (which is why I've called it a "default default").
>>>
>>> A weakly informative prior will typically have a scale set to some value larger than 1, on the assumption that the data have been scaled so that parameters should not be much more than 1 in absolute value.  Even after rescaling, though, parameters often _can_ be much less than 1, for example .01 or .001 or even closer to 0).  For this reason, our weakly informative priors typically put a (soft) constraint on the parameter at the high end but not at the low end.  This is why a weakly informative prior can often be specified using just one hyperparameter.  This hyperparameter could have a default value of 10, but for some classes of models that we understand well, we might recommend a smaller value for the default scale, for example 2.5 for logistic regression coefficients.
>>>
>>> An informative prior will typically have two hyperparameters, which can be conceptualized as a prior estimate and uncertainty, or as a lower and upper prior bound.
>>>
>>> And there are various intermediate steps.  For example, we can be moderately informative, using some subject-matter knowledge to (soft)-constrain a prior distribution but without trying to fully include all prior knowledge.  This can make sense in settings where default weakly informative priors don't regularize enough, but where we don't want to put in the effort to fully quantify our prior information.
>>>
>>> I've struggled for years to put all this in a theoretical framework, and I'm still struggling.  Still, I think what I'm saying is reasonable.
>>>
>>> Also, the side note that in some settings we might want boundary-avoiding priors for point estimation (for example, to keep hierarchical variance parameters away from 0) while in other settings we might be happy for point estimates to be on the boundary or to hit some special value (for example, in lasso regression where it is considered desirable to get coefficient estimates of 0).
>>>
>>> There's also this attached paper by Sander Greenland who recommends the log-F family of priors, which he says has better properties than the Cauchy which I've been recommending.  He may well be right; I'd never thought that hard about the functional form but I agree that Cauchy is pretty extreme for most applications.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Using stan as an MCMC kernel within a bigger algorithm
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Using stan as an MCMC kernel within a bigger algorithm
messages.body_plain:
Bob, I'm afraid I don't know exactly what you mean by 'ensemble' and 'interweaving'. But maybe this will help:

- I use multiple chains (8, for no particular reason), and parallelise at the likelihood function level, not the chain level. So I loop over steps, and for each step I loop over chains. I choose at random (with sampler weights) for each step/chain what sampler I am using, so for a given step there are multiple samplers, and of course the NUTS sampler takes a lot longer than the DREAM sampler, but that is OK because of the way I parallelise. It would be hopeless if I parallelised at the chain level.

- there are several different versions of DREAM. Some sample from other chains at the same step, others sample from a store of previous steps (DREAMZ). I use both methods. In pure DREAM, the problem with sampling from other chains is the one I mentioned, getting stuck in the same hyperplane, and they have various methods to overcome this, none of which I like. They are Gibbs-like, which is hopeless if the likelihood is not aligned with the axes. But by combining with NUTS, this problem is avoided. All the complexity of DREAM (choosing subsets of parameters, adding in a bit of random walk) can be avoided.

- I have a feeling, and it is no more than that, that DREAM sampling from other chains has a more satisfactory detailed balance proof, hence why I use multiple chains. But I may be wrong. the 'proofs' in DREAM are rather sketchy.

- whether the DREAM family, or my combined approach, strictly obey the necessary rules, is not something I am qualified to discuss. But in my tests they successfully reproduce the analytical results for complex high dimensional problems, which is more than good enough for my audience.

- speed and performance is critical in my application, it is an interactive tool for engineers which repeats MC many times, so I have to make some compromises to get the performance. Whether the compromises are real or imaginary I don't know (see above!), but without performance nobody would use it.

My video http://www.youtube.com/channel/UCQbRkgaevt0TSDzipvmtMKQ

shows, for EssRisk64DNormal, this combined approach for a 64 dimensional multivariate normal. In this case I have one chain, and DREAM samples from the store. Blue jumps are DREAM, green jumps are NUTS.

For the Haario problem (64 dimensional, each pair of parameters is a 2D Haario function, so it is much harder than the published function) DREAM works much less well, for obvious reasons. But my algorithm can recognise this, and adjust the amount of DREAM usage accordingly.

In concept, I guess you could say NUTS does the exploration, and other samplers fill in the gaps.

Also, when you combine samplers, you may need to look at modifying the algorithms for the individual samples, as I did for DREAM.  This is just the same when, for example, you combine evolutionary algorithm optimisers with local gradient optimisers - just plugging the two together is not a satisfactory solution, they have influence on each other, and opportunities also.

I really must look at Goodman-Weare in more detail one day.

Nigel

On Wednesday, 23 July 2014 05:58:21 UTC+1, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> How do you deal with the interleaving when DREAM assumes an ensemble
> and HMC/NUTS don't?  And just to be clear here, DREAM isn't a random
> walk algorithm in the same way as Metropolis and Gibbs are.
>
> We're working on some ensemble samplers now, starting with the Goodman-Weare
> versions, but we'll probably also implement differential evolution (which in my
> understanding is like DREAM w/o the detailed-balance violating heuristics).
>
> - Bob
>
>
> On Jul 22, 2014, at 2:27 PM, Nigel Goodwin <goo...@essence-property.com> wrote:
>
> > I'm not a stan user, but I have implemented NUTS together with other samplers, particularly DREAM (and RWM). The reason is two-fold - DREAM can handle, at least to some degree, discrete parameters and multi-modal situations. Secondly, when DREAM works well, it works well, and can be faster than NUTS. So I mix randomly DREAM and NUTS, in concept NUTS is used to generate a good population, and then DREAM is used to sample and difference from that population. This is all done randomly at each step and for each chain.
> >
> > This also avoids one of the main pitfalls of DREAM, IMHO, that heuristic tricks have to be used to make it go outside of the hyperplane defined by the chains at the current step. The inclusion of NUTS means that those tricks are no longer needed.
> >
> > In addition, I examine the acceptance rate for DREAM, and vary the proportion of time spent in DREAM according to how close the acceptance rate is to the theoretical value for normal distributions. I use dual averaging for the DREAM step (i.e. the scaled difference).
> >
> > Remarkably, the dual averaging generated a step size almost identical to the theoretical value for a normal test problem. Well, I'm always surprised when theory meets practice.
> >
> > So, long story short, I found value in mixing samplers. It's the same when you mix optimisation algorithms, they all have different good and bad behaviours, and a mixture is more robust.
> >
> >
> > On Tuesday, 22 July 2014 14:40:05 UTC+1, david...@gmail.com wrote:
> >
> > Random walk on the hyperparameters isn't going to do anyone any good.  Certainly in the worst case HMC reduces to a random walk, so why not just use it in the first place?
> >
> >
> > I believe its the overhead of HMC.  On a per iteration basis I agree random walk Metropolis has no advantage - but random walk Metropolis will iterate faster...  but see the conclusion of Filippone rather than have me paraphrase...
> >
> >  Of course any algorithm will work well in some circumstances, but we're (okay, maybe I should just speak for myself) interested in algorithms that work well with great generality,
> > and Gibbs is not going to be that algorithm, especially for modern applied problems.
> >
> >
> > I take your point completely - but would still like to be able to use Gibbs/single component Metropolis for problems that I don't know how to do anything else with - and for which there is some sort of track record of at least moderate performance....
> >
> > I really look forward to modifications to rstan that make this possible.  Thanks again for your advice and pointers!
> >
> > Cheers,
> > David

messages.body_plain:
Agreed!

On Wednesday, July 23, 2014 1:15:21 AM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:

> Indeed.  This is important.
>
> Thanks again for the ongoing tutorials!
>
> - Bob
>
> On Jul 22, 2014, at 10:01 AM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>
> > +1
> > On Jul 22, 2014, at 1:27 AM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> >> For what it's worth, I like to classify priors by the different criteria
> >> used to chose them.
> >>
> >> The "non informative" priors are all dependent on the chosen parameterization (one
> >> of the reasons why we keep getting confused between the Stan default being uniform
> >> on the constrained or uniform on the unconstrained scale).  Essentially you're choosing
> >> a distinguished parameterization as somehow identifying the right sense of ignorance.
> >>
> >> Weakly informative priors set a scale to the problem, identifying "small" and "big" but
> >> being relatively ignorant beyond that.  These are nice because they provide a means
> >> of actually converting domain knowledge into mathematical constructions.
> >>
> >> Informative priors, as Andrew notes, add structure beyond the choice of scale.
> >>
> >>
> >> On Jul 21, 2014, at 11:45 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
> >>
> >>> Hmm, let me make some recommendations:
> >>>
> >>> First, the general ladder of priors:
> >>> 1.  Noninformative
> >>> 2.  Weakly informative
> >>> 3.  Informative
> >>>
> >>> A noninformative prior is typically uniform; it's what we get when no prior is specified at all (which is why I've called it a "default default").
> >>>
> >>> A weakly informative prior will typically have a scale set to some value larger than 1, on the assumption that the data have been scaled so that parameters should not be much more than 1 in absolute value.  Even after rescaling, though, parameters often _can_ be much less than 1, for example .01 or .001 or even closer to 0).  For this reason, our weakly informative priors typically put a (soft) constraint on the parameter at the high end but not at the low end.  This is why a weakly informative prior can often be specified using just one hyperparameter.  This hyperparameter could have a default value of 10, but for some classes of models that we understand well, we might recommend a smaller value for the default scale, for example 2.5 for logistic regression coefficients.
> >>>
> >>> An informative prior will typically have two hyperparameters, which can be conceptualized as a prior estimate and uncertainty, or as a lower and upper prior bound.
> >>>
> >>> And there are various intermediate steps.  For example, we can be moderately informative, using some subject-matter knowledge to (soft)-constrain a prior distribution but without trying to fully include all prior knowledge.  This can make sense in settings where default weakly informative priors don't regularize enough, but where we don't want to put in the effort to fully quantify our prior information.
> >>>
> >>> I've struggled for years to put all this in a theoretical framework, and I'm still struggling.  Still, I think what I'm saying is reasonable.
> >>>
> >>> Also, the side note that in some settings we might want boundary-avoiding priors for point estimation (for example, to keep hierarchical variance parameters away from 0) while in other settings we might be happy for point estimates to be on the boundary or to hit some special value (for example, in lasso regression where it is considered desirable to get coefficient estimates of 0).
> >>>
> >>> There's also this attached paper by Sander Greenland who recommends the log-F family of priors, which he says has better properties than the Cauchy which I've been recommending.  He may well be right; I'd never thought that hard about the functional form but I agree that Cauchy is pretty extreme for most applications.
> >>>
> >>>
> >>> On Jul 14, 2014, at 7:31 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> >>>
> >>>> We still have uniform priors on intervals in examples.
> >>>>
> >>>> I've been waiting to hear from you on what I should replace them with
> >>>> in the manual examples.  You hinted at a blog post forthcoming.
> >>>>
> >>>> Most of the examples are for example models, like linear regressions,
> >>>> so the priors should just be default family recommendations.
> >>>>
> >>>> lognormal?
> >>>>
> >>>> exponential?
> >>>>

Hi Marcus,

Excellent advices. Thank you for trying the data and model.

I have applied your advices and here are the results and some questions:

- The most noticeable impact was by changing the algorithm from BFGS to LBFGS. It got faster by 1 order.

- By adjusting convergence tests, do you mean the optional arguments of optimizing() function, such as tol_rel_obj and tol_rel_grad? How can they be turned off? The rdoc says: 'tol_rel_grad (double, default to 1e7), for BFGS and LBFGS, see the manual of Stan', but I couldn't find these in stan manual.

- I still get line search errors for some random seeds.

- Consider generalizing this problem in two directions:

(1) y_1 = x * beta_1, y_2 = x * beta_2, ..., y_n = x * beta_n
(2) y = x_1 * beta_1, y = x_2 * beta_2, ..., y = x_m * beta_m

Would these problem solving time in stan increase linearly by n (or m), or is there anything that stan can do to avoid re-computations? For instance, in problem (1), x is shared between all equations, when n is about 1e3, how can we take advantage of this shared predictor x?

On Tuesday, July 22, 2014 8:29:39 PM UTC+1, Marcus wrote:
> Hi David,
>
> So I took a look at what was going on with this case and I've found a few things
>
> - The optimal solution (from nnls) is very sparse, i.e., all but maybe a dozen coefficients are zero.  This solution is going to be very hard (if not impossible) for Stan to reach using the parameterization (using lower=0) that you used in the basic model.  This is because in the unconstrained domain, a parameter needs to effectively get to infinity for it to be zero.  Worse though is that it is definitely possible for it to converge to bad solution due to numerical issues.  This happens when the unconstrained parameter x becomes sufficiently negative that exp(x) underflows and is numerically zero.  The problem is that then the derivative wrt x becomes zero and this parameter will *never* change again.  So, if the optimizer over shoots for a parameter, it can get stuck in a bad place.  Worse, this can't be easily diagnosed because it's gradient will appear to be zero!
>
> To summarize for users:  If you are optimizing and expect your solution to end up on a constraint boundary, *do not* use Stan's "lower=" or "upper=" constraints.  They will almost certainly result in failures and it's likely that it there will be no obvious indication that it's failed.
>
> For stan-dev:  It would be really nice if we could handle simple bound constraints directly in the optimizer.  One more thing to put on the (ever-growing) todo list...  Also, it may be worth checking for underflow in exp() and throwing an exception.  I hate to do it because it's going to potentially really hurt performance, but issues like this seem to pop up more than I'd like.
>
> - Using a squared or fabs parameterization avoids this issue for the most part.  You can't use init=0 in this case because the gradients are all zero there, but otherwise it will work better.  However for it to have a chance of working, you need to normalize your data a bit.  Right now the scale on the data is huge which is blowing out the gradients and making it difficult for the optimizer to make initial progress.  You should normalize your data to have a std dev of 1.  Note that this can even be done in the transformed data block of the Stan model to make it easier.
>
> - This model is sufficiently large that you'll want to use LBFGS instead of BFGS.  On my machine LBFGS is about 40 times faster for your data.  As an added bonus, because LBFGS is often better at adapting to curvature changes, it actually gets to a better optimum for me.
>
> - Also, be aware of the convergence criteria.  They are set to values which are reasonable but certainly may need to be adjusted for different problems.  If the optimizer is stopping but not at the right solution, consider adjusting (or turning off) some of the convergence tests.  E.G., for your data and model I found turning off the relative convergence tests to be useful.  See also normalizing your data.
>
> - The model could be made a bit faster by using squared_distance() instead of dot_self().  (Not a huge speedup, but it will help a little bit.)
>
> Play around a bit with normalizing your data, using the squared() parameterization and LBFGS and let us know how it goes.
>
> Cheers,
> Marcus

messages.body_plain:
What I meant is how do you combine HMC and ensemble methods.

An ensemble method uses K ensemble members, each being
a complete set of parameter values, whereas HMC works for a
single value of the parameters.  The entire ensemble is what
makes up the Markov chain in the ensemble method --- the
individual ensemble members do not form a Markov chain by
themselves.

You can find the detailed balance proofs for the simplified
version in ter Braak's paper on differential evolution.

- Bob

On Jul 23, 2014, at 6:39 AM, Nigel Goodwin <goo...@essence-property.com> wrote:

> Bob, I'm afraid I don't know exactly what you mean by 'ensemble' and 'interweaving'. But maybe this will help:
>
> - I use multiple chains (8, for no particular reason), and parallelise at the likelihood function level, not the chain level. So I loop over steps, and for each step I loop over chains. I choose at random (with sampler weights) for each step/chain what sampler I am using, so for a given step there are multiple samplers, and of course the NUTS sampler takes a lot longer than the DREAM sampler, but that is OK because of the way I parallelise. It would be hopeless if I parallelised at the chain level.
>
> - there are several different versions of DREAM. Some sample from other chains at the same step, others sample from a store of previous steps (DREAMZ). I use both methods. In pure DREAM, the problem with sampling from other chains is the one I mentioned, getting stuck in the same hyperplane, and they have various methods to overcome this, none of which I like. They are Gibbs-like, which is hopeless if the likelihood is not aligned with the axes. But by combining with NUTS, this problem is avoided. All the complexity of DREAM (choosing subsets of parameters, adding in a bit of random walk) can be avoided.
>
> - I have a feeling, and it is no more than that, that DREAM sampling from other chains has a more satisfactory detailed balance proof, hence why I use multiple chains. But I may be wrong. the 'proofs' in DREAM are rather sketchy.
>
> - whether the DREAM family, or my combined approach, strictly obey the necessary rules, is not something I am qualified to discuss. But in my tests they successfully reproduce the analytical results for complex high dimensional problems, which is more than good enough for my audience.
>
> - speed and performance is critical in my application, it is an interactive tool for engineers which repeats MC many times, so I have to make some compromises to get the performance. Whether the compromises are real or imaginary I don't know (see above!), but without performance nobody would use it.
>
> My video http://www.youtube.com/channel/UCQbRkgaevt0TSDzipvmtMKQ
>
> shows, for EssRisk64DNormal, this combined approach for a 64 dimensional multivariate normal. In this case I have one chain, and DREAM samples from the store. Blue jumps are DREAM, green jumps are NUTS.
>
> For the Haario problem (64 dimensional, each pair of parameters is a 2D Haario function, so it is much harder than the published function) DREAM works much less well, for obvious reasons. But my algorithm can recognise this, and adjust the amount of DREAM usage accordingly.
>
> In concept, I guess you could say NUTS does the exploration, and other samplers fill in the gaps.
>
> Also, when you combine samplers, you may need to look at modifying the algorithms for the individual samples, as I did for DREAM.  This is just the same when, for example, you combine evolutionary algorithm optimisers with local gradient optimisers - just plugging the two together is not a satisfactory solution, they have influence on each other, and opportunities also.
>
> I really must look at Goodman-Weare in more detail one day.
>
> Nigel
>
>
> On Wednesday, 23 July 2014 05:58:21 UTC+1, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> How do you deal with the interleaving when DREAM assumes an ensemble
> and HMC/NUTS don't?  And just to be clear here, DREAM isn't a random
> walk algorithm in the same way as Metropolis and Gibbs are.
>
> We're working on some ensemble samplers now, starting with the Goodman-Weare
> versions, but we'll probably also implement differential evolution (which in my
> understanding is like DREAM w/o the detailed-balance violating heuristics).
>
> - Bob
>
>
> On Jul 22, 2014, at 2:27 PM, Nigel Goodwin <goo...@essence-property.com> wrote:
>
> > I'm not a stan user, but I have implemented NUTS together with other samplers, particularly DREAM (and RWM). The reason is two-fold - DREAM can handle, at least to some degree, discrete parameters and multi-modal situations. Secondly, when DREAM works well, it works well, and can be faster than NUTS. So I mix randomly DREAM and NUTS, in concept NUTS is used to generate a good population, and then DREAM is used to sample and difference from that population. This is all done randomly at each step and for each chain.
> >
> > This also avoids one of the main pitfalls of DREAM, IMHO, that heuristic tricks have to be used to make it go outside of the hyperplane defined by the chains at the current step. The inclusion of NUTS means that those tricks are no longer needed.
> >
> > In addition, I examine the acceptance rate for DREAM, and vary the proportion of time spent in DREAM according to how close the acceptance rate is to the theoretical value for normal distributions. I use dual averaging for the DREAM step (i.e. the scaled difference).
> >
> > Remarkably, the dual averaging generated a step size almost identical to the theoretical value for a normal test problem. Well, I'm always surprised when theory meets practice.
> >
> > So, long story short, I found value in mixing samplers. It's the same when you mix optimisation algorithms, they all have different good and bad behaviours, and a mixture is more robust.
> >
> >
> > On Tuesday, 22 July 2014 14:40:05 UTC+1, david...@gmail.com wrote:
> >
> > Random walk on the hyperparameters isn't going to do anyone any good.  Certainly in the worst case HMC reduces to a random walk, so why not just use it in the first place?
> >
> >
> > I believe its the overhead of HMC.  On a per iteration basis I agree random walk Metropolis has no advantage - but random walk Metropolis will iterate faster...  but see the conclusion of Filippone rather than have me paraphrase...
> >
> >  Of course any algorithm will work well in some circumstances, but we're (okay, maybe I should just speak for myself) interested in algorithms that work well with great generality,
> > and Gibbs is not going to be that algorithm, especially for modern applied problems.
> >
> >
> > I take your point completely - but would still like to be able to use Gibbs/single component Metropolis for problems that I don't know how to do anything else with - and for which there is some sort of track record of at least moderate performance....
> >
> > I really look forward to modifications to rstan that make this possible.  Thanks again for your advice and pointers!
> >

Hi Bob,

First thanks for the reply!

I think I forgot to point out that I would like to sample from only the positive solution space of Ax = b. For example, if A is a 1 by 3 matrix whose entries are all 1 and b is 1, then I want to sample uniformly from the triangle connecting (1, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0) and (0, 0, 1). Of course, A may have more than one one row and so may b. Moreover, I will make sure that the input I supply has a finite measure. Do you know how to add that constraint of positivity?

Yuanchu

On Wednesday, July 23, 2014 12:20:22 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> If you can write down an expression proportional to a
> proper log posterior, then Stan should be able to sample
> from it (with some caveats about posterior curvature).
>
> It may seem like this model would work:
>
> data {
>   int<lower=1> K;
>   vector[K] b;
> }
> parameters {
>   matrix[K] A;
> }
> transformed parameters {
>   vector[K] x;
>   x <- A \ b;
> }
> model {
> }
>
> The way this works, though, is that an empty model means a
> uniform distribution on the parameters.  So that would be
> uniform in A, which is improper (uniforms are only proper on
> finite-volume subsets).
>
> To make it uniform in x, you need to add the log Jacobian
> determinant of the transform from A to x into the model:
>
>   increment_log_prob(log_det_J);
>
> I'm not good enough at linear algebra to tell you what that
> is without spending all day on it, and I'm also not sure offhand
> if the posterior will be proper.
>
> - Bob

On Tuesday, July 22, 2014 12:41:40 PM UTC, david...@gmail.com wrote:
> Thanks for the responses Michael,
>
> I certainly defer to you, Girolami and the rest of the Stan team on these issues.  From a quick skim of the paper it seems the argument is that centring is only possible under limited circumstances...  I agree it is a good paper, and will go back to it when I get the chance...  so far I have read Murray's and Filippone's paper - rather than yours.  Filippone's paper recommends interweaving using HMC for latent variables and plain old random walk Metropolis for hyperparameters.
>
> Obviously conditional Gibbs sampling or single component Metropolis sampling is a compromise - but its a compromise that has served some of us quite well at times.
>
> I would like to implement the model described here.  http://people.ee.duke.edu/~lcarin/PoissonProcess.pdf
> It doesn't have to be using their sampler which involves both Metropolis Hastings and HMC steps - and involves trans-dimensional steps - but my first thought was to just use their sampler, and I thought Stan could help with the HMC part - but right now this appears to be not easy.

Thanks for sharing that, I was not aware of the sampling of event times by thinning.  If you are willing to take a step back from the full GP version and don't need to simulate events from the IHPP it looks like Stan can work just fine.  I've done a little proof of concept that this is reasonable in Stan by representing the intensity function as a spline with smoothness provided by a GP on the knot weights.  That gets you an arbitrarily fine intensity function and reduces the dimension of the GP to the number of knots (rather than the number of data points).  Once you estimate the spline you could even simulate from the poisson process by thinning as suggested by Adams et al.  I'm attaching some code so it's a little more concrete, not that I'm claiming this to be a _good_ model for the simulated data but Stan does pretty well, all things considered.

>
> OTOH If you think it can be completely done in Stan then I would be fascinated!
>
> BTW for reference it seems that you have been over this issue just a few weeks back (sorry) see Krzysztof Sakrejda's post and the responses which gives some detail about why the above doesn't work...
> https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/stan-users/HBewhdW1u88
>

I appreciate it getting re-hashed in more detail.  In my case I think one of the solutions is not sticking to discretized time survival models quite so much.

Krzysztof

>
>
> On Tuesday, July 22, 2014 9:27:58 PM UTC+10, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> >
> > > My hope was primarily to deal with models changing dimension and with discrete latent variables...   but I put in a couple of other suggestions ...  (I agree the annealing bit is particularly questionable)...  On the other hand Mark Girolami actually recommends interweaving here: http://www.dcs.gla.ac.uk/publications/PAPERS/9382/tech_rep_lgms.pdf .  Iain Murray argues running HMC on the full posterior for latent variable Gaussian process hierarchical  models doesn't work so well - but I must admit I don't understand why.
> > >
> > > It is fairly common that a published algorithm uses HMC as a kernel in combination with standard Metropolis-Hastings or Gibbs kernels...  it would be surprising if this were _never_ a good idea....   It would really be wonderful to be able to use Stan to make the HMC part easier...  but it looks like that is at least not easy right now...  although I am still a little puzzled as to why...
> > >
> > > Thanks again, for the feed back and for Stan!
> >
> > Well, if it matters at all I work for Mark, so I'm not coming from an orthogonal direction!
> >
> > Firstly, the big issue here is sampling jointly or sampling conditionally.  Sampling conditionally is always going to bring in problems when the target measure has large correlations, i.e. any realistic problem.  HMC appears to use a Gibbs step to sample the auxiliary momenta, but technically that sampling is doing something else.  Ignoring the technical details, HMC is making a joint update of all the model parameters which is what is important.
> >
> > This leaves two issues: hierarchical modes are hard and discrete models are harder.
> >
> > We review hierarchical models thoroughly in http://arxiv.org/abs/1312.0906, in particular we address why Euclidean HMC can run into problems.  A common approach that people take, starting with Radford Neal way back when he was first introducing HMC into stats, is to sample from the hyperparameters conditional on the local parameters,
> > but this inevitably leads to large autocorrelations because of the strong dependencies between the hyperparameters and the local parameters.  What you'd really want to do is sample from the marginal distribution of the hyperparameters, but computing that distribution is a tremendously difficult task.  Pseudomarginal methods are trying to solve this, but they are hard to make general and can run into their own pathologies.  As noted in the paper, Riemannian HMC solves many of these problems by construction, and it's coming soon to Stan.  At the moment your best bet is to find a good non-centered parameterization.
> >
> > Everyone wants discrete parameters but everyone also needs to understand the underlying problems.  Without the nice structure of a continuous measure, it's very, very hard to construct an efficient sampler.  Moreover, if you split your parameters into continuous and discrete then you're doing conditional updates, which will be slow as discussed above.  We've seen lots of success when the discrete parameters can be marginalized out to give a fully continuous model amenable to HMC.  This includes discrete latent models, provided there aren't too many possible states.
> >
> > You can certainly use Stan as a sampling API and stick it into a bigger sampler, but without addressing the fundamental problems with discrete variables and conditional updates you're only going to be able to go so far.
> >

messages.body_plain:
On Wednesday, July 23, 2014 7:14:22 PM UTC+1, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
>
> On Jul 23, 2014, at 12:22 PM, David C Cohen <buend...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> > On Jul 23, 2014, at 10:32 AM, David C Cohen <buend...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > > - Consider generalizing this problem in two directions:
> > >
> > > (1) y_1 = x * beta_1, y_2 = x * beta_2, ..., y_n = x * beta_n
> > > (2) y = x_1 * beta_1, y = x_2 * beta_2, ..., y = x_m * beta_m
> > >
> > > Would these problem solving time in stan increase linearly by n (or m), or is there anything that stan can do to avoid re-computations? For instance, in problem (1), x is shared between all equations, when n is about 1e3, how can we take advantage of this shared predictor x?
>
> ...
>
> > Sorry, I should have made it clear: y and beta are column vectors, x is a matrix with each column being a predictor. So the below products do not apply.
>
> Then there's no way to speed up (1) other than using a loop ---
> we don't have any specialized tensor operations.
>
> Just doing 1000 matrix multiplications on their own isn't going
> to be super fast.
>
> I don't understand (2), because x[1] will be a row vector and beta[1]
> a scalar, so y would have to be a row vector, too.  And why is y
> being reassigned?

(2) is just like (1), with one difference that y is constant, and x changes. This simply implies fitting the same response y with multiple groups of predictors x_i.

>
> - Bob

messages.subject: Sampling chains in parallel with rstan under windows
messages.subject_clean: Sampling chains in parallel with rstan under windows
messages.body_plain:
I've been grateful for everyone (especially Bob Carpenter) who's patiently answered my stan questions. I hope sharing my experiences getting multiple chains running in parallel under windows will return some of those favors and be useful.

I have been playing with sampling stan chains in parallel under Windows for long computations. There is some documentation on the rstan site about running parallel chains, but because windows doesn't allow unix-style forking processes, things are more complicated. I have tried several parallel R packages with varying results. Snow works all right, and is simple to invoke, but the default of "SOCKS" communication produces intermittent but annoyingly frequent interprocess communication glitches that waste time when I have to restart runs. Snow doesn't work with MPI under windows, at least not for me, even when rmpi is installed and working. So recently, I tried pbdMPI (pbd = "programming with big data": see http://r-pbd.org/ and http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/pbdMPI/index.html ). This is harder to code with, but once you have the hang of it, it's pretty straightforward to get multiple stan chains running in parallel.

I'm using the R pbdMPI library with the Microsoft High Performance Computing MPI package ( http://technet.microsoft.com/en-us/library/cc514029.aspx ). Microsoft HPC is free as an MPI package that runs multiple processes on multiple processors on a single computer. To get a cluster going with multiple computers, you would need to get MS's HPC server (but I can't see why anyone would want to run huge numbers of chains). Alternately, all this should work with OpenMPI under Linux and MacOS either on a single computer or in a cluster.

I am attaching an example of a toy R script that just runs the 8schools model with either 4 parallel chains (if use.mpi is either undefined or set to TRUE when the script is loaded) or 4 sequential chains (if use.mpi is set to FALSE when the script is loaded). It should serve as a template in which you can substitute your own model for the 8schools one. Running the 8schools model with 4 chains of 1 million iterations (absurdly large, but long processing times reduce the noise due to random stuff at initialization and termination) on a rather modest workstation with four cores takes 115 seconds in normal single-process mode and 32 seconds with parallel processing (this is the time for sampling, not including the time for compiling the model with stan and gpp).

For most small models, there is no benefit to running chains in parallel: the time to compile the stan model takes up the lion's share of processor time for small models. But for big models that take hours to converge, cutting the sampling time by a factor of three or more by running chains in parallel may make it worth the hassle of running the chains in parallel.

The key here are the pbdMPI functions bcast() and task.pull(). The function bcast() broadcasts a value from one thread (process #0, the master process, by default) to all other threads. This is how you initialize variables and compile the stan model once, and then pass the R stanmodel object to all the processes. The function task.pull() tells the worker threads to start executing a function N times. If N <= # threads, all the tasks run simultaneously. If N > # threads, each worker thread executes one task and then when it's done, asks (pulls) a new task from the master thread until all tasks are done. The master thread collects the results and returns them as a list, which can be assembled into a stanfit object using the rstan sflist2stanfit() function.  It is possible to pass parameters to the worker tasks using ellipsis arguments in R functions, but I found it easier to pass them as global variables that I initialize for each thread using bcast().

pbdMPI does not want to run in interactive mode (e.g., RStudio), so you need to invoke it via the mpiexec command from a command prompt or batch file/shell script. The best thing to do is run the stan computation under mpiexec and and have the script save the stanfit object as a .RData file, which you can read into an interactive session to analyze.

When using pbdMPI, some terminology that may be confusing is that the process number (0, 1, 2, ...) is referred to throughout the documentation as the "rank" of the process, so you get the thread # by calling comm.rank(). The rank-zero process is, by default, the master and the higher-rank processes are worker/slave threads. If you have code (such as compiling a stan model) which you only want one thread to execute, you can enclose it in an if(comm.rank() == 0) statement.

To get this going from scratch (assuming you're running windows and have already got R and rstan installed):

1. Download and install the Microsoft HPC pack
2. Install pbdMPI either from CRAN or from the r-pbd web site
3. From the command line, in the directory where the attached script lives (the -np option indicates the number of processes to start):
mpiexec -np 5 Rscript.exe MPI_schools.R

To run in single-process mode, invoke the script thus:
Rscript -e "use.mpi <- FALSE; source('MPI_schools.R')"

One thing that's not obvious is that if you want to run full out with one chain on each core, then you want the number of processes (the -np option for mpiexec) to be one greater than min(#  processors, # chains) because one process (thread) will be the master and the rest will be workers that execute the chains, so you need n+1 processors to run n threads full-out on n cores while the master waits for the workers to finish. Thus, to run 4 chains on 4 cores, you would use -np 5. To run 3 chains on 4 cores, you'd use -np 4.

On Jun 17, 2014, at 10:41 AM, Fei He <hefeif...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Dear STAN team,
>
> I am recently learning to use STAN. There is a classic Theophylline example in NONMEM, so I just want to redo it in STAN. But a couple of problems arise, so I really need your help.

Great --- we'd love to get some of those examples working.

We should be rolling out a diff-eq solvers before the end of
this year.

> Background:
> We have 12 subjects, each with 11 observations.
> theta1 ,theta2, theta3 are fixed effects.
> eta1, eta2, eta3 are random effects with mean 0.
> sigma is the error term and Omega is the covariance matrix.
>
> I want to have the estimates of 3 fixed effects, 1 error term and 6 covariance parameters and code are in newtest.stan.
>
> Problems are:
> 1. If I specify Omega as cov_matrix[3], I got 3 kinds of the messages: (1) Error in function stan::prob::normal_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): Location parameter is inf:0, but must be finite! (2) Error in function stan::prob::multi_normal_prec_log(d): LDLT_Factor of precision parameterunderlying matrix is not positive definite. LDLT_Factor of precision parameterlast conditional variance is 180.4616997051736. and

These first two aren't necessarily a problem if they don't persist across
iterations.

> (3) Optimization terminated with error:  Line search failed to achieve a sufficient decrease, no more progress can be made

This is more of a problem.

> The result in output.csv is not in accordance with NONMEM output

NONMEM does marginal maximum likelihood for random effects, which is
not what Stan does (at least not yet, though it's in the works).
Right now, we have only a simple (penalized) maximum likelihood estimator.

What that's likely to do in practice for hierarchical models is
drive the hierarchical variance to 0, because it drives up the likelihood.

>
> 2. If I specify Omega as matrix[3,3], I got the message: Error in function stan::prob::multi_normal_prec_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): Precision matrixPrecision matrix is not symmetric. Precision matrix[1,2] is -14.756310354014762:0, but Precision matrix[2,1] element is -14.7563:0

We're hoping to fix this issue with Stan 2.4 by only using the
lower triangular portion and thus enforcing symmetry in the
function itself.

> Optimization terminated normally:  Convergence detected: change in objective function was below tolerance

> Even though it is converged, but result in output.csv is not in accordance with NONMEM output

See above.  If you have a covariance matrix parameter, as Omega is,
you really need to declare it as such.  If it's a generated quantity or
transformed parameter, it's not a  big deal, as uses of it will
enforce its structure.

> Question:
> Did I make some mistakes or Could you please give me some suggestions?

I suspect the problem here is really trying to apply maximum likelihood
in a situation where you need marginal maximum likelihood (integrates out
the low-level parameters, optimizes the marginal of the high-level
parameter, then uses those to estimate low-level parameters).

You could try running with NUTS in sampling mode.  That can deal
with hierarchical models.  It'll be slower, but should work.

We'd also recommend using unconstrained parameters rather than putting
upper and lower bounds on them;  if you use bounded parameters, you
should be careful you're not getting estimates up against a boundary.

Also, if Omega is truly a covariance matrix (and not a precision matrix),
then you should use multi_normal, not multi_normal_prec.  Sorry for the
confusion with the variable type being named cov_matrix --- it should
just be spd_matrix, for symmetric-positive-definite matrix.  We're going
to change it in the future and deprecate the "cov_matrix" type (and
then eventually get rid of it).

- Bob

>
> Thank you so much!
>
> Bests,
> Fei
>
> PS: theo5.nmctl.txt is the NONMEM file and theo5.ext.txt is the NONMEM output
>

messages.body_plain:
Do you get warnings printed out as you go about failures
in the covariance matrix tests?

I'm hoping the problem is that our covariance matrix and
correlation matrix consistency checks are too stringent and
causing unnecessary failures.  That's been the case before.

The underlying problem with more variables is that floating
point arithmetic just isn't that precise, and when you have
lots of operations (as in Cholesky factor multiplication
and solvers converting the constrained/unconstrained), the
results vary from what you'd get from infinite-precision
arithmetic in that we can lose symmetry or positive definiteness.

Another problem is if estimates get pushed up against boundaries
(here correlation = 1 or -1, sd = 0 or +infinity).  This is
also very unstable arithmetically.

You might want to try again with Stan 2.4 --- we tried to clean
some of these things up, but we probably still have a ways to go.

- Bob
