messages.body_plain:
On Jul 19, 2014, at 2:45 PM, Katherine Grace Jonas <katherine....@gmail.com> wrote:

> Thanks for the suggestions.  Using only one scale parameter helped.  In this model (attached), the priors on bi_raw and bi_scale are constrained so that bi + bj will be appropriately ordered.  The item cutpoints are declared and fixed as per your suggestion.  With those changes, STAN is producing fewer errors (just one or two per warm up period per chain).
>
> The traces look better than before, but still aren't mixing well (a few from bi are attached).  Rhats are still high, from 1.3 to 20.  However, the bi estimates themselves are generally in the right range.  At least, they tend to be of the same sign as the simulated values.

If the model's converging properly, all R-hat values should be under 1.05,
and ideally very close to 1.

Very high R-hats often signal non-identifiabilities in the model, especially
if other parameters do converge reasonably.

> Another possible hiccup is in the response data.  Some simulated respondents never use certain response categories, due to response style.  It would be very difficult to estimate the third threshold (bi[,3]) for someone who never uses the highest response category.  Simulating more extreme vignettes helps, but in the real world there are often respondents with this sort of response data.  It may call for a ragged array.

You just want to be sure to avoid things like separability.  You need
stronger priors to overcome them and still sample efficiently.

- Bob

>
>
> On Fri, Jul 18, 2014 at 7:43 PM, Joshua Rosenau <josh.r...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hmm, it looks like you’re scaling each cutpoint separately, which would seem like it would leave the vector bi[] not being ordered in at least some cases. Shouldn’t you be multiplying by a single value (or a single value per item, at least)?
>
> Also, I think that’s not the best way to fix a value for bj[1,2]. Better to construct bj in the transformed parameters block, which would require a bit of reorganization of the code, but would allow you to simply assign 0 to bj[1,2]. You’d do something like declare parameters:
>
> ordered[K-1] bj_raw[J-1];
> real<upper=0> bj_init_a;
> real<lower=0> bj_init_b;
>
> Then in the transformed parameters, declare vector[K-1] bj[J], and:
>
> bj[1,1]<-bj_init_a; bj[1,2]<-0; bj[1,3]<-bj_init_b;
> for (j in 2:J) {
> bj[j]<-bj_raw[j-1];
> }
>
> and put the necessary priors on all the declared parameters (bj_raw, bj_init_a, bj_init_b).
>
> Hope that helps.
>
> Josh
>
> On Jul 18, 2014, at 4:27 PM, Katherine Grace Jonas <katherine....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>> Hello All,
>>
>> First off, thank you to everyone who's contributed to this list.  Searching through the questions and answers has helped me solve a number of problems with this model.
>>
>> The model I'm working on (a version and simulated data are attached) is a graded response IRT model, where the difficulty parameter is decomposed into two components: an item component and a person component.  The person component would theoretically encompass response styles.  I am hoping to capture response style by having respondents answer items with regard to themselves, as well as a vignette (or three, in this case).  Response styles should remain constant across self-report, vignettes, and items.
>>
>> The model shows poor convergence across parameters.  Rhat is large for most parameters, n_effs can be 2, and the chains wander about.  The problem seems to be caused by difficulties estimating the person difficulties (bi), because RStan frequently warns that the category cutpoints are not appropriately ordered.  The model will converge without bi, or if bi_scale is given a very tight prior.  My hunch is that there is a better way to parameterize bi.  The category cutpoints (bj) can be declared as ordered vectors, but the person parameters can't, so the sum of bi and bj is not always ordered.  The prior on bi_scale (uniform(0,3*N)) should keep bi in about the right range, given the distance between category cutpoints, but that doesn't seem to be enough.
>>
>> I'd really appreciate your thoughts.  Thanks again to all the list contributors.
>>
>> Katherine

messages.body_plain:
OK, I think I understand, the ensemble is the set of chains.

As I say, I trample all over the theory, in an attempt to get something which is useable by engineers, and much better than what they had before (RWM).

I think I can see your worry - but it will need some further thought to see if it clearly breaks the detailed balance proof. I have of course read most of the DREAM papers and tried to understand the detailed balance proofs. I still have an ensemble, but different members use different samplers at different steps.

DREAMZ does not, as far as I recall, rely on the ensemble for detailed balance proof, it uses a store of previous samples.

NUTS by itself is too slow for me and doesn't handle discrete cases, and my implementation has been in commercial use for over a year now, and cash flow is king. No doubt something better will emerge over time. For at least the next year my focus will be on dissemination rather than major changes to algorithms.

On Wednesday, 23 July 2014 19:47:21 UTC+1, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> What I meant is how do you combine HMC and ensemble methods.
>
> An ensemble method uses K ensemble members, each being
> a complete set of parameter values, whereas HMC works for a
> single value of the parameters.  The entire ensemble is what
> makes up the Markov chain in the ensemble method --- the
> individual ensemble members do not form a Markov chain by
> themselves.
>
> You can find the detailed balance proofs for the simplified
> version in ter Braak's paper on differential evolution.
>
> - Bob
>
> On Jul 23, 2014, at 6:39 AM, Nigel Goodwin <goo...@essence-property.com> wrote:
>
> > Bob, I'm afraid I don't know exactly what you mean by 'ensemble' and 'interweaving'. But maybe this will help:
> >
> > - I use multiple chains (8, for no particular reason), and parallelise at the likelihood function level, not the chain level. So I loop over steps, and for each step I loop over chains. I choose at random (with sampler weights) for each step/chain what sampler I am using, so for a given step there are multiple samplers, and of course the NUTS sampler takes a lot longer than the DREAM sampler, but that is OK because of the way I parallelise. It would be hopeless if I parallelised at the chain level.
> >
> > - there are several different versions of DREAM. Some sample from other chains at the same step, others sample from a store of previous steps (DREAMZ). I use both methods. In pure DREAM, the problem with sampling from other chains is the one I mentioned, getting stuck in the same hyperplane, and they have various methods to overcome this, none of which I like. They are Gibbs-like, which is hopeless if the likelihood is not aligned with the axes. But by combining with NUTS, this problem is avoided. All the complexity of DREAM (choosing subsets of parameters, adding in a bit of random walk) can be avoided.
> >
> > - I have a feeling, and it is no more than that, that DREAM sampling from other chains has a more satisfactory detailed balance proof, hence why I use multiple chains. But I may be wrong. the 'proofs' in DREAM are rather sketchy.
> >
> > - whether the DREAM family, or my combined approach, strictly obey the necessary rules, is not something I am qualified to discuss. But in my tests they successfully reproduce the analytical results for complex high dimensional problems, which is more than good enough for my audience.
> >
> > - speed and performance is critical in my application, it is an interactive tool for engineers which repeats MC many times, so I have to make some compromises to get the performance. Whether the compromises are real or imaginary I don't know (see above!), but without performance nobody would use it.
> >
> > My video http://www.youtube.com/channel/UCQbRkgaevt0TSDzipvmtMKQ
> >
> > shows, for EssRisk64DNormal, this combined approach for a 64 dimensional multivariate normal. In this case I have one chain, and DREAM samples from the store. Blue jumps are DREAM, green jumps are NUTS.
> >
> > For the Haario problem (64 dimensional, each pair of parameters is a 2D Haario function, so it is much harder than the published function) DREAM works much less well, for obvious reasons. But my algorithm can recognise this, and adjust the amount of DREAM usage accordingly.
> >
> > In concept, I guess you could say NUTS does the exploration, and other samplers fill in the gaps.
> >
> > Also, when you combine samplers, you may need to look at modifying the algorithms for the individual samples, as I did for DREAM.  This is just the same when, for example, you combine evolutionary algorithm optimisers with local gradient optimisers - just plugging the two together is not a satisfactory solution, they have influence on each other, and opportunities also.
> >
> > I really must look at Goodman-Weare in more detail one day.
> >
> > Nigel
> >
> >
> > On Wednesday, 23 July 2014 05:58:21 UTC+1, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > How do you deal with the interleaving when DREAM assumes an ensemble
> > and HMC/NUTS don't?  And just to be clear here, DREAM isn't a random
> > walk algorithm in the same way as Metropolis and Gibbs are.
> >
> > We're working on some ensemble samplers now, starting with the Goodman-Weare
> > versions, but we'll probably also implement differential evolution (which in my
> > understanding is like DREAM w/o the detailed-balance violating heuristics).
> >
> > - Bob
> >
> >
> > On Jul 22, 2014, at 2:27 PM, Nigel Goodwin <goo...@essence-property.com> wrote:
> >
> > > I'm not a stan user, but I have implemented NUTS together with other samplers, particularly DREAM (and RWM). The reason is two-fold - DREAM can handle, at least to some degree, discrete parameters and multi-modal situations. Secondly, when DREAM works well, it works well, and can be faster than NUTS. So I mix randomly DREAM and NUTS, in concept NUTS is used to generate a good population, and then DREAM is used to sample and difference from that population. This is all done randomly at each step and for each chain.
> > >
> > > This also avoids one of the main pitfalls of DREAM, IMHO, that heuristic tricks have to be used to make it go outside of the hyperplane defined by the chains at the current step. The inclusion of NUTS means that those tricks are no longer needed.
> > >
> > > In addition, I examine the acceptance rate for DREAM, and vary the proportion of time spent in DREAM according to how close the acceptance rate is to the theoretical value for normal distributions. I use dual averaging for the DREAM step (i.e. the scaled difference).
> > >
> > > Remarkably, the dual averaging generated a step size almost identical to the theoretical value for a normal test problem. Well, I'm always surprised when theory meets practice.
> > >
> > > So, long story short, I found value in mixing samplers. It's the same when you mix optimisation algorithms, they all have different good and bad behaviours, and a mixture is more robust.
> > >
> > >
> > > On Tuesday, 22 July 2014 14:40:05 UTC+1, david...@gmail.com wrote:
> > >
> > > Random walk on the hyperparameters isn't going to do anyone any good.  Certainly in the worst case HMC reduces to a random walk, so why not just use it in the first place?
> > >
> > >
> > > I believe its the overhead of HMC.  On a per iteration basis I agree random walk Metropolis has no advantage - but random walk Metropolis will iterate faster...  but see the conclusion of Filippone rather than have me paraphrase...
> > >
> > >  Of course any algorithm will work well in some circumstances, but we're (okay, maybe I should just speak for myself) interested in algorithms that work well with great generality,
> > > and Gibbs is not going to be that algorithm, especially for modern applied problems.
> > >
> > >
> > > I take your point completely - but would still like to be able to use Gibbs/single component Metropolis for problems that I don't know how to do anything else with - and for which there is some sort of track record of at least moderate performance....
> > >
> > > I really look forward to modifications to rstan that make this possible.  Thanks again for your advice and pointers!
> > >
> > > Cheers,
> > > David
> > >

Good catch! Indeed, Sage is for some reason building R without any optimization when it has -O2 by default. It is a bit disturbing that we can't build rstan without optimization (which would be useful for debugging at some point), but it is more disturbing that Sage would turn off optimization by default when building R.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for your code Krzysztof, I didn't expect this!

It doesn't run out of the box for me, I will try tweaking it to try to work out what you have done.

I hadn't thought about using splines, but it is not clear to me if doing so solves everything.  Maybe you can analytically integrate under a non-negative function of them which would change things....

For this model, the likelihood contains the following terms

1 ~ poisson(sigmoid(lambda))
0 ~ poisson(sigmoid(-latent))

lambda is the size of the data set, where latent is of variable size (which is the big problem for Stan I think).

The reason for the use of the 1/0 is that for a point process there is a small number of locations where a single event happens and everywhere else nothing happens - you never evaluate the poisson with a count greater than 1.

it looks to me like you are instead modelling

count[ii] ~ poisson(lambda(ii))

which appears at face value to be a different model.  Apologies, in advance if I have misunderstood...  Maybe we should talk more about this out of the thread...  my email is david...@gmail.com.

Cheers,
David

On Thursday, July 24, 2014 6:16:54 AM UTC+10, Krzysztof Sakrejda wrote:
> On Tuesday, July 22, 2014 12:41:40 PM UTC, david...@gmail.com wrote:
> > Thanks for the responses Michael,
> >
> > I certainly defer to you, Girolami and the rest of the Stan team on these issues.  From a quick skim of the paper it seems the argument is that centring is only possible under limited circumstances...  I agree it is a good paper, and will go back to it when I get the chance...  so far I have read Murray's and Filippone's paper - rather than yours.  Filippone's paper recommends interweaving using HMC for latent variables and plain old random walk Metropolis for hyperparameters.
> >
> > Obviously conditional Gibbs sampling or single component Metropolis sampling is a compromise - but its a compromise that has served some of us quite well at times.
> >
> > I would like to implement the model described here.  http://people.ee.duke.edu/~lcarin/PoissonProcess.pdf
> > It doesn't have to be using their sampler which involves both Metropolis Hastings and HMC steps - and involves trans-dimensional steps - but my first thought was to just use their sampler, and I thought Stan could help with the HMC part - but right now this appears to be not easy.
>
> Thanks for sharing that, I was not aware of the sampling of event times by thinning.  If you are willing to take a step back from the full GP version and don't need to simulate events from the IHPP it looks like Stan can work just fine.  I've done a little proof of concept that this is reasonable in Stan by representing the intensity function as a spline with smoothness provided by a GP on the knot weights.  That gets you an arbitrarily fine intensity function and reduces the dimension of the GP to the number of knots (rather than the number of data points).  Once you estimate the spline you could even simulate from the poisson process by thinning as suggested by Adams et al.  I'm attaching some code so it's a little more concrete, not that I'm claiming this to be a _good_ model for the simulated data but Stan does pretty well, all things considered.
>
> >
> > OTOH If you think it can be completely done in Stan then I would be fascinated!
> >
> > BTW for reference it seems that you have been over this issue just a few weeks back (sorry) see Krzysztof Sakrejda's post and the responses which gives some detail about why the above doesn't work...
> > https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/stan-users/HBewhdW1u88
> >
>
> I appreciate it getting re-hashed in more detail.  In my case I think one of the solutions is not sticking to discretized time survival models quite so much.
>
> Krzysztof
>
> >
> >
> > On Tuesday, July 22, 2014 9:27:58 PM UTC+10, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> > >
> > > > My hope was primarily to deal with models changing dimension and with discrete latent variables...   but I put in a couple of other suggestions ...  (I agree the annealing bit is particularly questionable)...  On the other hand Mark Girolami actually recommends interweaving here: http://www.dcs.gla.ac.uk/publications/PAPERS/9382/tech_rep_lgms.pdf .  Iain Murray argues running HMC on the full posterior for latent variable Gaussian process hierarchical  models doesn't work so well - but I must admit I don't understand why.
> > > >
> > > > It is fairly common that a published algorithm uses HMC as a kernel in combination with standard Metropolis-Hastings or Gibbs kernels...  it would be surprising if this were _never_ a good idea....   It would really be wonderful to be able to use Stan to make the HMC part easier...  but it looks like that is at least not easy right now...  although I am still a little puzzled as to why...
> > > >
> > > > Thanks again, for the feed back and for Stan!
> > >
> > > Well, if it matters at all I work for Mark, so I'm not coming from an orthogonal direction!
> > >
> > > Firstly, the big issue here is sampling jointly or sampling conditionally.  Sampling conditionally is always going to bring in problems when the target measure has large correlations, i.e. any realistic problem.  HMC appears to use a Gibbs step to sample the auxiliary momenta, but technically that sampling is doing something else.  Ignoring the technical details, HMC is making a joint update of all the model parameters which is what is important.
> > >
> > > This leaves two issues: hierarchical modes are hard and discrete models are harder.
> > >
> > > We review hierarchical models thoroughly in http://arxiv.org/abs/1312.0906, in particular we address why Euclidean HMC can run into problems.  A common approach that people take, starting with Radford Neal way back when he was first introducing HMC into stats, is to sample from the hyperparameters conditional on the local parameters,
> > > but this inevitably leads to large autocorrelations because of the strong dependencies between the hyperparameters and the local parameters.  What you'd really want to do is sample from the marginal distribution of the hyperparameters, but computing that distribution is a tremendously difficult task.  Pseudomarginal methods are trying to solve this, but they are hard to make general and can run into their own pathologies.  As noted in the paper, Riemannian HMC solves many of these problems by construction, and it's coming soon to Stan.  At the moment your best bet is to find a good non-centered parameterization.
> > >
> > > Everyone wants discrete parameters but everyone also needs to understand the underlying problems.  Without the nice structure of a continuous measure, it's very, very hard to construct an efficient sampler.  Moreover, if you split your parameters into continuous and discrete then you're doing conditional updates, which will be slow as discussed above.  We've seen lots of success when the discrete parameters can be marginalized out to give a fully continuous model amenable to HMC.  This includes discrete latent models, provided there aren't too many possible states.
> > >
> > > You can certainly use Stan as a sampling API and stick it into a bigger sampler, but without addressing the fundamental problems with discrete variables and conditional updates you're only going to be able to go so far.
> > >

messages.body_plain:
Hello guys,

my issue is the following. I have several 'populations' of individuals of variable size but with known covariance matrices.
Suppose individuals from different populations are independent and it would be thus more efficient to sample conditional on the
populations instead of sampling from a huge block diagonal matrix with lots of zeros. How can I achieve this in RStan?

As an R user, two possibilities come to my mind:
1) Using a list of matrices and sampling from one after the other
2) Subsetting a huge block diagonal matrix appropriately when sampling

I appreciate your help,
Dominik

messages.subject: Re: Efficient sampling from a block diagonal (known) covariance matrix
messages.subject_clean: Efficient sampling from a block diagonal (known) covariance matrix
messages.body_plain:
On Thursday, July 24, 2014 6:33:29 AM UTC-4, dominom...@googlemail.com wrote:
> my issue is the following. I have several 'populations' of individuals of variable size but with known covariance matrices.
> Suppose individuals from different populations are independent and it would be thus more efficient to sample conditional on the
> populations instead of sampling from a huge block diagonal matrix with lots of zeros. How can I achieve this in RStan?
>
> As an R user, two possibilities come to my mind:
> 1) Using a list of matrices and sampling from one after the other
> 2) Subsetting a huge block diagonal matrix appropriately when sampling

Subsetting is more tedious in Stan than it is in R, so I would go with option 1). You need to declare an array of covariance matrices in the data block like

data {
  int<lower=1> n_populations;
  int<lower=2> n_variables;
  cov_matrix[n_variables] Sigma[n_populations];
}
...

And then include a list of those covariance matrices as an element of the data list when you call stan() from R.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: Sampling chains in parallel with rstan under windows
messages.subject_clean: Sampling chains in parallel with rstan under windows
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

In case anybody needs below is R code to run chains in parallel (in simplest sense when chains don't talk with each other) in windows.  I am using the code to ensure that convergence is reached for multiple chains.

library (parallel)

stanmod <- function (chain, file, sm, data, warmup, n.draws, pars, init) {
    if (length (init) == 1) {
        if (init == "random") {
            init <- "random"
        } else {
            init <- list (init [[chain]])
        }
    } else {
        init <- list (init [[chain]])
    }
    sampling (sm, data = data, pars = pars, chains = 1,
        iter = warmup + n.draws, warmup = warmup,
        init = init,
        diagnostic_file = paste (file, chain, "d.txt", sep = ""),
        sample_file = paste (file, chain, "s.txt", sep = ""),
        verbose = TRUE, refresh = max ((warmup + n.draws) / 10, 1),
        chain_id = chain)
}
par.stan <- function (file, code, data, warmup, n.draws, chains, pars,
    init)
{
    # translate model to C++
    rt <- stanc (file, model_code = code, model_name = file)
    if (rt$status == FALSE) return (NULL)
    # compile C++ code
    sm <- stan_model (stanc_ret = rt, verbose = FALSE)
    cat ("COMPILED\n")
    cl <- makePSOCKcluster (chains,
        outfile = paste (file, "out.txt", sep = ""))
    setDefaultCluster (cl)
    clusterExport (NULL, c ('stanmod'))
    clusterEvalQ (NULL, library (rstan))
    posterior <- parLapply (NULL, 1 : chains, stanmod, file, sm, data, warmup,
        n.draws, pars, init)
    stopCluster (cl)
    return (posterior)
}

Linas

On Wednesday, July 23, 2014 5:19:59 PM UTC-4, Jonathan Gilligan wrote:
> I've been grateful for everyone (especially Bob Carpenter) who's patiently answered my stan questions. I hope sharing my experiences getting multiple chains running in parallel under windows will return some of those favors and be useful.
>
> I have been playing with sampling stan chains in parallel under Windows for long computations. There is some documentation on the rstan site about running parallel chains, but because windows doesn't allow unix-style forking processes, things are more complicated. I have tried several parallel R packages with varying results. Snow works all right, and is simple to invoke, but the default of "SOCKS" communication produces intermittent but annoyingly frequent interprocess communication glitches that waste time when I have to restart runs. Snow doesn't work with MPI under windows, at least not for me, even when rmpi is installed and working. So recently, I tried pbdMPI (pbd = "programming with big data": see http://r-pbd.org/ and http://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/pbdMPI/index.html ). This is harder to code with, but once you have the hang of it, it's pretty straightforward to get multiple stan chains running in parallel.
>
> I'm using the R pbdMPI library with the Microsoft High Performance Computing MPI package ( http://technet.microsoft.com/en-us/library/cc514029.aspx ). Microsoft HPC is free as an MPI package that runs multiple processes on multiple processors on a single computer. To get a cluster going with multiple computers, you would need to get MS's HPC server (but I can't see why anyone would want to run huge numbers of chains). Alternately, all this should work with OpenMPI under Linux and MacOS either on a single computer or in a cluster.
>
> I am attaching an example of a toy R script that just runs the 8schools model with either 4 parallel chains (if use.mpi is either undefined or set to TRUE when the script is loaded) or 4 sequential chains (if use.mpi is set to FALSE when the script is loaded). It should serve as a template in which you can substitute your own model for the 8schools one. Running the 8schools model with 4 chains of 1 million iterations (absurdly large, but long processing times reduce the noise due to random stuff at initialization and termination) on a rather modest workstation with four cores takes 115 seconds in normal single-process mode and 32 seconds with parallel processing (this is the time for sampling, not including the time for compiling the model with stan and gpp).
>
> For most small models, there is no benefit to running chains in parallel: the time to compile the stan model takes up the lion's share of processor time for small models. But for big models that take hours to converge, cutting the sampling time by a factor of three or more by running chains in parallel may make it worth the hassle of running the chains in parallel.
>
> The key here are the pbdMPI functions bcast() and task.pull(). The function bcast() broadcasts a value from one thread (process #0, the master process, by default) to all other threads. This is how you initialize variables and compile the stan model once, and then pass the R stanmodel object to all the processes. The function task.pull() tells the worker threads to start executing a function N times. If N <= # threads, all the tasks run simultaneously. If N > # threads, each worker thread executes one task and then when it's done, asks (pulls) a new task from the master thread until all tasks are done. The master thread collects the results and returns them as a list, which can be assembled into a stanfit object using the rstan sflist2stanfit() function.  It is possible to pass parameters to the worker tasks using ellipsis arguments in R functions, but I found it easier to pass them as global variables that I initialize for each thread using bcast().
>
> pbdMPI does not want to run in interactive mode (e.g., RStudio), so you need to invoke it via the mpiexec command from a command prompt or batch file/shell script. The best thing to do is run the stan computation under mpiexec and and have the script save the stanfit object as a .RData file, which you can read into an interactive session to analyze.
>
> When using pbdMPI, some terminology that may be confusing is that the process number (0, 1, 2, ...) is referred to throughout the documentation as the "rank" of the process, so you get the thread # by calling comm.rank(). The rank-zero process is, by default, the master and the higher-rank processes are worker/slave threads. If you have code (such as compiling a stan model) which you only want one thread to execute, you can enclose it in an if(comm.rank() == 0) statement.
>
> To get this going from scratch (assuming you're running windows and have already got R and rstan installed):
>
> 1. Download and install the Microsoft HPC pack
> 2. Install pbdMPI either from CRAN or from the r-pbd web site
> 3. From the command line, in the directory where the attached script lives (the -np option indicates the number of processes to start):
> mpiexec -np 5 Rscript.exe MPI_schools.R
>
> To run in single-process mode, invoke the script thus:
> Rscript -e "use.mpi <- FALSE; source('MPI_schools.R')"
>
> One thing that's not obvious is that if you want to run full out with one chain on each core, then you want the number of processes (the -np option for mpiexec) to be one greater than min(#  processors, # chains) because one process (thread) will be the master and the rest will be workers that execute the chains, so you need n+1 processors to run n threads full-out on n cores while the master waits for the workers to finish. Thus, to run 4 chains on 4 cores, you would use -np 5. To run 3 chains on 4 cores, you'd use -np 4.

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have a question - I have found that using uniform (0,1) sometimes dosn't work for standard deviations (when sd > 1, no surprise).  I really don't know a structured way how to estimate sd in advance.  Therefore I rely on cauchy(0,5) for simplicity.  I assume there is a better practice and I would like to hear about it.

Thanks for any advice,
Linas

On Monday, July 21, 2014 6:45:47 PM UTC-4, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> Hmm, let me make some recommendations:
>
> First, the general ladder of priors:
> 1.  Noninformative
> 2.  Weakly informative
> 3.  Informative
>
> A noninformative prior is typically uniform; it’s what we get when no prior is specified at all (which is why I’ve called it a “default default”).
>
> A weakly informative prior will typically have a scale set to some value larger than 1, on the assumption that the data have been scaled so that parameters should not be much more than 1 in absolute value.  Even after rescaling, though, parameters often _can_ be much less than 1, for example .01 or .001 or even closer to 0).  For this reason, our weakly informative priors typically put a (soft) constraint on the parameter at the high end but not at the low end.  This is why a weakly informative prior can often be specified using just one hyperparameter.  This hyperparameter could have a default value of 10, but for some classes of models that we understand well, we might recommend a smaller value for the default scale, for example 2.5 for logistic regression coefficients.
>
> An informative prior will typically have two hyperparameters, which can be conceptualized as a prior estimate and uncertainty, or as a lower and upper prior bound.
>
> And there are various intermediate steps.  For example, we can be moderately informative, using some subject-matter knowledge to (soft)-constrain a prior distribution but without trying to fully include all prior knowledge.  This can make sense in settings where default weakly informative priors don’t regularize enough, but where we don’t want to put in the effort to fully quantify our prior information.
>
> I’ve struggled for years to put all this in a theoretical framework, and I’m still struggling.  Still, I think what I’m saying is reasonable.
>
> Also, the side note that in some settings we might want boundary-avoiding priors for point estimation (for example, to keep hierarchical variance parameters away from 0) while in other settings we might be happy for point estimates to be on the boundary or to hit some special value (for example, in lasso regression where it is considered desirable to get coefficient estimates of 0).
>
> There’s also this attached paper by Sander Greenland who recommends the log-F family of priors, which he says has better properties than the Cauchy which I’ve been recommending.  He may well be right; I’d never thought that hard about the functional form but I agree that Cauchy is pretty extreme for most applications.
>

For a scale parameter, uniform(0,infinity) is the default default and will often work just fine.  A default weakly informative prior would be something like Cauchy+(0,10), where Cauchy+ is the Cauchy defined on (0,infinity).  I’m assuming the variable is scaled so that values on the order of magnitude 1 will be reasonable.

messages.body_plain:
Looking again at the Braak 2006 Stat Comp paper,he says quote ".... and the distribution of e is symmetric........For the third condition it is required that any state can be reached with positive probability and this is guaranteed by the unbounded support of the distribution of e (which is N(0, b))" Now if e is a NUTS step (or any other valid sampler) rather than a RWM step, does this invalidate the proof? It isn't obvious to me, but I'm not an expert. Is the problem that the NUTS is not a symmetric distribution?

I somehow thought that if you have an ensemble, so long as each individual step conformed to the rules, the ensemble would conform to the rules, so it didn't matter if individual steps and members of the ensemble used different samplers.

I guess clarification of this would help those of us doing what this thread is about, using NUTS as a sampler within a bigger algorithm.

On Thursday, 24 July 2014 00:34:11 UTC+1, Nigel Goodwin wrote:
> OK, I think I understand, the ensemble is the set of chains.
>
> As I say, I trample all over the theory, in an attempt to get something which is useable by engineers, and much better than what they had before (RWM).
>
> I think I can see your worry - but it will need some further thought to see if it clearly breaks the detailed balance proof. I have of course read most of the DREAM papers and tried to understand the detailed balance proofs. I still have an ensemble, but different members use different samplers at different steps.
>
> DREAMZ does not, as far as I recall, rely on the ensemble for detailed balance proof, it uses a store of previous samples.
>
> NUTS by itself is too slow for me and doesn't handle discrete cases, and my implementation has been in commercial use for over a year now, and cash flow is king. No doubt something better will emerge over time. For at least the next year my focus will be on dissemination rather than major changes to algorithms.
>
> On Wednesday, 23 July 2014 19:47:21 UTC+1, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > What I meant is how do you combine HMC and ensemble methods.
> >
> > An ensemble method uses K ensemble members, each being
> > a complete set of parameter values, whereas HMC works for a
> > single value of the parameters.  The entire ensemble is what
> > makes up the Markov chain in the ensemble method --- the
> > individual ensemble members do not form a Markov chain by
> > themselves.
> >
> > You can find the detailed balance proofs for the simplified
> > version in ter Braak's paper on differential evolution.
> >
> > - Bob
> >
> > On Jul 23, 2014, at 6:39 AM, Nigel Goodwin <goo...@essence-property.com> wrote:
> >
> > > Bob, I'm afraid I don't know exactly what you mean by 'ensemble' and 'interweaving'. But maybe this will help:
> > >
> > > - I use multiple chains (8, for no particular reason), and parallelise at the likelihood function level, not the chain level. So I loop over steps, and for each step I loop over chains. I choose at random (with sampler weights) for each step/chain what sampler I am using, so for a given step there are multiple samplers, and of course the NUTS sampler takes a lot longer than the DREAM sampler, but that is OK because of the way I parallelise. It would be hopeless if I parallelised at the chain level.
> > >
> > > - there are several different versions of DREAM. Some sample from other chains at the same step, others sample from a store of previous steps (DREAMZ). I use both methods. In pure DREAM, the problem with sampling from other chains is the one I mentioned, getting stuck in the same hyperplane, and they have various methods to overcome this, none of which I like. They are Gibbs-like, which is hopeless if the likelihood is not aligned with the axes. But by combining with NUTS, this problem is avoided. All the complexity of DREAM (choosing subsets of parameters, adding in a bit of random walk) can be avoided.
> > >
> > > - I have a feeling, and it is no more than that, that DREAM sampling from other chains has a more satisfactory detailed balance proof, hence why I use multiple chains. But I may be wrong. the 'proofs' in DREAM are rather sketchy.
> > >
> > > - whether the DREAM family, or my combined approach, strictly obey the necessary rules, is not something I am qualified to discuss. But in my tests they successfully reproduce the analytical results for complex high dimensional problems, which is more than good enough for my audience.
> > >
> > > - speed and performance is critical in my application, it is an interactive tool for engineers which repeats MC many times, so I have to make some compromises to get the performance. Whether the compromises are real or imaginary I don't know (see above!), but without performance nobody would use it.
> > >
> > > My video http://www.youtube.com/channel/UCQbRkgaevt0TSDzipvmtMKQ
> > >
> > > shows, for EssRisk64DNormal, this combined approach for a 64 dimensional multivariate normal. In this case I have one chain, and DREAM samples from the store. Blue jumps are DREAM, green jumps are NUTS.
> > >
> > > For the Haario problem (64 dimensional, each pair of parameters is a 2D Haario function, so it is much harder than the published function) DREAM works much less well, for obvious reasons. But my algorithm can recognise this, and adjust the amount of DREAM usage accordingly.
> > >
> > > In concept, I guess you could say NUTS does the exploration, and other samplers fill in the gaps.
> > >
> > > Also, when you combine samplers, you may need to look at modifying the algorithms for the individual samples, as I did for DREAM.  This is just the same when, for example, you combine evolutionary algorithm optimisers with local gradient optimisers - just plugging the two together is not a satisfactory solution, they have influence on each other, and opportunities also.
> > >
> > > I really must look at Goodman-Weare in more detail one day.
> > >
> > > Nigel
> > >
> > >
> > > On Wednesday, 23 July 2014 05:58:21 UTC+1, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > > How do you deal with the interleaving when DREAM assumes an ensemble
> > > and HMC/NUTS don't?  And just to be clear here, DREAM isn't a random
> > > walk algorithm in the same way as Metropolis and Gibbs are.
> > >
> > > We're working on some ensemble samplers now, starting with the Goodman-Weare
> > > versions, but we'll probably also implement differential evolution (which in my
> > > understanding is like DREAM w/o the detailed-balance violating heuristics).
> > >
> > > - Bob
> > >
> > >
> > > On Jul 22, 2014, at 2:27 PM, Nigel Goodwin <goo...@essence-property.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > > I'm not a stan user, but I have implemented NUTS together with other samplers, particularly DREAM (and RWM). The reason is two-fold - DREAM can handle, at least to some degree, discrete parameters and multi-modal situations. Secondly, when DREAM works well, it works well, and can be faster than NUTS. So I mix randomly DREAM and NUTS, in concept NUTS is used to generate a good population, and then DREAM is used to sample and difference from that population. This is all done randomly at each step and for each chain.
> > > >
> > > > This also avoids one of the main pitfalls of DREAM, IMHO, that heuristic tricks have to be used to make it go outside of the hyperplane defined by the chains at the current step. The inclusion of NUTS means that those tricks are no longer needed.
> > > >
> > > > In addition, I examine the acceptance rate for DREAM, and vary the proportion of time spent in DREAM according to how close the acceptance rate is to the theoretical value for normal distributions. I use dual averaging for the DREAM step (i.e. the scaled difference).
> > > >
> > > > Remarkably, the dual averaging generated a step size almost identical to the theoretical value for a normal test problem. Well, I'm always surprised when theory meets practice.
> > > >
> > > > So, long story short, I found value in mixing samplers. It's the same when you mix optimisation algorithms, they all have different good and bad behaviours, and a mixture is more robust.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > On Tuesday, 22 July 2014 14:40:05 UTC+1, david...@gmail.com wrote:
> > > >
> > > > Random walk on the hyperparameters isn't going to do anyone any good.  Certainly in the worst case HMC reduces to a random walk, so why not just use it in the first place?
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > I believe its the overhead of HMC.  On a per iteration basis I agree random walk Metropolis has no advantage - but random walk Metropolis will iterate faster...  but see the conclusion of Filippone rather than have me paraphrase...
> > > >
> > > >  Of course any algorithm will work well in some circumstances, but we're (okay, maybe I should just speak for myself) interested in algorithms that work well with great generality,
> > > > and Gibbs is not going to be that algorithm, especially for modern applied problems.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > I take your point completely - but would still like to be able to use Gibbs/single component Metropolis for problems that I don't know how to do anything else with - and for which there is some sort of track record of at least moderate performance....
> > > >
> > > > I really look forward to modifications to rstan that make this possible.  Thanks again for your advice and pointers!
> > > >
> > > > Cheers,
> > > > David
> > > >

Yes --- you can interleave steps from Markov chains
with the right stationarity properties (i.e., the
stationary distribution of the chain is the posterior
p(theta)).  So you can alternate differential evolution
and RWM or HMC or NUTS and the combination still has
the right stationarity properties.

The detailed balance proof for NUTS is rather complicated,
but similar in many ways to the arguments involved for
slice sampling, which Radford Neal goes over in his paper
introducing slice sampling.

- Bob

>

RStan 2.3 didn't depend on BH, but I believe 2.4 (or the release
after) will depend on BH and RcppEigen (although I hate the dependencies,
it seems the only way to get it into CRAN, which should hopefully simplify
some of the installs).

For one, Andrew would kill us if we got rid of the install script.
That's because it's cleaned up most of the install procedures for
"standard" installations, which are very fiddly and error prone.

We figured people running non-standard installs would be able to
deal with a little more customization on their own.

Having said that, I have no idea what Sage is (other than what
I see on their home page: http://www.sagemath.org).  Maybe we just need to
build Stan into Sage so nobody has to install it manually.  Isn't that
the point of these mega-integrations?

Having said that, we can add special instructions for special versions
of R.

- Bob

If you have managed to find an analytic integral that removes the doubly intractable problem for even a grossly simplified model that would be quite remarkable...

Its not a problem to integrate under a standard GP (for some covariance functions e.g. gaussian), but once you apply a non-negative transform (log, square or sigmoid) it becomes intractable AFAICT and right now I don't see how using a spline will help... I can't spend too much time on this right now, but we should keep talking about this at a later date...

Cheers,
David

I agree it is a good paper, and will go back to it when I get the chance...  so far I have read Murray's and Filippone's paper - rather than yours.  Filippone's paper recommends interweaving using HMC for latent variables and plain old random walk Metropolis for hyperparameters.
> > > >
> > > > Obviously conditional Gibbs sampling or single component Metropolis sampling is a compromise - but its a compromise that has served some of us quite well at times.
> > > >
> > > > I would like to implement the model described here.  http://people.ee.duke.edu/~lcarin/PoissonProcess.pdf

That gets you an arbitrarily fine intensity function and reduces the dimension of the GP to the number of knots (rather than the number of data points).  Once you estimate the spline you could even simulate from the poisson process by thinning as suggested by Adams et al.  I'm attaching some code so it's a little more concrete, not that I'm claiming this to be a _good_ model for the simulated data but Stan does pretty well, all things considered.

> > > >
> > >
> > > I appreciate it getting re-hashed in more detail.  In my case I think one of the solutions is not sticking to discretized time survival models quite so much.
> > >
> > > Krzysztof
> > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > On Tuesday, July 22, 2014 9:27:58 PM UTC+10, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> > > > >
> > > > > > My hope was primarily to deal with models changing dimension and with discrete latent variables...   but I put in a couple of other suggestions ...  (I agree the annealing bit is particularly questionable)...  On the other hand Mark Girolami actually recommends interweaving here: http://www.dcs.gla.ac.uk/publications/PAPERS/9382/tech_rep_lgms.pdf .  Iain Murray argues running HMC on the full posterior for latent variable Gaussian process hierarchical  models doesn't work so well - but I must admit I don't understand why.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > It is fairly common that a published algorithm uses HMC as a kernel in combination with standard Metropolis-Hastings or Gibbs kernels...  it would be surprising if this were _never_ a good idea....   It would really be wonderful to be able to use Stan to make the HMC part easier...  but it looks like that is at least not easy right now...  although I am still a little puzzled as to why...
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Thanks again, for the feed back and for Stan!
> > > > >
> > > > > Well, if it matters at all I work for Mark, so I'm not coming from an orthogonal direction!
> > > > >
> > > > > Firstly, the big issue here is sampling jointly or sampling conditionally.  Sampling conditionally is always going to bring in problems when the target measure has large correlations, i.e. any realistic problem.  HMC appears to use a Gibbs step to sample the auxiliary momenta, but technically that sampling is doing something else.  Ignoring the technical details, HMC is making a joint update of all the model parameters which is what is important.
> > > > >
> > > > > This leaves two issues: hierarchical modes are hard and discrete models are harder.
> > > > >
> > > > > We review hierarchical models thoroughly in http://arxiv.org/abs/1312.0906, in particular we address why Euclidean HMC can run into problems.  A common approach that people take, starting with Radford Neal way back when he was first introducing HMC into stats, is to sample from the hyperparameters conditional on the local parameters,
> > > > > but this inevitably leads to large autocorrelations because of the strong dependencies between the hyperparameters and the local parameters.  What you'd really want to do is sample from the marginal distribution of the hyperparameters, but computing that distribution is a tremendously difficult task.  Pseudomarginal methods are trying to solve this, but they are hard to make general and can run into their own pathologies.  As noted in the paper, Riemannian HMC solves many of these problems by construction, and it's coming soon to Stan.  At the moment your best bet is to find a good non-centered parameterization.
> > > > >
> > > > > Everyone wants discrete parameters but everyone also needs to understand the underlying problems.  Without the nice structure of a continuous measure, it's very, very hard to construct an efficient sampler.  Moreover, if you split your parameters into continuous and discrete then you're doing conditional updates, which will be slow as discussed above.  We've seen lots of success when the discrete parameters can be marginalized out to give a fully continuous model amenable to HMC.  This includes discrete latent models, provided there aren't too many possible states.
> > > > >
> > > > > You can certainly use Stan as a sampling API and stick it into a bigger sampler, but without addressing the fundamental problems with discrete variables and conditional updates you're only going to be able to go so far.
> > > > >

Thanks for the feedback, it seems I'm not obviously doing anything ridiculous, and alternating samplers is, in principle, OK.

Just like the no free lunch theorem (which I've seen used to justify all kinds of nonsense) in optimisation, different samplers may be suitable for different problems, and then the trick is to automatically adjust the proportion of the time spent in different samplers according to the problem. This was the main trick I used with DREAM, by examining the step size from dual averaging v. the theoretical step size for normal distributions. In practice, it means that if the hessian is fairly stable, DREAM dominates, if not NUTS dominates. It is easy to see why DREAM is hopeless with severe bananas..

On Friday, July 25, 2014 2:34:46 AM UTC-4, Emmanuel Charpentier wrote:
> It seems that my problem (and problems with installing other libraries after enabling parallel compilation) might have been caused by this (undocumented) leftover of the installation of Rstan 3.2 -O3 is a bit *too* optimizing for complex tasks...

-O3 may be too extreme for some other R packages, but I don't think that is the problem with the rstan installation. If R from Sage were picking up the -O3 flag, then there would have been a -O3 in each call to g++ while it was compiling rstan. There was no -O at all, which is equivalent to -O0, which does not work for rstan with g++ for some unknown reason, like Mav mentioned when he linked to

https://travis-ci.org/stan-dev/rstan/builds/30479408

The install_rstan() function explicitly ignores ~/.R/Makevars because people (mostly Windows people) mess that file up by including -g in the CXXFLAGS, in which case mingw is unable to compile it. By ignoring ~/.R/Makevars, install.packages() reverts to the CXXFLAGS that were used to compile R, which is somehow empty when run from the Sage beta (after I mv ~/.R/Makevars out of the way)

> system(paste0(Sys.getenv('R_HOME'), "/bin/R", " CMD config CXXFLAGS"))

>
> BTW : could you explicitely state this in the rstan install document

yes

> make rstan depend on CRAN's Rcpp, inline and BH,

it does (for rstan 2.4.0)

> source("http://mc-stan.org/rstan/install.R", max.deparse.length = 1500, echo = TRUE)

> install_rstan <- function() {
+   on.exit(Sys.unsetenv("R_MAKEVARS_USER"))
+   on.exit(Sys.unsetenv("R_MAKEVARS_SITE"), add = TRUE)
+
+   try(remove.packages("rstan"), silent = TRUE)
+   Sys.setenv(R_MAKEVARS_USER = "foobar")
+   Sys.setenv(R_MAKEVARS_SITE = "foobar")
+   install.packages(c("inline", "BH", "RcppEigen"))
+   install.packages("Rcpp", type = "source")
+   library(inline)
+   library(Rcpp)
+   src <- '
+     std::vector<std::string> s;
+     s.push_back("hello");
+     s.push_back("world");
+     return Rcpp::wrap(s);
+   '
+   hellofun <- cxxfunction(body = src, includes = '', plugin = 'Rcpp', verbose = FALSE)
+   test <- try(hellofun())
+   if(inherits(test, "try-error")) stop("hello world failed; ask for help on Rcpp list")
+
+   options(repos = c(getOption("repos"),
+           rstan = "http://rstan.org/repo/"))
+   install.packages("rstan", type = 'source')
+   library(rstan)
+   set_cppo("fast")
+   if (any(grepl("^darwin", R.version$os, ignore.case = TRUE))) {
+     cat('\nCC=clang', 'CXX=clang++ -arch x86_64 -ftemplate-depth-256',
+         file = "~/.R/Makevars", sep = "\n", append = TRUE)
+   }
+   return(invisible(NULL))
+ }

> use a simpler install command (see above) AND GET RID OF THE DAMN INSTALL SCRIPT ?
>
> Just my two cents... What do you think ?

I think I have been advocating getting rstan onto CRAN for more than two years

https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-dev/wIpu_otqK10/H5OZnHOX5PQJ

and am the only Stan developer that is strongly in favor of getting rstan onto CRAN, so you are shouting at the wrong person. BH 1.54.0-x was the first version of the BH package that would build rstan and rstan 1.0.1 was rejected from CRAN on September 15, 2012 largely for bundling the necessary parts of Boost. Since then, we have dealt with one installation problem after another on Windows and Mac OSX (and occasionally Linux) that has culminated in the script you are keen to get rid of, which has reduced installation problems of rstan 2.3.0 and rstan 2.4.0 to a trickle. We don't permanently drop anything. We ignore ~/.R/Makevars by instead searching for foobar inside the install_rstan() function and then read from it thereafter

  ...
  on.exit(Sys.unsetenv("R_MAKEVARS_USER"))

  on.exit(Sys.unsetenv("R_MAKEVARS_SITE"), add = TRUE)

  Sys.setenv(R_MAKEVARS_SITE = "foobar")
  ...

The rstan package should install with R's CXXFLAGS. It is a very minor rstan bug that it currently does not install if R's CXXFLAGS are empty, in which case g++ compiles at -O0. It is a less minor bug in Sage that it builds R with empty CXXFLAGS. You can work around both bugs by filling out ~/.R/Makevars however you like (excluding CXXFLAGS=-O0 if CXX=g++) and installing rstan without the install_rstan() function.

I think you are objecting to the set_cppo() function, which is called by install_rstan() after rstan is installed and modifies ~/.R/Makevars so that it is correctly formatted and by default uses -O3 because that makes Stan programs run slightly faster than -O2 and much faster than any other optimization level. Setting -O3 probably breaks some other R packages, which I would be sympathetic to if that happened on your system, but it changes a  non-executable file, is documented and also prints a message to the console when it is called.

>

> > +   install.packages("Rcpp", type = "source")

No:

http://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/R-exts.html#Package-Dependencies

> "Field ‘Depends’ should nowadays be used rarely, only for packages which are intended to be put on the search path to make their facilities available to the end user (and not to the package itself)"

and later on in that same section

> A package that wishes to make use of header files in other packages needs to declare them as a comma-separated list in the field ‘LinkingTo’ in the DESCRIPTION file. For example
> LinkingTo: link1, link2
>
> As from R 3.0.2 the ‘LinkingTo’ field can have a version requirement which is checked at installation. (In earlier versions of R it would cause the specification to be ignored.)
>
> Specifying a package in ‘LinkingTo’ suffices if these are C++ headers containing source code or static linking is done at installation: the packages do not need to be (and usually should not be) listed in the ‘Depends’ or ‘Imports’ fields. This includes CRAN packages BH <http://CRAN.R-project.org/package=BH> and almost all users of RcppArmadillo <http://CRAN.R-project.org/package=RcppArmadillo> and RcppEigen <http://CRAN.R-project.org/package=RcppEigen>.
which is exactly what the DESCRIPTION file in rstan does

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/stan-dev/rstan/develop/rstan/rstan/DESCRIPTION

Depends: R (>= 3.0.2), Rcpp (>= 0.9.10), utils, inline, methods
LinkingTo: Rcpp, RcppEigen, BH (>= 1.54)
Suggests: RUnit, RcppEigen, BH (>= 1.54), parallel

with the added Suggests line to work around the undocumented fact that the rstan vignette would not build without it.

You just have to be careful to do all this balancing
during warmup, throw away the warmup samples, and then
used fixed parameters during actual sampling.

If you adjust ratios after warmup, then you break
detailed balance and almost certainly the
break the stationary distribution for MCMC, except
under circumstances where the adjustment tails off
fast enough in magnitude or the adjustments themselves
are reversible.

- Bob

This was the main trick I used with DREAM, by examining the step size from dual averaging v. the theoretical step size for normal distributions. messages.body_plain:
On Friday, July 25, 2014 2:53:59 PM UTC-4, Emmanuel Charpentier wrote:
> Dear Ben :
> A couple more datapoints :
> 1) Sages'R indeed needs -O2 (or -O3, but I'd settle for -O2 since -O3 leads to invalid objects for other libraries, such as nloptr, which is the workhorse of a lot of other packages...).

OK

> 2) I did not (yet) found a way to pass it from R to an installation od rstan othar than via "./RMakevars". GCC mysteries...

I suspect there is something suboptimal in the Sage build. A plain ./configure on the r-devel tree results in

R is now configured for x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu

  Source directory:          .
  Installation directory:    /usr/local

  C compiler:                gcc -std=gnu99  -g -O2
  Fortran 77 compiler:       gfortran  -g -O2

  C++ compiler:              g++  -g -O2
  C++ 11 compiler:           g++  -std=c++11 -g -O2
  Fortran 90/95 compiler:    gfortran -g -O2

So, someone would have to do something other than a plain ./configure to remove the -O2.

> 3) System's R does not seem to *need* -O2|3, but gives a couple of warnings about 'exceeded limits. Retrying without limits".

I get those also with g++, and I think they are harmless because it succeeds on the retry. They do not appear with clang++.

> 4) GCC mysteries : any compilation of rstan seem to need about 2 Gb (!!!) of memory. Parallelizing it seriously accelerates the process, but needs as much as 11,2 Gb (!!!!) of RAM.

Not a mystery or at least this is something we have known to be the case for 3 years. With clang++, it is much better in terms of RAM usage. With g++-4.9, you can add the flags -flto and -ffat-lto-objects (see https://gcc.gnu.org/gcc-4.9/changes.html) to CXXFLAGS in ~/.R/Makevars and it is a lot better but not quite as good as clang++.

> 5) Consequences of 4) : any model compilation (even a small one) on a 2 Gb machine leads to swapping.

I would install clang++ from the Debian repositories and set CC=clang and CXX=clang++ in ~/.R/Makevars

> [...]

> Rstan 2.3 still left me with .//Makevars... (notwithstanding the set_cppo hypothesis).

Yes, so there is some chance that it will break other packages, and I would understand if CRAN makes us get rid of set_cppo() if / when we retry to upload it to CRAN. But set_cppo() in rstan 2.3.0 should have produced a valid ~/.R/Makevars for installing rstan. It is just we can't ensure that ~/.R/Makevars is valid on every user's machine so install_rstan() ignores it in favor of whatever settings R was built with (which are amenable to installing rstan for any binary install of R or a sane source install of R but apparently not Sage's).

> Shouldn't setting this option be *internal* to rstan's wrapper functions ? Again, the idea is to avoid to modify the state of thge user's computer. To your garden-variety biostatistician, GCC is something like an endemic disease (fortunately non-mortal (usually...)) ; the CXXFLAGS some sort of prognostic factor. The Stan USER should NOT have to worry with such technical details -but these should be documented for the special cases).

I don't think there is a way to pass a particular set of flags when internally calling stan_model() (to compile the program) that wouldn't get superseded by what is in ~/.R/Makevars because the compilation is actually done with a separate R process. For most users that do not want to worry about such technical details, calling set_cppo() once solves that problem, but it is somewhat evil to the extent it breaks other R packages.

>  [...]

>
> I think you are objecting to the set_cppo() function, which is called by install_rstan() after rstan is installed and modifies ~/.R/Makevars

>
> That might be the case. I didn't think of that... But this should be documented as a potentially serious side effect. And, if possible at all, limited in scope by the R wrapper functions.
>
> > so that it is correctly formatted and by default uses -O3 because that makes Stan programs run slightly faster than -O2 and much faster than any other optimization level. Setting -O3 probably breaks some other R packages, which I would be sympathetic to if that happened on your system,
>
> It did. More than once ...

Sorry. We were aware of the potential for this problem, but were not aware of particular packages that do not work under -O3. If you could tell us what those were, we could add a warning about that to the documentation. If you call set_cppo("presentation2"), it should set it back to -O2.

>
> > but it changes a  non-executable file, is documented and also prints a message to the console when it is called.
>
> Not during installation !

It isn't read during installation, but it is modified by install_rstan() after the installation. There should be a message like "mode fast without NDEBUG for compiling C++ code is set".

> >
> > > [ ... ]
> > >
> > > > +   install.packages(c("inline", "BH", "RcppEigen"))
> > > > +   install.packages("Rcpp", type = "source")
> > >
> > > No : here, you unconditionally install whatever Rcpp and BH version happens to be available on CRAN at install time. You should install use the "Depends" field of the DESCRIPTION file, which would install the packages *if necessary* (even with version constraints if necessary).
> >
> > No:
> >
> > http://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/R-exts.html#Package-Dependencies
> >
> > > "Field ‘Depends’ should nowadays be used rarely, only for packages which are intended to be put on the search path to make their facilities available to the end user (and not to the package itself)"
> >
> > and later on in that same section
> >
> > > A package that wishes to make use of header files in other packages needs to declare them as a comma-separated list in the field ‘LinkingTo’ in the DESCRIPTION file. For example
> > > LinkingTo: link1, link2
> > >
> > > As from R 3.0.2 the ‘LinkingTo’ field can have a version requirement which is checked at installation. (In earlier versions of R it would cause the specification to be ignored.)
> > >
> > > Specifying a package in ‘LinkingTo’ suffices if these are C++ headers containing source code or static linking is done at installation: the packages do not need to be (and usually should not be) listed in the ‘Depends’ or ‘Imports’ fields. This includes CRAN packages BH <http://CRAN.R-project.org/package=BH> and almost all users of RcppArmadillo <http://CRAN.R-project.org/package=RcppArmadillo> and RcppEigen <http://CRAN.R-project.org/package=RcppEigen>.
> > which is exactly what the DESCRIPTION file in rstan does
> >
> > https://raw.githubusercontent.com/stan-dev/rstan/develop/rstan/rstan/DESCRIPTION
> >
> > Depends: R (>= 3.0.2), Rcpp (>= 0.9.10), utils, inline, methods
> > LinkingTo: Rcpp, RcppEigen, BH (>= 1.54)
> > Suggests: RUnit, RcppEigen, BH (>= 1.54), parallel
> >
> > with the added Suggests line to work around the undocumented fact that the rstan vignette would not build without it.
>
> Okay. So why unconditionally install BH and RcppEigen ?

Because BH and RcppEigen are not only needed when the package is built / installed but also when stan_model() is called to compile the user's program. So, you could install rstan but not use it unless BH and RcppEigen are on the disk. CRAN's DESCRIPTION file does not have an idiom for this case. (Re)Installing them unconditionally isn't harmful but wastes a little bandwidth if they are already installed. I suppose I could write some logic to check whether they are installed and what version they have, but I haven't gotten around to it.

Ben

messages.subject: Stan 2.4 now available
messages.subject_clean: Stan 2.4 now available
messages.body_plain:
As usual, instructions for all three interfaces (RStan, PyStan,
CmdStan) are available starting from the Stan home page:

   http://mc-stan.org/

Appended below are the release notes indicating what's new.

- Stan Development Team

v2.4.0 (20 July 2014)
======================================================================

New Features
------------
* L-BFGS optimization (now the default)
* completed higher-order autodiff (added all probability functions,
  matrix functions, and matrix operators);  tested up to 3rd order
* enhanced effective range of normal_cdf to prevent underflow/overflow
* added von Mises RNG
* added ability to use scalars in all element-wise operations
* allow matrix division for mixing scalars and matrices
* vectorization of outcome variates in multivariate normal with efficiency boosts
* generalization of multivariate normal to allow rwo vectors as means
  and

Reorganization
--------------
* move bin/print and bin/stanc to CmdStan;  no longer generating main
  when compiling model from Stan C++

New Developer
-------------
* Added Jeffrey Arnold as core Stan developer
* Added Mitzi Morris as core Stan developer

Bug Fixes
---------
* modified error messages so that they're all 1-indexed instead of 0-indexed
* fixed double print out of times in commands
* const added to iterators to allow VS2008 compiles
* fix boundary conditions on ordered tests
* fix for pow as ^ syntax to catch illegal use of vectors (which
  aren't supported)
* allow zero-length inputs to multi_normal and multi_student_t
  with appropriate log prob (i.e., 0)
* fixed bug in inverse-Wishart RNG to match MCMCPack results
  with slightly asymmetric inputs
* fixed problem with compiling user-defined function twice
* fixed problem with int-only parameters for user-defined functions
* fixed NaN init problems for user-defined functions
* added check that user variable doesn't conflict with user function + doc
* disallow void argument types in user-defined functions

Code Cleanup and Efficiency Improvements
----------------------------------------
* removed main() from models generated from C++ Stan (they are
  now available only in CmdStan); removed no_main command options
* reserve vector sizes for saving for sample recorder
* removing many instances of std::cout from API (more still to go)
* removed non-functional Nesterov optimization option
* optimization code refactoring for testing ease
* better constant handling in von Mises distribution
* removed tabs from all source files
* massive re-org of testing to remove redundant files and allow
  traits-based specializations, plus fixed for 1-indexing

Testing
-------
* added tests for log_softmax, multiply_lower_tri_self_transpose, tcrossprod
* break out function signature tests into individual files, add many
  more
* enhanced cholesky factor tests for round trip transforms and
  derivatives
* extensive unit testing added for optimization
* remove use of std::cout in all tests

Example Models
--------------
* lots of cleanup in links and models in ARM examples
* added BUGS litter example with more stable priors than in the
  BUGS version (the original model doesn't fit well in BUGS as is,
  either)

Documentation
-------------
* add infix operators to manual
* categorical_logit sampling statement
* Cholesky factor with unit diagonal transform example
* example of using linear regression for prediction/forecasting with
  notes
* clarified some relations of naive Bayes to clustering
  vs. classification and relation to non-identifiability
* new advice on multivariate priors for quad_form_diag
* fix typo in multiply_lower_self_transpose (thanks to Alexey Stukalov)
* fix formatting of reserved names in manual
* fixed typo and clarified effective sample size doc

On Jul 27, 2014, at 10:22 PM, Hiroki Mizukami <rocky...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi Bob
>
> The problem has gone!

Glad to hear it.

> Actually , I deal with it by followings,
>
> parameters{
> ...
>   positive_ordered[2] a[T];
> ...
> }
> transformed parameters{
> ...
>   vector[T] a1;
>   vector[T] a2;
>
>   for(t in 1:T){
>     a1[t] <- a[t,1];
>     a2[t] <- a[t,2];
>   }
> }
>
> ==
> Vectorizing is useful, but we have to gave the variable name explicitly , to understand the meaning of variables.

I don't see why.  a[,1] is just a2 and a[,2] is just your a1.
So it's not like they're getting lost.  Just renamed.

If you want to recover the a1 and a2 as above, then it's more
efficient to do it in the generated quantities block instead of
the transformed parameters block.  The issue with making it transformed
parameters is that it negatively impacts speed because any parameters,
including transformed parameters, get added to the expression graph for
the log probability and take up time during gradient calculations (here,
needless applications of the chain rule).

But, if you want to use a1 and a2 in the model, then they need to be
transformed parameters.

>  I really really appreciate you! thanks!
>

You're welcome!

- Bob

Hi Hiroki,

As Bob mentioned, if you just want to pick out the T-dimensional vector from ordered[2] a[T] it'll be much faster doing that in the "generated quantities" block instead of the "transformed parameters" block. All that means is you'll want to define a1 and a2 inside the generated quantities block and do the assignment there.

You're right that Stan doesn't have a good way of accessing a[,1] or a[,2].

Regarding vectorization:
- for loops in Stan are not slow.
- vectorization is faster in Stan when it can figure out how to not calculate expressions multiple times and/or it has special implementation that reduces the time it takes for automatic differentiation. The place where Stan does this the best is in its probability distributions.
- vectorization is convenient for writing out expressions

I guess the point I want to make is that the loops aren't slow in Stan and you should just use loops to set a1 and a2 without worry about trying to find a more efficient way to do it.

Daniel

messages.subject: Nice vectorized multi_normal speedup
messages.subject_clean: Nice vectorized multi_normal speedup
messages.body_plain:
With 2.4 out, I ran a quick test of how much speedup I could get by changing my old non-vectorized multi_normal sampling to the new vectorized form. I get a 40% time savings, without even trying hard. This is much better than I expected.

Timings with vectorized multi_normal:

#  Elapsed Time: 96.8564 seconds (Warm-up)
#                87.8308 seconds (Sampling)
#                184.687 seconds (Total)

Timings without vectorized multi_normal:

#  Elapsed Time: 168.544 seconds (Warm-up)
#                147.83 seconds (Sampling)
#                316.375 seconds (Total)

These timings are for a Gaussian mixed model with three random effects, 5000 cases, and 500 groups. The only difference between these two models was changing this line:

vary ~ multi_normal( rep_vector(0,3) , SIGMA );

to this line:

for ( j in 1:N_id ) vary[j] ~ multi_normal( rep_vector(0,3) , SIGMA );

Really nice stuff.

messages.body_plain:
The savings are proportionally bigger with higher dimensional
SIGMA, too.

You get the same kind of speedup vectorizing plain old normal, too.

The main reason is that the checks for well-formedness of Sigma
only need to be done once and that the autodiff is more efficient
because the expression tree getting built up has fewer nodes, and
hence fewer virtual function calls.

We still have some headroom to speed these things up --- the only
thing we're missing is programmer time!

- Bob

On Monday, July 28, 2014 4:02:12 PM UTC-4, Richard McElreath wrote:
> These timings are for a Gaussian mixed model with three random effects, 5000 cases, and 500 groups. The only difference between these two models was changing this line:
>
> vary ~ multi_normal( rep_vector(0,3) , SIGMA );
>
> to this line:
>
> for ( j in 1:N_id ) vary[j] ~ multi_normal( rep_vector(0,3) , SIGMA );
>
> Really nice stuff.

It is nice that multi_normal is vectorized now. But it is also important to keep in mind opportunities to avoid using it (can't quite tell which might be applicable in your situation, but as a general principle the following are true). If the LHS is a parameter, you can change it to a transformed parameter where

vary <- L * z;

such that L * L' = SIGMA, where L is a Cholesky factor, and z is a matrix whose elements are distributed iid standard normal a priori i.e. include

to_vector(z) ~ normal(0,1);

in the model block.

Or if SIGMA is unknown with an inverse-Wishart prior (which I am skeptical of), you can integrate it out according to Wikipedia <http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inverse-Wishart_distribution#Conjugate_distribution>

and obtain a prior distribution for the unknown X as a function of the degrees of freedom (nu) and scatter matrix (Psi). In the usual case where nu and Psi are known, this is proportional to a

increment_log_prob(-0.5 * (nu + n) * log_determinant(Psi + tcrossprod(X)));

So, I really don't use multi_normal() much.

Ben

messages.subject: update on uniformly sampling a convex polytope
messages.subject_clean: update on uniformly sampling a convex polytope
messages.body_plain:
I posted a question last week about uniformly sampling a convex polytope with Stan:
https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/stan-users/YCCOuUO4jgc

I am really thankful for the responses from the Stan community. Below is the code I currently use to sample points from a 20-dimensional simplex:

library(rstan)
library(MASS)
A <- matrix(1, nrow = 1, ncol = 20)
b <- 1
dim(b) <- 1
Ag <- ginv(A)
code <-'data {
  int<lower=1> m;
  int<lower=1> n;
  vector[m] b;
  matrix[m,n] A;
  matrix[n,m] Ag;
}
transformed data {
  matrix[n,n] ImAgA;
  vector[n] Agb;
  Agb <- Ag * b;
  ImAgA <- -Ag*A;
  for(i in 1:n) ImAgA[i,i] <- ImAgA[i,i] + 1.0;
}
parameters {
  vector[n] w;
}
transformed parameters {
  vector<lower=0>[n] x;
  x <- Agb + ImAgA * w;
}
model {
}'
d <- list(m = 1, n = 20, b = b, A = A, Ag = Ag)
fit <- stan(model_code = code, data = d, init="0", chains = 1, iter = 2000)
x <- extract(fit)$x

Except for some uninvited informational messages (running R from cmd does partially solve the problem as Ben kindly suggests), the sampling looks alright. So I went on to evaluate the sampling quality using coda package which implements Gelman-Rubin diagnostic. I created five mcmc objects with methods in the coda package, each from a single chain with 1000 points. Then I combined them into a mcmc list and passed it to Gelman - Rubin test. Here is the specific code:

library(coda)
m1 <- as.mcmc(extract(stan(model_code = code, data = d, init="0", chains = 1, iter = 2000))$x)
m2 <- as.mcmc(extract(stan(model_code = code, data = d, init="0", chains = 1, iter = 2000))$x)
m3 <- as.mcmc(extract(stan(model_code = code, data = d, init="0", chains = 1, iter = 2000))$x)
m4 <- as.mcmc(extract(stan(model_code = code, data = d, init="0", chains = 1, iter = 2000))$x)
m5 <- as.mcmc(extract(stan(model_code = code, data = d, init="0", chains = 1, iter = 2000))$x)
mclist.stan <- mcmc.list(m1, m2, m3, m4, m5)
gelman.diag(mclist.stan, multivariate = FALSE)

According to my understanding, an upper bound of 1 for Gelman-Rubin statistic indicates good mixing while a result substantially larger than 1 implies poor convergence. Below is what I got for each of the 20 dimensions (first column shows point estimates and second column shows the upper limit of 95% C.I.):

      Point est. Upper C.I.
 [1,]       1.81       3.19
 [2,]       1.39       1.97
 [3,]       2.19       4.28
 [4,]       1.25       1.59
 [5,]       1.10       1.25
 [6,]       1.22       1.58
 [7,]       1.65       2.70
 [8,]       2.42       5.13
 [9,]       1.08       1.22
[10,]       1.44       2.02
[11,]       1.18       1.49
[12,]       2.13       3.71
[13,]       2.00       3.62
[14,]       1.13       1.30
[15,]       1.84       3.08
[16,]       1.22       1.66
[17,]       2.43       4.28
[18,]       2.37       4.83
[19,]       1.22       1.59
[20,]       2.06       3.32

I accidentally came across another package - limSolve - with a function called "xsample" which does exactly uniform sampling under linear constraints. For default setting, "xsample" adopts mirror algorithm which "uses the inequality constraints as reflecting planes along which jumps are reflected" and thus has an exponential complexity with respect to input dimensions. Below is how I approached the same 20-dimensional simplex sampling problem with "xsample" in limSolve package and how I examined its performance:

library(limSolve)
dimen <- 20
E <- matrix(1, nrow = 1, ncol = dimen)
F <- c(1)
G <- diag(1, nrow = dimen, ncol = dimen)
H <- matrix(0, nrow = dimen, ncol = 1)
s1 <- as.mcmc(xsample(E = E, F = F, G = G, H = H, iter = 2000, outputlength = 1000)[[1]])
s2 <- as.mcmc(xsample(E = E, F = F, G = G, H = H, iter = 2000, outputlength = 1000)[[1]])
s3 <- as.mcmc(xsample(E = E, F = F, G = G, H = H, iter = 2000, outputlength = 1000)[[1]])
s4 <- as.mcmc(xsample(E = E, F = F, G = G, H = H, iter = 2000, outputlength = 1000)[[1]])
s5 <- as.mcmc(xsample(E = E, F = F, G = G, H = H, iter = 2000, outputlength = 1000)[[1]])
mclist.xsam <- mcmc.list(s1, s2, s3, s4, s5)
gelman.diag(mclist.xsam, multivariate = FALSE)

And here is the Gelman-Rubin test score for sampling with limSolve:

      Point est. Upper C.I.
 [1,]       1.00       1.00
 [2,]       1.00       1.01
 [3,]       1.01       1.01
 [4,]       1.02       1.03
 [5,]       1.00       1.01
 [6,]       1.00       1.01
 [7,]       1.01       1.02
 [8,]       1.00       1.01
 [9,]       1.00       1.00
[10,]       1.00       1.01
[11,]       1.00       1.01
[12,]       1.00       1.01
[13,]       1.00       1.00
[14,]       1.00       1.01
[15,]       1.00       1.01
[16,]       1.00       1.01
[17,]       1.00       1.00
[18,]       1.00       1.00
[19,]       1.00       1.00
[20,]       1.00       1.00

Maybe it's my fault, but it does appear that "xsample" outperforms Stan by this measure. However, I really want to use Stan to solve my uniform sampling problem (not just from simplex but more generally from convex polytope), because Stan seems more systematic and professional at sampling various distributions. I wonder if there should be some smarter ways of tackling this problem with Stan.

I saw in the forum FAQ that adding a new distribution to Stan with C++ is easy, so can uniform sampling be cracked this way? I also learned that Stan's sampling scheme over a finite interval consists of mapping the interval to some unconstrained space and then using logistic sampler before finally converting the sampled result back to the designated interval. Will this process get in the way of uniformity? Or maybe we can just add some tailored functionality to Stan for a more satisfactory solution?

The above paragraph is just my random thoughts which may or may not be relevant. Again, every suggestion on the central problem of better sampling the positive solution space of Ax=b with Stan is greatly appreciated.

messages.body_plain:
How are you comparing speed?  The only measure that makes
sense is effective samples per second (or seconds per effective
sample).

If you can share the Stan model, we could tell you more.
There are various "tricks" to implementing such models having
to do with reparameterizations --- there's a discussion in the manual,
which also has a pointer to the Betancourt and Girolami arXiv paper, with
a much deeper analysis of hierarchical models in HMC.

- Bobp
