messages.body_plain:
Just to check if I'm understanding your code: your model predicts counts using a Poisson, with a log-linear predictor that involves both a random intercept (alpha) and slope (gamma*diameter), where you've set the prior mean for the random slope to zero (why?)).

In the generated quantities you simulate both posterior predictive values (i.e. "counts_rep": random counts given the fitted mu for each data point) and mixed prior-posterior predictive values (i.e. "counts_rep1": random counts given independently re-sampled random effects and given the fitted fixed effects).

My first thought is there may be considerable correlation between the two random effects alpha and gamma, which you are not capturing in your posterior predictive checks. Solution would be to explicitly model alpha and and gamma from a bivariate normal distribution, and using the estimated hyperparameters of this bivariate distribution to generate alpha and gamma in the generated quantities block.

I'm not sure how to interpret the plots that you've produced. What does a data point represent? The average of the posterior? I would somehow expect "error-bars" for each data point to illustrate the variation of the discrepancy measure over all the samples of the posterior. A good starting point for me is usually to plot the replicated data (y-axis) against the observed data (x-axis), and then go on to discrepancy measures. It might also be helpful to plot the results of different lots with different colors or symbols.

Best,

Luc

messages.body_plain:
It would help if you told us in formulas what you want
the posterior to be.  I didn't understand the rather
ad-hoc looking use of weights in the glm() function in R:

  Non-NULL weights can be used to indicate that different observations
  have different dispersions (with the values inweights being inversely
  proportional to the dispersions); or equivalently, when the elements of
  weights are positive integers w_i, that each response y_i is the mean
  of w_i unit-weight observations. For a binomial GLM prior weights are
  used to give the number of trials when the response is the proportion
  of successes: they would rarely be used for a Poisson GLM.

If you just want to treat each instance as the equivalent of
weights[i] fractional instances, then what you have is correct.

But instead of this:

   la <- exp(a);
   for(i in 1:N) {

       ll <- poisson_log(counts[i],la);
       increment_log_prob(weights[i] * ll);

you're better off for arithmetic statiblity using

   for (i in 1:N)
     increment_log_prob(weights[i] * poisson_log_log(counts[i], a));

That is, use the log-scale version of Poisson.

I'd also recommend tighter priors than normal(0,100) unless
your data is on that scale.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I have no idea about the modeling, but as far as the Stan
code goes, rather than writing this:

  log_lik [i] <- poisson_log (counts [i], exp (mu [i]));

you could write:

  log_lik[i] <- poisson_log_log(counts[i], mu[i]);

This takes a parameter on the log scale and does the exp transform
internally, which is less likely to cause arithmetic problems.

(I find the spaces make the code very hard to read.)

There's no reason to define the mu as a transformed parameter rather
than a local variable unless you need it in the output.

We don't have a poisson_log_rng, but we probably should.
Basically, anywhere you see an exp() in a program you should
be nervous about arithmetic behavior.  Ditto an inverse() for
matrices.

- Bob

Thanks for the clarification. I know see that gamma is vector[N], not vector[NL]. Not so sure whether you need to pursue the bivariate modeling of alpha and gamma. You might want to check first whether the posterior estimates of each alpha and gamma are correlated between lots. If so, you may want to model alpha and gamma bivariately, specifying gamma conditional on alpha:

Copied and pasted from: http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multivariate_normal_distribution#Bivariate_conditional_expectation

Here, X1 is gamma[i], X2 is the lot-specific alpha[lot[i]], sigma1 and sigma2 are the marginal standard deviations of gamma and alpha (both 1 in your model), mu2 is the mean of prior for alpha (zero), and rho is a correlated parameter that needs to be estimated. The implementation in your model is straightforward if you let go the Matt trick (the multiplication of a N(0,1) random value with some scale parameter). If you want to hold on to the Matt trick because your dataset is small, you would have to figure out some smart coding, which should be doable.

What I meant by "A good starting point..." was to plot the posterior of the replicated data (as mean or median + error bars for 95% credible interval) on the y-axis against the observed data on the x-axis. Telling me that you derived the plots from "Bayesian Modeling with WinBUGS" doesn't really help me understand them. Can you be more specific about what you plotted?

Best,

messages.body_plain:
Again looking at the second plot of NewLots.jpg, I start wondering what went into the calculation of the discrepancy metric (squared residuals?) for each axis. I'm guessing that for the replicate data, you did (data_rep - mu_rep)^2, where mu_rep includes the resampled random effects (i.e. mixed prior-posterior predictive check);  and that for the observed data, you calculated (data - mu_rep)^2.

If this is so, one should expect that discrepancy metric for the observed data is always going to be much and much larger than for the replicated data. So I'm not sure (and really don't know) whether you are calculating your discrepancy metrics in the right way. I often get terribly confused when I try to think about posterior predictive checks, and it's happening again now :). Really, we want someone like Andrew Gelman to chime in at this point!

What I think is the correct way to calculated discrepancy metric T for your mixed prior-posterior predictive check is:

T_rep = (data_rep - mu_fit)^2, where data_rep includes resampled random effects
T_obs = (data_obs - mu_fit)^2

T = T_obs - T_rep

Then, if T for any data-point is often > 0, it means that the observed data are rather far away from the model. You could also sum your T_rep and T_obs per cluster and then compare whether some clusters lie within a plausible distance from the model.

messages.body_plain:
So a common issue with posterior predictive checks for hierarchical models is that the the classic approach gives results that are far too optimistic (e.g. compared to cross-validation). When you only replicate data from the fitted mu's, you are essentially overestimating the model fit in your PPC. That's exactly what you see in the first plot: perfect correlation. No single model is really that good! The second model looks much more like something that you would expect from a cross-validation exercise, although it's hard to see which sets of green and red data-points actually represent a single observations. Error-bars would be great :), as in dx.doi.org/10.1371/journal.pntd.0002168.g004 <http://dx.doi.org/10.1371/journal.pntd.0002168.g004>, just to blatantly quote myself. I don't have the code around though, otherwise I'd happily share it with you.

Now about that discrepancy test that you used for NewLots.jpg in your original post: did you calculate Pearson residuals relative to mu_rep or mu_fit? I.e., what "mu" are you feeding into the function in "fit.r" from your original post? You should be feeding it fitted values of mu and replicated data based on replicated values of mu (i.e. mu including new random effects).

Hope this clarifies things.

Luc

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: goodness of fit for mixed model
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: goodness of fit for mixed model
messages.body_plain:
Hi Linus,

Like I said, you should always be using the fitted mu to calculate your discrepancy test, also for your "new lots". So for mixed prior/posterior predictive checks, the Pearson residuals are: (data_obs - mu_fit) / mu_fit and (data_rep - mu_fit) / mu_fit, where data_rep is based on mu_rep.

"I think that I need to look for a better model since the full predictive distribution is too optimistic."

The way you calculate the residuals for your "existing lots" is too optimistic. That in itself does not mean that your model is wrong. You need to make a better comparison, which is why you should be (and are) doing a mixed prior/posterior predictive check (i.e. as above in bold). .

"My observation is that for a wide range of observed values prediction is pretty much the same.  Are there any techniques to make prediction more sensitive to observed values?"

Keep in mind that have a Poisson model. So when you simulate replicate data from mu 1.6 and 1.8, the generated values will look pretty much the same because of Poisson sampling error. Given that your model also included overdispersion, the variation in your simulated replicate data should be large! You may want to check whether the overdispersion term is really necessary in your case.

That plot looks great. For interpretability, you may want to log-transform both axes and add an identity line (y=x). Judging from the plot, it seems that the random intercepts explains most of the variation in the data (the data seem very neatly grouped by color), and within lots, there seem to be relatively little variation in predicted values. Do the length and diameter covariates really explain anything?

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Adding weight to the likelihood as glm in R does
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Adding weight to the likelihood as glm in R does
messages.body_plain:
You mean in this section:

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weighted_least_squares#Weighted_least_squares

I couldn't quite understand the least-squares formulation.

Andrew might jump in with a more Bayesian model-based solution,
because the application looks to my untrained eye a lot like his pet
example, 8 schools.

The way to work out what happens in Stan is to just look
at the posterior.  If you have a standard linear regression with
no priors and coefficient and noise scale parameters beta and sigma,
then the log posterior is proportional to

  log p(beta,sigma|y,x) propto SUM_n log normal(y[n] | x[n] * beta, sigma)

                        =     SUM_n -log(sigma) - [0.5 * (y[n] - x[n] * beta) / sigma)]^2

Where I'm using propto loosely on the log scale to mean equal up to
an additive constant that doesn't depend on beta or sigma.

So if you do

  for (n in 1:N)
    increment_log_prob(normal_log(y[n], x[n] * beta, sigma));

this is the posterior you get.

If you multiply the term added to the log prob by w[i], as in

 for (n in 1:N)
    increment_log_prob(w[n] * normal_log(y[n], x[n] * beta, sigma));

then the posterior will be

  log p(beta, sigma | y, x, w) propto

    SUM_n w[n] * { -log(sigma) - [0.5 * (y[n] - x[n] * beta) / sigma)]^2 }

If that's what you want, then you're good to go.

Even if you think it's right analytically, I would run some tests
on problems with known answers to make sure you're getting the
right answers.  (Of course, that's tricky because the MLE isn't
necessarily close to the posterior mean until you get a lot of data.)

- Bob

If you want to do inference, you need a probability model, and in that case you can still do this but then you have to think a bit more carefully about what your model is.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Julia C++ FFI interface
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Julia C++ FFI interface
messages.body_plain:
Clearly this is of great interest to Julia's Stan.jl package (and I'm following it quite closely). It is closer to Rcpp.

Last week a new (v0.0.2) version of Stan.jl was tagged and pushed to METADATA, tested and available on Julia's 0.3_RC1 on OSX.

Version 0.0.2 version returns the sampling, diagnose and optimize results as an array of dictionaries (one dictionary for each chain), similar to a companion package Jags.jl (not yet published but available at https://github.com/goedman/Jags.jl.git ).

All 0.0.x releases do break compatibility as the Julia interface takes shape. Only after the 0.1.0 release I plan to start using the deprecate.jl abilities to alleviate the pain.

Version 0.0.3, in about 10 days, will generate input data from a dictionary and, if necessary, regenerate and compile model files based on a Stan model defined as a Julia string. Similar code is working in Jags.jl.

Version 0.0.4 will focus on plotting of the results, similar to Julia's (unpublished yet) Mamba.jl package using Gadfly.jl and Winston.jl.

It is the intention that some of FFI stuff will be part of the first 0.1.0 release later this year.

I also expect to take a closer look at Tim Holy's (and others) HDF5.jl package (more so if Stan would go there).

A final consideration is if 'bottling' CmdStan is a viable option (and/or a Homebrew formula?). Time frame tbd.

For both 'bottling' and FFI I want to make sure it is robust and kind of hidden from end-users.

Regards,
Rob J. Goedman
goe...@icloud.com

On Jul 30, 2014, at 1:15 PM, andre.p...@googlemail.com wrote:

>
>  for (n in 1:N)
>     increment_log_prob(normal_log(y[n]*w[n], (x[n] * beta) * w[n], mean(w[n]*sigma));
>

I don't understand the term mean(w[n] * sigma) because the argument is
just a scalar.

If you work through what that does (dropping the mean), then you get

   -log(w[n] * sigma) - ((w[n] * y[n] - w[n] * x[n] * beta) / w[n] * 2 * sigma)^2

=  -log(w[n]) - log(sigma) - w[n]^2 * ((y[n] - x[n] * beta) / 2 * sigma)^2

which isn't quite the same as multiplying the original log prob by w[n].

If you just want to weight the instances so that they count as w[n]
instances, then you do just want to multiply the original log prob.

If that's not what's going on (and I didn't understand the Wikipedia article),
then you have to figure out the posterior log probability you want and
code that up.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: goodness of fit for mixed model
messages.body_plain:
I'm not sure what you mean with "random effects for diameter and length". Previously, you had fixed effects for diameter and length. Did you change your model? Just in case: in your posterior predictive checks, you shouldn't resample the coefficients for diameter and length. If you do (and also resample the sigma's), you step into the arena of prior predictive checks (which I've never used before, but there's plenty of literature on it if you want to find out what it's for).

What do you mean by decent in "SSQ of Pearson residuals or just SSQ for new batches don't provide decent  p-value (not equal 0 or 1)"? You want your p-value to be far away from 0 and 1, right? I.e. you don't want large differences between the observed and replicated data, relative to the fitted model.

Regarding checking for overdispersion, the first thing would be to use common sense: check the scale of the overdispersion parameter. Is it close to zero? Next, you could use an information criterion to compare models with and without the overdispersion parameter (the WAIC has been suggested before elsewhere on this list). You might even be able to do some sort posterior predictive check with a clever discrepancy test to see whether the overdispersion makes sense (although I would have to think longer about that, have to run now).

Luc

Most of the optional parameters are exactly the same as for BFGS, in fact they're all detailed together in the manual.  The only one that's special for L-BFGS is the history_size parameter which specifies how many update vectors to keep around.  The default value of 5 is usually sensible but if you're seeing slow progress (lots of steps with alpha < 1) then you could try increasing this.

Marcus

Sorry---I hadn't installed RStan 2.4 yet.

One of "Newton", "BFGS", and "LBFGS" indicating which optimization algorithm is used. The default is BFGS.

and here are the parameters:

Other optional parameters.

	• iter (integer), the maximum number of iterations

	• save_iterations (logical), whether to save the iterations

	• refresh (integer)

	• init_alpha (double, default to 0.001), for BFGS and LBFGS, see manual of Stan

	• tol_obj (double, default to 1e-12), for BFGS and LBFGS, see the manual of Stan

	• tol_grad (double, default to 1e-8), for BFGS and LBFGS, see the manual of Stan

	• tol_param (double, default to 1e-8), for BFGS and LBFGS, see the manual of Stan

	• tol_rel_obj (double, default to 1e4), for BFGS and LBFGS, see the manual of Stan

	• tol_rel_grad (double, default to 1e7), for BFGS and LBFGS, see the manual of Stan

	• history_size (integer, default to 5), for LBFGS, see the manual of Stan

The manual reference should be to Stan, but we don't have that info in
the Stan manual yet --- it moved with other command doc to CmdStan, and we
need to pull it back out into the main manual for the next release.  The link
to the CmdStan manual is:

http://mc-stan.org/cmdstan.html

The tolerances are absolute or relative for the objective function (log prob),
parameter distance, and gradient vector length.  (Though it looks like

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for being persistent.  I just went and looked at the code:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/blob/develop/src/models/ARM/Ch.17/17.6_multilevel_ordered_categorical.stan

It looks like a literal translation of the BUGS code in Andrew
and Jennifer's book, and is not at all how you'd want to implement
this model in Stan.

Here are things wrong with that model at a glance:

1.  Stan has a built-in ordered logit distribution and you really want
to be using that.

2.  If you have a variable with constrained support, as in T[1,100] in
this model, then the parameters need to be declared to have matching
support, or you'll have a hard time with inits and/or sampling.

3.  If you have truncations and have the support defined properly, then
you never need to have a T[...] truncation with just constants.

4.  Rather than doing transpose(row(P,i)), which involves lots of extra
copying, it's better to set up the data structure for P so that it is
an array of vectors.  See the manual chapter (near the beginning) on
arrays vs. vectors.

Mitzi's taking a pass through the ARM models, and will probably get
around to fixing this one.  Peter might have time to fix it before then.

In the interim, I'd suggest looking at section 5.6 of the Stan 2.4
manual, which has a simple example of how to do ordered logit in
Stan.

- Bob

messages.subject: Rhat for lp__
messages.subject_clean: Rhat for lp__
messages.body_plain:
Forgive me if this is a dumb question (and if it is, please let me know why so I can correct my confusion).

For a model I’m running, the parameters I’m interested in are all showing good convergence (high n_eff, Rhat near 1, traceplots look well-mixed), but Rhat for lp__ is 1.60. Does that indicate that I should let the model run longer, or is it not crucial that lp__ converge as long as everything else converges?

Thanks.

Josh

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Rhat for lp__
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Rhat for lp__
messages.body_plain:
I don't think it's a dumb question.  It's something we should
answer in our doc, because I think it's a common occurrence.

I too wonder why we always see Rhat so high for lp__ and if it
should be a concern.  It's definitely a concern if you want to
estimate lp__ accurate.   So the real question is whether we can
trust parameter estimates with high Rhat values for lp__.

I'll write the answer into the manual.

lp__ the log posterior up to a constant.  Because it's
a highly non-linear combination of the parameters, there's
no reason to expect it to have the same convergence properties.

Another case to think about is X^2.  That's what you need to
converge to get a good estimate of the posterior variance of X.
And it will often converge more slowly than X does (I don't know
if the reverse will ever be true).

- Bob
